`vendor/rea-docs/docs/agent-environments.md`:

```md
# Agent environments from recorded captures

Use `rea environment-serve` to serve an environment manifest as an agent
environment: an MCP server whose tools answer from the records of one retained
web network capture, plus the environment card the agentenv framework reads to
discover it. Nothing is fetched from the recorded application; every answer is
retained Evidence. `rea environment-export` writes the same pair as a bundle
folder `agent-env run` builds and runs; see [Export a bundle](#export-a-bundle).

```sh
rea inspect-web-network-capture /absolute/session.har har --format json > capture.json
rea inspect-analysis-view view.json --format json > manifest.json
rea environment-serve manifest.json --evidence capture.json --port 8765
```

The first command inspects the capture; the second projects the
[environment manifest](web-network-captures.md#environment-manifest) view from
it, where `view.json` wraps the capture Evidence as the inline source:

```json
{
  "source": { "kind": "inline", "evidence": { "evidence_id": "ev_…" } },
  "view": {
    "kind": "environment-manifest",
    "template_rules": ["after-uid-literal", "opaque-token", "sibling-variance"]
  }
}
```

The third command serves that manifest. Both served files are complete REA
Evidence JSON as the commands write it with `--format json`; the `evidence`
member of `view.json` is the whole of `capture.json`.

## From a browser scenario

The capture can also come from REA itself: a
[browser scenario](browser-scenario-contract.md) records a scripted session
in a browser REA launches, and its Evidence is a manifest parent like a HAR
inspection. Select the `network` event family and response bodies. A replayed
reply carries up to 256 KiB of a recorded body, but the scenario keeps at most
`max_network_body_bytes` of each body (64 KiB by default), and only within its
allocation budgets: base64 is charged about 11 bytes per body byte, and
redaction more the shorter a declared secret is (about 35 bytes per body byte
for a 12-character `admin_password`). A body over
`max_network_body_allocation_bytes` (1 MiB by default) is kept as `unavailable`
with that reason; one over `max_event_allocation_bytes` (4 MiB) or
`max_total_event_allocation_bytes` (16 MiB) loses its whole content event,
headers included, which the capture lists among its omissions. Either way its
tool replays no body. The example raises all four so that 256 KiB bodies are
kept when the declared secret has at least 12 characters:

```json
{
  "browser": { "mode": "launch", "executable_path": "/usr/bin/chromium" },
  "start_url": { "url": "http://127.0.0.1:5230/auth", "query": [] },
  "secrets": [
    { "secret_id": "admin_password", "environment_variable": "APP_PASSWORD" }
  ],
  "actions": [
    {
      "step_id": "user",
      "action": "fill",
      "locator": { "kind": "css", "selector": "input[name=username]" },
      "value": { "source": "literal", "value": "admin" }
    },
    {
      "step_id": "password",
      "action": "fill",
      "locator": { "kind": "css", "selector": "input[type=password]" },
      "value": { "source": "secret", "secret_id": "admin_password" }
    },
    {
      "step_id": "sign-in",
      "action": "press",
      "locator": { "kind": "css", "selector": "input[type=password]" },
      "key": "Enter"
    },
    {
      "step_id": "first-memo",
      "action": "goto",
      "destination": { "url": "http://127.0.0.1:5230/m/1", "query": [] },
      "wait_until": "load"
    }
  ],
  "capture": {
    "events": ["network"],
    "network": {
      "request_body": true,
      "response_body": true,
      "header_values": false
    },
    "limits": {
      "max_network_body_bytes": 262144,
      "max_network_body_allocation_bytes": 12582912,
      "max_event_allocation_bytes": 12582912,
      "max_total_event_allocation_bytes": 67108864
    }
  }
}
```

```sh
APP_PASSWORD=… rea capture-browser-scenario scenario.json --format json > capture.json
rea inspect-analysis-view view.json --format json > manifest.json   # view.json wraps capture.json as before
rea environment-serve manifest.json --evidence capture.json --port 8765
```

Each network transaction becomes one record, in request order, and the
record's ordinal is its zero-based position; a transaction whose URL carried a
redacted secret is left unrepresented rather than templated, and one the
capture cannot attribute to a single request and response is left
unrepresented too. Tools are chosen by response media type, so a scenario that
selected neither response bodies nor header values is refused. The browser
scenario redacts credential headers and the secrets it declares; values the
application returns in response bodies, such as session tokens, are kept, and
the replayed body is the bytes the browser exposes for each response, with any
declared secret replaced by its redaction marker (a body that redaction had to
empty replays no body).

## What a manifest is

An environment manifest is a projection of one application's recorded request
lines into a tool surface: one tool per method and path template on the
primary origin, with inferred path parameters, observed query parameter
names, value-free body shapes and pointers to the parent records each tool
cites. It carries no bodies and no headers. The manifest's
`parent_evidence_id` names the capture Evidence it was projected from; the
serve command refuses a manifest whose parent is not the supplied `--evidence`
file with an `invalid_request` error naming both identifiers, so a manifest can
never be served from records it did not cite.

The MCP catalog and environment card use a 1 KiB UTF-8 budget for each
captured display sample. Observation, body-key and cited-record lists show
whole values with omission counts; long method, path and query-name displays
show a marked prefix. Complete values remain in manifest Evidence. Argument
names longer than 64 characters use collision-safe `path_<n>` or `query_<n>` aliases; replay maps
those aliases to the complete captured names.

Discovery is admitted as a complete catalog under a 1 MiB serialization
reservation before the listener binds. Reservation charges up to six bytes per
UTF-16 code unit for JSON escaping/UTF-8 expansion, plus schema overhead;
a catalog may therefore be refused even when its compact JSON is smaller.
This was calibrated with 1500 query fields and eight concurrent SDK discovery
requests (183,798-byte card, 507.27 MiB sampled process-family RSS). Over-capacity
catalogs return `resource_constraint`, retain complete input Evidence, and require
a smaller capture or manifest. Fields and tools are never silently omitted.

## What replay means and does not mean

Each MCP tool call selects one of the records its manifest tool cites and
returns that record's recorded response. Selection compares the supplied path
parameters against the record's path segments at the parameter indexes, then
the supplied query values against the record's query string, and keeps the
record with the most matches; ties keep manifest order. The result reports
where the answer came from:

```json
{
  "status": 200,
  "content_type": "application/json",
  "body": { "id": 2, "login": "probe" },
  "replay": {
    "record_ordinal": 5,
    "evidence_id": "ev_…",
    "exact_match": true,
    "recorded_path": "/api/users/2",
    "recorded_query": null,
    "recorded_line_truncated": false,
    "body_recorded": true,
    "body_encoding": "utf-8",
    "truncated": false
  }
}
```

`exact_match` is true when every supplied path parameter and query value
equals the recorded one; it says nothing about parameters the caller omitted.
Recorded query parsing runs only when supplied query arguments affect selection.
A path value matches a recorded segment as written or after percent-decoding;
when both kinds of match are available, the record whose segment equals the
value as written is chosen. `recorded_query` keeps the `?` of an explicit empty
query, and a recorded path or query longer than 1 KiB is cut in the reply with
`recorded_line_truncated: true`; selection always uses the full recorded line.
`content_type` also has a 1 KiB display bound with `content_type_truncated`; body
interpretation uses the full recorded media type.
When no record matches, the tool still answers from the tool's first cited
record and reports `exact_match: false`. `body` is parsed JSON when the
recorded content type is JSON-like (`application/json`, `application/*+json`,
`text/plain`, `text/markdown`) and the text parses with safe numeric conversion; otherwise
it is the recorded text. Large integer IDs and other numbers that would lose
information stay in the original JSON text. Bodies over 256 KiB are cut at a UTF-8 boundary and returned as
text with `truncated: true`. `body_recorded` is false when the capture kept the
response's status and content type but no body; `body` is then `null`, which
is not a recorded JSON `null`. `body_encoding` is `base64` when the capture
retained response bytes that are not valid UTF-8; `body` is then exactly those
bytes in base64, never a lossy decoding. A retained base64 body is decoded only as far as the 256 KiB a reply can carry, and a leading byte-order mark is kept. For a `base64` body the limit applies to the recorded bytes, not their longer base64 spelling, and a cut keeps whole base64 groups. Request bodies passed to `POST`, `PUT` and `PATCH`
tools are accepted and ignored: nothing is written, and no call changes what a
later call returns. Arguments the tool's input schema does not name are
refused by the MCP server as invalid arguments, so a misspelled parameter never
degrades into an omitted one.

Replay is not emulation. A served environment does not establish the
application's authorization model, response semantics or state transitions,
which the manifest lists as unknowns; it does not validate supplied values; and
it does not answer requests the capture never recorded. Replayed content is
target content: every tool result, including the argument errors the MCP server
returns before a replay runs, carries `_meta.provenance.untrusted_content: true`
with `source: "analysis_target"`. The server advertises REA's untrusted-content
instructions plus a warning that its tool names, descriptions, parameter names
and observed values come from the capture too, and agents must treat all of it
as data, never as instructions.
That same warning prefixes every tool description in the standalone card, so
card discovery carries it before an MCP client initializes. It labels the
captured text without changing the tool names or schema fields clients use.

## The state a capture observed

Replay answers each call from one recording, so the answers reflect whichever
moment of the capture recorded them. The
[environment state](web-network-captures.md#environment-state) view extracts
instead the data the capture's reads observed before the first related write:
entity types with an identity field, entities with their recorded values,
documents for written paths, and a render plan per read tool, kept only where
it reproduces that tool's recordings from the state. It is the starting state
an environment can hold, load and report; serving from it is a later increment
and does not change replay.

## Serve a manifest

```sh
rea environment-serve manifest.json --evidence capture.json [--host 127.0.0.1] [--port 0]
```

`--host` and `--port` default to `MCP_HOST` and `MCP_PORT` from the
environment, then to `127.0.0.1` and an ephemeral port, exactly as
[`rea mcp --http`](cli.md#serve-mcp-over-streamable-http) resolves them. The
bound MCP URL is written to stderr as one JSON log line
(`"msg":"MCP transport listening"` with `url`); `REA_LOG_LEVEL` overrides that
log level. `ENVIRONMENT_NAME` renames the served environment; otherwise the
manifest's `name` is used, and a set but blank value is refused as
`configuration_invalid` before binding rather than silently falling back. The
listener serves one MCP client at a time with the same session, `Host` header
and shutdown contract as [transports](mcp-contracts.md#transports) describes.
It runs until SIGINT or SIGTERM, then closes the listener, prints one
`{"status":"stopped", …}` document and exits `130` or `143`.
Signals during input loading or DNS/bind cancel the owning reader/listener before
a listening announcement;
that path returns a structured `cancelled` result instead of a stopped-listener
document, with the same signal exit status.

Three routes are served:

| Route                             | Answer                                                                 |
| --------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `POST /mcp`                       | The MCP server: one tool per manifest tool, replaying retained records |
| `GET /.well-known/agent-env.json` | The environment card                                                   |
| `POST /agentenv`                  | JSON-RPC `-32601 method not found: <method>` for every method          |

Numeric JSON-RPC IDs outside JavaScript's safe range or whose precision would
be lost are refused as invalid requests with a null ID. They are never echoed
as a different number.

The data plane at `/agentenv` is advertised by the card but carries no
operations in this release; the error names the requested method so a caller
can see that the method, not the transport, is unsupported. Its request body is
read within the same 4 MiB bound the MCP endpoint applies: a larger body is
answered `413` with a JSON-RPC `-32000` error before any of it is parsed, and a
body that is not JSON is answered `400` with `-32700`. A notification (no `id`)
gets `202` and no body, a batch gets one reply per request in it, and an empty
batch, a batch of more than 100 messages, or a message that is not a JSON-RPC
request (including an `id` that is not a string, number or null, or `params`
that are not an object or array) gets `-32600 invalid request`.

## The environment card

The card is the discovery document the agentenv framework reads before
connecting to `/mcp`:

```json
{
  "name": "grafana-example",
  "protocolVersion": "1.0",
  "url": "/agentenv",
  "preferredTransport": "JSONRPC",
  "additionalInterfaces": [{ "url": "/mcp", "transport": "mcp" }],
  "capabilities": {
    "extensions": null,
    "tools": [
      {
        "name": "get_users_by_id",
        "description": "GET /api/users/{numeric}; replays retained records [5, 6]; evidence ev_…",
        "inputSchema": {
          "type": "object",
          "properties": {
            "id": {
              "type": "string",
              "description": "Path segment 2 (numeric); observed: 2, 3"
            }
          },
          "required": ["id"],
          "additionalProperties": false
        }
      }
    ],
    "operations": []
  },
  "children_environments": null
}
```

`capabilities.tools` lists the same names, descriptions and input schemas that
`tools/list` advertises over MCP. Path parameters are required strings whose
description names the segment index, the templating rule and the observed
values (sampled within the list budget above; the manifest keeps them all);
query parameter names are optional strings; write methods accept an
optional `body` object described by the recorded top-level key types. Each
input keeps its own argument: a query name equal to a path parameter's name is
advertised as `query_<name>`, a query name longer than 64 characters as
`query_<n>` (its position) with the captured name sampled in its description,
and the write body as `request_body` when a query parameter is named `body`. Every
schema closes with `additionalProperties: false`, a key the echo example's
schema does not carry.
`extensions`, `operations` and `children_environments` are fixed to `null`,
`[]` and `null`: a replay environment declares no extensions, no data-plane
operations and no children.

## Export a bundle

`rea environment-export` writes the same pair as a bundle folder the agentenv
framework runs directly, shaped like its own echo example:

```sh
rea environment-export manifest.json --evidence capture.json ./grafana-example --json
agent-env run ./grafana-example
```

```text
grafana-example/
  README.md                                 provenance, replay limits, run command, rights note
  envs/grafana-example/Dockerfile           pinned image: node:24.18.0-bookworm-slim + rea-agents@<this version>
  envs/grafana-example/env.toml             environment_name = "grafana-example"
  envs/grafana-example/manifest.json        byte-exact copy of manifest.json
  envs/grafana-example/evidence.json        byte-exact copy of capture.json
  artifacts/check_grafana-example/verify.py the replay verifier
  tasks/smoke.json                          deploy_env (local sandbox), then env_outcome_verifier
```

The command reads each file once, after checking that reading and parsing the
whole file, including sealing traversal, fits the process's live heap headroom (a file that does not is
refused as a `resource_constraint` before it is read), then authenticates and cross-checks the
pair as `environment-serve` does, so a manifest projected from another capture
is refused with the same `invalid_request` before anything is written, and the
bytes it copies are the bytes it authenticated. The bundle directory must be
absent or empty; an occupied directory is refused and nothing in it changes.
The complete tool catalog must also fit the server's advertised catalog budget
before any files are written. Privately parsed JSON is sealed once so authentication
and replay share immutable response trees rather than copying the capture repeatedly.
`--name` replaces the manifest's portable kebab-case name as the env folder and env id
(Windows device names such as `con` and `lpt1` are refused);
`--package-tarball <path>` copies a packed `rea-agents` tarball into the env
folder and makes the Dockerfile install it instead of the registry package and
remove it in the same layer, which is how a checkout rather than a release is
run. The command prints the
written files with their sizes and the pinned package source.

Export uses the shared output-tree owner to check directory identities around
exclusive creates, verify written bytes, and reject unowned entries before
reporting success. It does not delete an inspectable partial folder on failure.
Node's portable pathname APIs leave a syscall-boundary race, so the output's
parent directories must be trusted. On POSIX output files use mode `0600`;
Windows inherits ACLs and REA does not establish owner-only access there. Choose
an already private Windows destination when captured content needs it.

The Dockerfile sets `MCP_HOST=0.0.0.0` and `MCP_PORT=18765`, the port the
framework maps for an MCP server env; the framework's own deploy supplies
`MCP_HOST`, `MCP_PORT` and `ENVIRONMENT_NAME`, so the served card carries the
env's name. It installs Debian's `python3` because the framework's local
sandbox probes a container's readiness with `python3` inside it, which the slim
Node image lacks. It copies the two inputs owned by the image's non-root `node`
user, so a private host umask cannot leave them unreadable, runs as that user and starts
`rea environment-serve /env/manifest.json --evidence /env/evidence.json`. The
`env.toml` names the environment because the framework otherwise reads the
name from Python sources the image does not have.

`verify.py` is the framework's `async def verify(mcp_url)` shape over its
Python MCP client: it lists the tools and checks the count equals the
manifest's, calls the first `GET` tool without path parameters with no
arguments and checks the call did not fail and its replayed `status` equals the
recorded status of that tool's first cited record (an unknown recorded status
stays unknown; it is not borrowed from another record), and returns one
`replay` result whose description
reports both checks. A manifest with no such tool yields a verifier that checks
the count only and says so. `tasks/smoke.json` deploys the env on the local
sandbox and runs that verifier against the env's MCP endpoint; the first run
also builds the framework's own infrastructure, and the run tears everything
down when it ends.

The README written into the bundle records the capture artifact's SHA-256, the
capture and manifest Evidence ids, the manifest view digest, the tool count and
the package source, and states that the recorded content belongs to the
captured application and must not be published without the rights to it.

## Compatibility verification

`npm run verify:agentenv:environment` is the hosted `real-agentenv` lane
described in [testing](testing.md#exported-environment-bundles). It projects
the Grafana-shaped source-owned capture through the built CLI, packs the
checkout, exports a bundle with `--package-tarball`, runs it with the pinned
`agentenv-framework` release on the runner's Docker and requires the smoke task
to pass with no container left behind other than the framework's own
image-registry helper, which the receipt reports. It proves that one exported bundle runs
on one framework release; it does not claim any hosted platform or other
framework versions.

## Resource and lifecycle boundaries

Both Evidence files are read once at startup through the bounded JSON input
reader and authenticated as Evidence before the listener binds; a file that is
not Evidence, a manifest of another view kind, a capture of another format, or
a manifest projected from a different capture is refused before any port is
opened. Because authentication covers the capture's records, a manifest whose
parent check passes cites only records the capture retains. The server keeps
only the cited records' request lines and response text in memory. No outbound
network request is made, no process is launched and nothing is written to
disk. A listener that fails after binding is logged and ends the command with
a `resource_constraint` error and exit `1` instead of serving nothing.

```

`vendor/rea-docs/docs/android-analysis.md`:

```md
# Static Android APK analysis

REA wraps an existing headless JADX engine through `src/android/`. Its source is
kept as an unmodified, commit-pinned Git submodule; see
[upstream provenance](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/third_party/README.md). CLI and MCP use the same
application workflow and return artifact-bound Evidence inline.

This family is present on repository main and in npm 4.1.0. Check the
[released package boundary](installation.md#released-package-and-main) and the
connected server's tool list before selecting it.

On Linux, JADX launches an REA-owned process and requires a procps-compatible
`ps` on REA's `PATH`; see the shared
[Linux process prerequisite](installation.md#linux-owned-process-prerequisite).

## Optional package delivery

The MCP `inspect_android_package` request keeps complete output when `detail` is
omitted or `"complete"`. Select `detail: "summary"` explicitly to receive all
package, SDK and permission declarations, engine identity and class/resource
counts without decoded manifest text or duplicate raw provider replies. A
retaining session keeps the complete original Evidence and returns a distinct
linked `inspect_analysis_view` summary. This changes delivery, not JADX analysis.

Use the returned `normalized_result.parent_evidence_id` with
`inspect_analysis_view`, source kind `retained-evidence`, and
`view: {kind: "android", facet: "manifest", offset: 0, limit: 4096}` to read the
exact decoded manifest without reopening the APK. Offsets and limits count UTF-16
code units; follow `coverage.next_offset`. The page preserves `source_status` and
`reported_total_bytes`: exhausting retained text does not make a partial decoded
manifest complete. Complete source Evidence remains exportable under the existing
session lifetime. Servers without retention reject summary before starting JADX.
One-shot CLI output remains complete. Older servers require the existing complete
request after schema discovery. APK authenticity and runtime behavior remain
unverified.

## Supply tools

Use a **full JDK 17 or newer** (including its compiler module) and
[**jadx-headless-mcp 0.7.1**](https://github.com/1013503897/jadx-headless-mcp/releases/download/v0.7.1/jadx-headless-mcp-0.7.1-all.jar).
Verify the downloaded JAR's SHA-256 against
[REA's pinned release metadata](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/src/android/JadxRelease.ts)
before using it. The following download and verification commands work for npm
package consumers as well as repository checkouts; the repository-only
`npm run fixtures:android` helper is not included in the npm package.

On macOS or Linux, choose a destination and verify the pinned digest:

```sh
mkdir -p "$HOME/.local/share/rea/android" &&
cd "$HOME/.local/share/rea/android" &&
curl -fL -o jadx-headless-mcp-0.7.1-all.jar https://github.com/1013503897/jadx-headless-mcp/releases/download/v0.7.1/jadx-headless-mcp-0.7.1-all.jar &&
if command -v sha256sum >/dev/null; then
  echo '6e5eacf500b64292bfb73c49797c1958f6ee44646e43e868039ae7feb573ff75  jadx-headless-mcp-0.7.1-all.jar' | sha256sum -c -
else
  echo '6e5eacf500b64292bfb73c49797c1958f6ee44646e43e868039ae7feb573ff75  jadx-headless-mcp-0.7.1-all.jar' | shasum -a 256 -c -
fi &&
export REA_JADX_MCP_JAR="$PWD/jadx-headless-mcp-0.7.1-all.jar"
```

On Windows, run the equivalent in PowerShell:

```powershell
$jar = Join-Path $HOME '.local\share\rea\android\jadx-headless-mcp-0.7.1-all.jar'
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force (Split-Path $jar) | Out-Null
Invoke-WebRequest -Uri 'https://github.com/1013503897/jadx-headless-mcp/releases/download/v0.7.1/jadx-headless-mcp-0.7.1-all.jar' -OutFile $jar
if ((Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 $jar).Hash.ToLowerInvariant() -ne '6e5eacf500b64292bfb73c49797c1958f6ee44646e43e868039ae7feb573ff75') { throw 'JADX JAR SHA-256 does not match REA pinned metadata' }
$env:REA_JADX_MCP_JAR = $jar
```

REA runs its packaged Java metadata bridge in source-file mode against the
unmodified engine JAR. REA does not install Java, an Android SDK, JADX, a device
service or an emulator. Set the path in the shell or MCP server environment:

```sh
export REA_JADX_MCP_JAR=/absolute/path/jadx-headless-mcp-0.7.1-all.jar
# Optional: select an existing JDK rather than java on PATH.
export JAVA_HOME=/absolute/path/existing-jdk
```

On Windows x64, use a REA package with its matching bundled Windows native
controls **including owned protocol stdin support**. This Windows boundary is
new on repository main; an older released package can still reject this host.
PowerShell accepts paths containing spaces without additional escaping
inside these environment values:

```powershell
$env:REA_JADX_MCP_JAR = 'D:\tools\jadx-headless-mcp-0.7.1-all.jar'
$env:JAVA_HOME = 'D:\tools\jdk-21'
rea inspect-android-package 'D:\targets\Example.apk'
```

REA selects `JAVA_HOME\bin\java.exe`, or resolves `java.exe` on the selected
Windows `PATH`. A missing or mismatched native artifact reports the package
prerequisite rather than attempting an unowned Java launch. Windows arm64 is
outside this provider's current native boundary.

Readiness checks the selected JAR's ZIP directory for the classes consumed by
REA's metadata bridge, as well as Java's compiler and version modules. It does
not load an APK or execute engine code. Invalid archives and missing bridge
classes report JAR-specific recovery; classpath inventory alone does not prove
that every class or engine operation will load successfully. Discovery limits
each ZIP metadata read to 8 MiB before allocation; a larger directory reports
the exhausted read budget and the selected JAR path.

The filtered class-page bridge (protocol 2) is verified on Linux x86-64 with
Temurin 21, public Appium ApiDemos 6.0.18 and NewPipe 0.29.1 APKs. Earlier
metadata-bridge records covered macOS arm64/OpenJDK 21 and Windows x64/JDK 21;
this protocol revision has not been rerun on those hosts or Linux/JDK 25.
Windows x64 uses an owned Job Object with bidirectional stdio, atomic job
assignment and kill-on-owner-close. Real Windows verification uses JDK 21 and
the pinned JADX 0.7.1 JAR; see the real verification lane below.

## Answer an analyst question

```sh
rea inspect-android-package /path/Example.apk
rea search-android-classes /path/Example.apk MainActivity
rea inspect-android-class /path/Example.apk example.MainActivity
rea inspect-android-method /path/Example.apk example.MainActivity onCreate
rea inspect-android-method /path/Example.apk example.MainActivity select --overload-index 1
rea trace-android-references /path/Example.apk example.MainActivity
rea trace-android-references /path/Example.apk example.MainActivity --method-name onCreate
rea trace-android-references /path/Example.apk example.MainActivity --method-name select --overload-index 1
```

Equivalent MCP methods are `inspect_android_package`, `search_android_classes`,
`inspect_android_class`, `inspect_android_method` and `trace_android_references`.
Every request includes `path`. Class/method operations use `class_name`,
`method_name` and optional `overload_index` as applicable. For example:

```json
{
  "name": "inspect_android_method",
  "arguments": {
    "path": "/path/Example.apk",
    "class_name": "example.MainActivity",
    "method_name": "select",
    "overload_index": 1
  }
}
```

Use `inspect_android_class` to choose an overload. REA rejects an ambiguous
method request rather than silently selecting the first match. Method reference
queries accept the same `overload_index`; the bridge resolves the selected
method node and the result reports its index and displayed signature. These
indices are tied to the current artifact and engine, not stable across builds.

Smali fallbacks select one complete block using the original method name and DEX
descriptor, before applying the source byte limit. This preserves the selected
overload even when Java code generation renames a method. If the selected Java
body was omitted, including a method merged into a synthetic bridge, REA returns
its original smali with the `java_body_unavailable` marker. The marker describes
missing Java; it does not infer why the method was omitted or name a replacement.
Unresolved or duplicate disassembly identities fail instead of attributing another
method's instructions to the selection.

Native and abstract methods are identified from access flags
captured before code generation. They report `body_status: "not_available"`, an
empty source, and the `native_method` or `abstract_method` marker; their declarations
are not passed through the engine's source slicer. Other missing decompiled bodies
do not establish either access flag.

Static initializers (`<clinit>`) return smali with the
`static_initializer_disassembly` marker. Java decompilation can move their
instructions into field declarations, leaving an empty or incomplete method
body. The selected method's disassembly preserves those instructions and retains
the same source byte limit and explicit truncation reporting.

## Interpret the result

- Package inspection retains decoded manifest XML, summary declarations,
  permissions and class/resource counts. Summary fields are extracted by the
  upstream engine and should be checked against the retained XML when needed.
  Signature verification is explicitly `not_performed`.
- Class search filters the engine's cached top-level names before transferring
  pages, then follows contiguous inventory positions without rescanning earlier
  rows. It checks selection, scope, examined ranges and counts before reporting
  complete coverage. Complete producer replies stay in Evidence; an empty `query`
  inventories all class-name rows; class names are decompiler representations.
  Repeated names remain repeated in `matches` so the inventory row count and
  producer evidence stay visible. `duplicate_names` identifies matching names
  with multiple rows and their occurrence counts; a name alone does not
  distinguish which provider class node a later lookup selects.
- Class inventories read parsed metadata without generating source and return
  full reported display types, fields and inner class names. Synthetic members
  that code generation hides can appear in the inventory; it stays consistent
  after method decompilation within the retained session.
  Exact DEX prototypes are reported from frozen JADX method metadata as
  `dex_descriptor`, for example `(I)V`. Display names can be JADX aliases;
  the descriptor alone is not a complete raw DEX method ID. Overload indices
  are tied to this artifact and engine, not stable identities across builds.
- Method inspection reports Java or smali, fallback markers and complete/partial
  returned text. Decompiled source is a derived representation. A complete text
  result does not establish complete semantics or a byte-identical reconstruction.
- Reference results are incoming static relationships between provider nodes.
  `reference_unit=using_node` means `total` counts containing JADX nodes, not
  individual invoke instructions; two calls from one method can appear as one
  entry. `coverage=complete` covers this node inventory only. For a method
  reference whose using node has raw code, `direct_invokes` lists matching DEX
  invoke instructions with their DEX entry, raw source method ID, code-unit
  offset, method index and opcode. An empty array means no direct invoke was
  matched in that node; `null` means raw code was unavailable or the using node
  was not a method. This list does not establish complete call-site coverage
  outside JADX's using-node inventory or through reflection and dynamic loading.
  A virtual or interface invoke also does not establish its runtime implementation.
  Source lines and the containing node's own `dex_offset` remain unknown.
  Method-reference results also carry the selected `dex_descriptor`;
  class-reference results report `null`.
  These relationships are not observed runtime calls.
- Original requests, APK SHA-256, actual engine JAR SHA-256 and raw producer
  responses remain in Evidence. Source revision is populated only for bytes
  matching the audited release JAR.

If a later step fails, the error's `details.partial_observation` retains the
selected and resolved APK paths, digest, observed provider identity and versions,
and each upstream request and reply collected before the failure. Failed replies
remain available even when their payload cannot be interpreted. Cancellation
also stops target hashing before provider admission.

These operations do not execute the APK or provide split APK/AAB handling,
signature validation, full resource-table semantics, native-library analysis or
Android runtime capture. An `.aab` suffix is a ZIP archive, not an APK, so
Android tools and the application graph do not treat it as a standalone APK.
Existing artifact inventory/extraction tools can supply archive evidence.
Inventory records an APK root only for ZIP bytes whose name ends in `.apk`.
The projection adds a limitation when no root `AndroidManifest.xml` was
observed, because such a ZIP may not be an APK. Nested members take a ZIP or
ASAR family from their bytes; an unread member keeps an unknown format.
Inventory keeps ZIP names that differ only in case and records that a
case-insensitive destination cannot store both spellings. Extraction fails
only when that destination directory cannot keep both names. Project that
Evidence with the execution-free inventory tool:

```sh
rea project-android-application-graph '{"inventory_evidence":[<inventory_artifact Evidence>]}'
```

```json
{
  "name": "project_android_application_graph",
  "arguments": {
    "inventory_evidence": ["<inventory_artifact Evidence>"]
  }
}
```

The projection reports exact component paths and hashes, runtime-family hints,
and path-based bridge hypotheses. File and slice occurrences supply component
endpoints; directory trees and symlinks retain their identities in the source
inventory without being classified as code files. It does not decode DEX or
claim observed runtime calls. DEX/JVM runtime hints summarize the classified
bytecode component lists. Framework hints match complete native library names,
such as
`libreactnativejni.so`, `libreactnative.so`, `libhermes.so`,
`libhermes_executor.so`, `libflutter.so`, and `libunity.so`; unrelated names
such as `libcommunity.so` and `libreactivity.so` do not identify those families.
The bridge basis is inferred from the native path and repeated for each managed
component, so it does not identify a specific JNI binding. Bridge hypotheses form a DEX/JVM-class by native-library
Cartesian product. The projection computes the product and exact serialized
candidate-array size before creating candidate objects, then retains a
deterministic prefix within a 2 MiB UTF-8 JSON budget. If candidates are omitted,
`bridge_candidate_coverage` reports total, emitted, and omitted counts; overall
coverage is `partial` while component arrays still include every component
from the supplied inventory pages. A path pair does not establish that a
managed declaration names, loads, or calls the native library.

## Resource and lifecycle limits

REA retains one serialized session with private, immutable APK, engine JAR and
metadata-bridge copies. Matching requests reuse the loaded engine. APK/engine
digests and JVM configuration are checked before reuse; changed inputs retire
the previous session. Sessions are cleaned after 60 seconds of inactivity, on
target/configuration changes, failure, timeout, cancellation, MCP disconnect or
server shutdown. One-shot CLI commands always join cleanup before returning.
REA never writes to the original APK or launches target code.

On Windows, stdin writes preserve stream backpressure and run outside the Node
event loop. Cancellation terminates the retained job, including descendants,
before workspace cleanup. On Windows, a detached REA helper owns the private
workspace's native directory handle. An abrupt CLI/server owner termination
closes the Java job and the helper's input pipe; the helper then removes the
workspace by handle. The real Windows lane checks both effects. If the helper
also dies or the host loses power before it finishes, private files can remain.

If Java cannot start the bridge, REA reports the selected executable and retained
startup diagnostics. Select a full JDK through `JAVA_HOME` or `PATH`, and use
`java --list-modules` to confirm `jdk.compiler` is present. A runnable JRE alone
cannot compile the bridge. Missing or ambiguous class and method selections are
input failures; discover names with `search_android_classes` and
`inspect_android_class` before correcting the selected argument.

If process cleanup cannot be confirmed, REA retains the workspace and reports its
location. That provider instance blocks subsequent engine launches until the
caller resolves the reported resources and starts a fresh instance.

The provider uses one JADX analysis worker independently of JVM processor and
garbage-collector settings. REA supplies no default heap or visible-CPU override;
Java uses its normal ergonomics and inherits caller JVM settings. Optional
provider settings add explicit JVM arguments:

```sh
export REA_JADX_HEAP_MIB=8192
# Optional, independent of the single JADX worker:
export REA_JADX_ACTIVE_PROCESSOR_COUNT=4
# Or select settings through Java's standard environment options:
export JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS=-Xmx8g
```

Both REA settings must be positive safe integers; processor counts must also fit
the JVM's signed 32-bit range. REA preserves
`JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS`, `JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS` and `_JAVA_OPTIONS` rather than replacing
them. Java's standard precedence applies: explicit command-line heap settings
override `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS`, while `_JAVA_OPTIONS` can override command-line
settings. Evidence reports the worker's observed `Runtime.maxMemory()` rounded
down to MiB and retains exact bytes, Java version and visible processors in its
raw runtime response. The observed allocatable heap can differ from configured
`-Xmx`, especially with Serial GC. Heap is not a total RSS cap: the JVM also
uses native memory. A typed JVM memory allocation failure during APK loading
reports `resource_constraint` with the observed maximum heap in bytes. Known
heap failures name `REA_JADX_HEAP_MIB` in remediation; other memory regions
remain unknown. A healthy doctor configuration check does not establish that
any particular APK fits. Failures before the bridge can report a typed result
and upstream errors from other operations retain their existing diagnostics;
error text alone does not establish memory exhaustion.

Independent REA instances have independent queues. Whole
operations have a **120-second** execution deadline by default, starting after
they reach the queue's front. For a known slow cold load, such as a large
multidex APK, select another finite deadline:

```sh
export REA_JADX_OPERATION_TIMEOUT_MS=600000
```

The value must be a decimal millisecond count from 1 to 2147483647; anything
else is refused before Java starts. The same deadline bounds each upstream
call, a timeout reports the selected value, and a passing JADX configuration
check in `rea doctor` reports the effective `operation_timeout_ms`. Explicit
cancellation still ends the operation immediately, and partial observations
and owned-process cleanup are unchanged. Raising the deadline does not extend
the bridge's 30-second startup handshake or the upstream **90-second**
decompilation limit. MCP clients enforce their own tool-call timeouts, and
setup's derived [client tool timeout](client-configuration.md) does not include
this setting, so also raise the client timeout when selecting a longer
deadline.

Decoded manifest and method text have a **1 MiB** upstream byte budget and report
truncation. Class-name pages use indexed slices of up to 4,096 names without changing the
complete, case-sensitive search contract. A protocol frame above **8 MiB**, or combined stdout/stderr above
**32 MiB per operation**, fails with a diagnostic instead of returning an incomplete inventory
as complete. These are memory-safety boundaries, not undocumented result caps.

## Real verification

Download the explicit public fixtures once; this installs no tools:

```sh
npm run fixtures:android
export REA_JADX_MCP_JAR="$PWD/_reference/apk-integration/jadx-headless-mcp-0.7.1-all.jar"
export REA_ANDROID_TEST_APK="$PWD/_reference/apk-integration/ApiDemos-debug.apk"
npm run verify:android
```

The main lane and Windows Java-selection checks validate the selected JDK and
engine archive through `validateVerifierJadxConfiguration`. This shared verifier
boundary supplies the production validator's resource owner and waits for
retained cleanup before proceeding. Failed closes retain their exact owners for
retry; prerequisite failures must not be mistaken for completed bridge tests.
Recovery checks match the typed Java or archive failure and its applicable
remediation.

The lane also uses the selected full JDK's `jlink` to create a disposable JRE
without the compiler module. It checks real Java startup failures, missing
selectors, recovery after failures, and CLI cancellation with owned cleanup.
The original APK and host Java configuration remain unchanged.

The same lane runs on Windows x64 with the bundled native controls and a full
JDK. It checks CLI/MCP results, real MCP cancellation and disconnect, and Java
exit and workspace removal after abrupt CLI owner termination. Windows forced
termination is checked separately from the POSIX CLI SIGTERM handler. A
synthetic two-owner test confirms that one owner's exit does not remove the
other owner's workspace. The lane does not claim a structured cancellation
result or power-loss recovery.

The download script verifies fixed SHA-256 values, reuses matching files and
refuses to overwrite a different existing file. APK/JAR files live under ignored
`_reference/` and are excluded from package contents. The lane exercises actual
REA CLI and MCP results with the real engine, separately from synthetic protocol
regressions. It needs no Gradle build, emulator, Android SDK or Ghidra.

Direct invoke sites retain exact DEX code-unit offsets separately from each
containing node's unknown `dex_offset`. `direct_invokes_exhaustive: false`
means instruction rows were bounded by the local bridge frame budget; `null`
means the producer did not establish instruction coverage. Using-node totals
and coverage do not imply complete instruction evidence.

`vendor/rea-docs/docs/apktool-resource-analysis.md`:

```md
# Apktool resource decoding

REA decodes Android resource tables and the binary manifest through the
caller's Apktool launcher. This completes the static triad for Android
targets: Java/Kotlin sources through the JADX family, engine-grade
decompilation through JEB, and resources through this family. REA never
installs Apktool or a Java runtime.

## Supply tools

Use Apktool 2.7.0 or newer (verified with 2.7.0 and 3.0.3 on Linux) and a Java runtime the
launcher can find. Select the launcher through the environment:

```sh
# Optional: absolute path to the apktool launcher (upstream wrapper or a
# java -jar script); without it, apktool resolves from PATH.
export REA_APKTOOL_COMMAND=/absolute/path/apktool
```

Readiness is `rea inspect-apktool-client`: it runs `apktool --version` and
reports the resolved launcher, its selection source, and its version. A
missing launcher reports `capability_unavailable` with the
`REA_APKTOOL_COMMAND` remediation rather than attempting an installation.
`binary_session` uses the same host probe for tool availability; it does not
validate a particular APK or guarantee that the selected input can be decoded.

Client inspection and decode results disclose the following reported-version
advisory windows without refusing otherwise compatible launchers:

| Advisory                                                                                              | Reported version window                          | Host scope |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ | ---------- |
| [CVE-2024-21633](https://github.com/iBotPeaches/Apktool/security/advisories/GHSA-2hqv-2xv4-5h5w)      | Before 2.9.2                                     | All        |
| [GHSA-vgwr-4w3p-xmjv](https://github.com/iBotPeaches/Apktool/security/advisories/GHSA-vgwr-4w3p-xmjv) | Before 2.9.3                                     | Windows    |
| [CVE-2026-39973](https://github.com/iBotPeaches/Apktool/security/advisories/GHSA-m8mh-x359-vm8m)      | 3.0.0 release line through versions before 3.0.2 | All        |

The 2026 advisory names 3.0.1 and its 3.0.2 fix. Inclusion of 3.0.0 is
source-derived: [tagged 3.0.0](https://github.com/iBotPeaches/Apktool/blob/f770b39e425af4fa6ac4ca1e9ea6c4824339c6d3/brut.apktool/apktool-lib/src/main/java/brut/androlib/res/table/ResTypeSpec.java)
passes type names through unchanged; the [3.0.2 patch](https://github.com/iBotPeaches/Apktool/commit/65dd8480dfcb63068562ffaa527f71bb0a9f772c)
validates those names at their owner before they reach the output-path producer.
Prereleases before the fixed release are conservatively disclosed; the exact
`-dirty` downstream marker is compared as a release while preserving its spelling.
This is version guidance, not verification of a particular prerelease or decoder.

A launcher version does not prove the decoder's contents, execution platform,
downstream backports, or overall safety. Windows applicability uses the selected
local host; an opaque wrapper may run another engine. A missing warning means
only that none of these version/host windows matched. Verify the selected
decoder's patches before decoding untrusted APKs; the compatibility floor above
is not a security recommendation. REA does not fetch advisories at runtime.

On Windows, a `.bat` or `.cmd` launcher (such as Chocolatey's `apktool.bat`)
runs through an explicit `cmd.exe /d /s /c` call. That call has no AutoRun,
no delayed expansion, and quotes every argument. A launcher path that
contains `"`, `%`, `^`, `!`, `&`, `|`, `<` or `>` is reported as
`not_configured` instead of being passed to `cmd.exe`. If REA's temporary
decode paths contain those characters, decoding through a batch launcher
reports `capability_unavailable`.

## Answer an analyst question

```sh
rea inspect-apktool-client
rea decode-android-resources /targets/Example.apk
rea decode-android-resources /targets/Example.apk --locale de
rea decode-android-resources /targets/Example.apk --locales de --locales pt-BR
rea decode-android-resources /targets/Example.apk --locales de --locales pt-BR --string-tables-only
rea decode-android-resources /targets/Example.apk --no-strings
```

Equivalent MCP methods are `inspect_apktool_client` and
`decode_android_resources`. The decode request takes `path`, an optional
primary `locale` (project `res/values-<locale>/strings.xml` instead of the default
table), `locales` (repeatable array of additional localized string tables to project
from the same single decode pass), and `include_strings` (default true). Regional locales such as `pt-BR`
select Android's `values-pt-rBR`. A three-digit region such as `es-419`
selects `values-b+es+419`; `es-r419` is rejected because Android's legacy
`-r` form requires a two-letter region. Android qualifiers such as `pt-rBR`
and `b+zh+Hans+CN` may also be supplied directly.

Set `string_tables_only: true` (CLI `--string-tables-only`) to return string
entries only inside `string_tables`, including when selecting a single table.
The top-level `strings` array is then empty by request; it does not establish
that the primary table is empty. Table status, counts and coverage still describe
the examined source. This avoids repeating primary entries in multi-locale
responses and charges the aggregate output budget for one copy per table.
Omitting the option preserves existing responses. `include_strings: false`
still suppresses all string projection, including in this mode.

## Interpret the result

- **An owned APK snapshot is digested and decoded.** `target.sha256` and
  `target.bytes` bind the observation to the exact APK that was decoded.
  The Evidence subject carries the same snapshot digest and caller-selected
  path, including when the original file changes during decoding.
- **Metadata comes from apktool.yml as apktool printed it.** Version codes
  keep their own spelling (`'7'` versus `7`); `package_name` is read from
  the decoded manifest, not inferred.
- **The manifest is the decoded text**, bounded at 512 KiB and reported as
  truncated when larger.
- **Strings are projected verbatim.** Escaped entities stay escaped, and
  entries containing nested markup (`<b>`, `<xliff:g>`) are counted as
  unparsed rather than flattened — the limitation names the examined count.
  Malformed XML and a wrong document root are whole-document projection
  failures: the result is partial, the failure reason is disclosed, and entry
  counts remain unknown. They are not counted as one unsupported string.
  The default table is bounded to 2000 entries with partial coverage when more
  exist. `locales` lists observed regular `strings.xml` tables whose exact
  `values-<locale>` directory is selectable by the request's locale grammar.
  Locale suffixes allow up to 23 ASCII characters, derived from Apktool's
  language, script, region, and variant fields; for example,
  `b+sr+Latn+RS+REVISED` selects that exact table.
  Other table directories, including combined qualifiers such as
  `values-en-rUS-v21` and `values-mcc310-fr`, are named in limitations with
  their source spelling. They are not advertised as selectable locales;
  REA does not infer Android's runtime resource matching. Non-regular
  strings-table paths are disclosed with partial coverage. Discovery uses
  the same bounded traversal as the file count; filesystem failures remain
  failures rather than being interpreted as missing tables.
  When multiple tables are requested with `locales`, `string_tables` records
  each projected table with its locale, status (`present`, `missing`,
  `oversized`, `malformed`, or `skipped`), entry counts, and coverage,
  bounded at an aggregate budget of 10,000 strings and 32 MiB XML. When `locales`
  is omitted and `string_tables_only` is not true, legacy single-table payloads are preserved
  without adding `string_tables`.
- **Smali is skipped by design** (`apktool d --no-src`): Java-source
  recovery belongs to the JADX family. Resource smali edits and rebuild are
  a follow-up lane with mutation authority.
- **Workspaces are owned and short-lived.** Decoding happens in a
  provider-owned temporary directory that is removed before the result is
  returned. The APK snapshot and framework cache both live inside this directory.
  If removal fails, the result names the residual path and the provider retains
  ownership for a cleanup retry on close, including failed decodes.

## Resource and lifecycle limits

- The decode runs with a 600 s deadline and a 4 MiB output capture budget;
  a stopped decode reports `provider_timeout` and exceeded budgets report
  `resource_constraint`.
- Manifest reads are bounded to 512 KiB before decoding UTF-8. Strings XML
  reads are bounded to 8 MiB; larger documents are skipped with partial
  coverage and an explicit limit, rather than reported as missing.
- `decoded_file_count` is capped at 100,000 files; the cap is reported in
  the limitations when hit.
- An ordinary nonzero decode exit surfaces as `unsupported_target` naming
  the caller-selected APK, with Apktool's diagnostic and captured output.
  Launcher startup, ownership preparation, signal termination and incomplete
  output collection remain provider failures; they do not establish that the
  selected APK is unsupported.

## Real verification

`npm run verify:apktool -- --apk PATH` exercises both operations against a
real launcher. Record: apktool 2.7.0-dirty (Debian packaging) on Linux with
OpenJDK 25 against a signed aapt2-built probe APK carrying two resource
locales — launcher version, on-disk digest agreement, apktool.yml metadata
(1.2.3, SDK 24–34), manifest package agreement, default and `de` string
tables projected. Parser goldens in the test suite come from the same
decode. See `docs/testing.md` for the lane summary.

Multi-locale and table-only projection were also verified through real CLI and
stdio MCP workflows on Linux with Apktool 3.0.3/JDK 21 against NewPipe 0.29.1,
ApiDemos 6.0.18 and Appium Settings 8.2.1. Independent XML projection checks,
exact facts/Evidence parity and bounded task costs are recorded in the
[shared-decode and table-only checkpoint](../experiments/analysis-efficiency/apktool-string-tables.md).
This qualifies selected resource facts, not application execution or independent
binary resource-decoder completeness.
