`capture.limits`. Omitted values use the defaults below; every supplied value
must be a positive safe integer, and callers can raise or lower a default.
Byte limits are conservative allocation-cost estimates for retained event
values, including UTF-16 storage and JSON expansion, rather than serialized
bytes or a promise about exact process memory. `events.omissions.by_kind`
reports counts and reasons for omitted event kinds. Its
`network_transactions` rows identify affected transaction IDs and omitted
event kinds; `network_transaction_range` identifies the contiguous IDs beyond
the transaction limit. Omission metadata is bounded by the selected
transaction limit. Other missing sections remain explicit and make the capture
ineligible for equality claims.

The default limits are 10,000 events, 4 MiB estimated allocation for one
event, 16 MiB estimated allocation across retained events, 1,024 network
transactions, 64 KiB of body bytes per transaction phase, 1 MiB estimated
allocation for body redaction/base64, 1 MiB for retained header values, and
1 MiB for network metadata. The same limits are included in the capture
Evidence. Playwright materializes response bodies before REA can inspect their
byte length; `max_network_body_bytes` bounds subsequent retained copies and
does not bound the browser API read itself. A body that exceeds its selected
limit has an explicit `body-size-limit` or `body-allocation-limit` unavailable
state with the observed and allowed values.

Additional implementation bounds are 16 simultaneous network-content reads,
a 5-second deadline for each provider API read, and 2,048 live event-listener
owners. These are not caller-selectable. The concurrency bound queues admitted
content jobs and does not itself omit observations; a provider read timeout
produces a typed unavailable state, while exceeding listener capacity produces
event-kind omission counts. A preflight avoids body redaction and base64 copies
when the currently available event budget already rejects the body.
Concurrent reads may each pass that check before their events are retained;
their retained-copy work is bounded by 16 times the selected per-body
allocation limit. The Playwright response Buffer itself is materialized before
REA can apply that limit. Requested artifacts and retained events are returned
inline within the declared limits.
Attach-mode captures also declare the unavoidable pre-attach event gap.

Selected event families are observed on the root page and discovered descendant
popups, including nested popups. Popup lifecycle records are emitted only when
`popups` is selected. Launch-mode network observation starts at the owned
context before navigation, so popup document requests, redirects, and responses
are included once. Connected contexts can contain unrelated tabs: only network
events with a frame belonging to the root or a discovered popup are retained.
Initial popup requests without a frame cannot be attributed in shared contexts
and are omitted; attach coverage remains incomplete.

Playwright reports new popup Pages after their first navigation has committed.
It buffers early console messages and page errors, but the pinned API cannot
recover every earlier frame, worker, WebSocket, or download event. If one of
those families is selected and a popup is discovered, REA reports the family gap
in `limitations`, marks `events` missing, and disables equality eligibility.
Later events remain available; no initial navigation is synthesized from the
popup's current URL.

Each request names the exact launch executable or loopback CDP endpoint, target,
actions, and capture behavior. Origin filters and environment-variable names
are included when the scenario needs them.
Launch owns a temporary profile; connect mode disconnects from the selected
external browser without closing it. The request itself defines the operation;
there is no additional REA grant step. The browser and host still enforce their
own access and process rules.

## Network evidence

`capture.events: ["network"]` retains request, response, completion, failure,
and unfinished-request metadata. Select content independently:

```json
{
  "browser": {
    "mode": "launch",
    "executable_path": "/absolute/path/to/chromium"
  },
  "start_url": { "url": "http://127.0.0.1:3000" },
  "actions": [
    {
      "step_id": "run",
      "action": "click",
      "locator": { "kind": "css", "selector": "#start" },
      "timeout_ms": 10000
    },
    {
      "step_id": "ready",
      "action": "wait_for",
      "locator": { "kind": "css", "selector": "#done" },
      "state": "visible",
      "timeout_ms": 10000
    }
  ],
  "capture": {
    "network": {
      "request_body": true,
      "response_body": true,
      "header_values": true
    }
  }
}
```

All three options default to `false`. Any selected network content also enables
network metadata observation; listing `network` in `events` is then optional.
Each observed request object receives a capture-scoped `transaction_id`.
Requests sharing a URL remain distinct. Redirects link to the preceding
transaction only when it was observed; a null predecessor does not establish
that no earlier hop existed. Request events require both transaction fields;
an absent ID is malformed capture data. `redirected_from_transaction_state`
records `root` when Playwright observed no predecessor and `unknown` when a
predecessor exists but was outside the capture. A linked predecessor is carried
by `redirected_from_transaction_id` with no state field. Older captures without
the state field retain the conservative meaning that a null predecessor is
unknown.

`scenario.network_content` records the resolved content selection. Comparing
captures with different selections reports network evidence as unknown with a
recovery instruction.
Capturing more data alone does not establish a website change.

`network-content` events reference the exact request or response event through
`source_event_sequence`. They include independently typed headers and body
states. Captured bodies retain base64 bytes, byte count, media type, and SHA-256
of the retained bytes. Request bytes are those exposed by Playwright; a
`not_exposed` request body does not prove absence or complete multipart file
coverage. Response bytes are the result of Playwright's `Response.body()` API.
Playwright may satisfy that API with a credentialed follow-up load of the
request URL when CDP has no response body. Event and transaction references
identify the associated Playwright response object, but do not verify that the
retained bytes came from the original network transaction. Successful selected
response bodies include this limitation in the capture. These bytes are not
the compressed wire representation.
Headers preserve producer order and duplicates. Authorization,
Proxy-Authorization, Cookie, and Set-Cookie values are null with
`redacted: true`; ordinary values remain intact. Declared UTF-8 secret values
and their standard URI/form or JSON-escaped representations are replaced without
decoding unrelated binary bytes. Other encodings are not interpreted. Digests describe the
retained representation after redaction.

Only completed responses are read. At the end of the final step, observation
stops; requests still in flight emit `request-unfinished`, and their observed
responses have explicitly unavailable bodies. Already-admitted content reads
drain before browser cleanup. At most 16 reads run at once; queued work is
bounded by the selected network-transaction limit and by successful admission
of its request or response event. Each provider API read has its own five-second
timeout once it starts, so queue wait adds to total drain and cleanup time; this
is not a five-second total capture cutoff. Cancellation interrupts active reads
and queued jobs produce cancelled states without calling their provider APIs.
This drain does not wait for long-lived unfinished streaming connections and
does not refetch unfinished response bodies. Failed or unexposed reads retain
per-content states and make selected event coverage incomplete. Body events can
arrive during later steps or final drain; event bounds describe receipt during
the step, while the source event reference establishes the transaction phase.
Comparison attributes content, like every other event of its transaction, to
the step that sent the request (the receipt step when that request was not
observed) and excludes the sequence reference from normalization.
Playwright scenario capture does not supply initiator stacks; passive CDP
observation retains its own initiator evidence.

## Scenario comparison

`compare_web_captures` and `compare-web-captures` also accept two complete
browser scenario captures. Steps align only by exact, unique `step_id`.
Duplicate IDs, missing counterparts, changed action kinds, and incompatible
browser/origin capture context are returned as alignment failures. They prevent
an unchanged claim; observed differences may still prove a changed result.

The comparison records its full normalization commitment and SHA-256 digest.
Built-in rules exclude step elapsed time and event sequence/index fields,
compare screenshots by content digest, and compare DOM/accessibility captures
by normalized text. Network events are grouped by transaction without their
capture-local transaction IDs, attributed to the step that sent the request,
and compared as an unordered collection after caller rules apply, because
concurrent responses arrive in any order and can land in a later step; a
redirect retains the complete predecessor ancestry, including each hop's own
request, response outcome, and selected network content. Each transaction's
capture-local IDs, sequence/index fields, and content source-sequence anchor
are removed. Caller rules normalize retained strings before hashing. The
`preserve_redirect_transaction_ancestry` built-in rule fingerprints each hop
as canonical SHA-256 of `{ events, redirected_from }`: `events` is the sorted
list of its normalized event SHA-256 digests, and `redirected_from` is its
predecessor fingerprint or null for a root. Selected transaction fingerprints
are sorted for the step's network comparison. Temporary numeric graph indices
are lookup references only and do not enter the final digest. Missing or cyclic
predecessor evidence yields unknown comparability instead of an unchanged claim.
Other events keep receipt order. Optional caller rules are bounded exact-literal
replacements over named artifact kinds. Rules and artifact-kind lists are
sorted canonically before application, making the same policy reproducible
regardless of input order. Rules operate only on already-redacted durable
capture fields and are preserved in the result.

Each aligned step reports changed, unchanged, or unknown. Changed and unknown
action, screenshot, DOM, accessibility, URL, history, storage, and event
artifacts carry their normalized before/after digests and capture states.
Every changed or unknown artifact record is returned inline for each aligned
step. Missing, truncated, or mismatched capture coverage remains unknown
instead of being treated as equality.

`scenario.event_families` records the sorted, de-duplicated `capture.events`
selection. Captures with different selections report event evidence as unknown
with a recovery instruction, even when no selected family emitted an event.
Captures written before this field existed omit it, so their event evidence is
also unknown.

Network normalization also commits the removal of capture-local transaction IDs,
attribution to the requesting step, and unordered transaction comparison. These
built-in rule identities participate in the normalization digest.

```

`vendor/rea-docs/docs/cli.md`:

```md
# CLI and Evidence

Use the CLI for a direct inspection or a script. It uses the same application
workflows and evidence contracts as REA's MCP server. Each CLI invocation is a
separate process; save results when you want to use them in a later command.

## Run a command

After [installing REA](installation.md), use `rea`. You can also run a command
without a global installation:

```bash
npx -y rea-agents@latest analyze-javascript-application /absolute/path/to/app --json
```

Use an extracted application directory or an ASAR as the target. Static
JavaScript analysis returns the application graph and Evidence directly.
Generic `rea analyze PATH` selects this workflow for directories and `.asar`
files when neither `--provider` nor `--snapshot` is supplied. See
[JavaScript artifact reconstruction](javascript-artifact-reconstruction.md)
for results, integrity checks and coverage.

The complete application Evidence can be hundreds of megabytes for a real
application. When an agent or a person reads the result, save it to a file and
project a summary, a module page or one module from the saved Evidence:

```bash
rea analyze-javascript-application /absolute/path/to/app --json > app-evidence.json
jq -c '{source: {kind: "inline", evidence: .}, view: {kind: "summary"}}' app-evidence.json > app-view.json
rea inspect-analysis-view app-view.json
```

The request can also name the saved file instead of embedding it:
`{"source": {"kind": "evidence-file", "path": "app-evidence.json"}, "view": {"kind": "summary"}}`.
The CLI resolves a relative path against the working directory; MCP clients
pass an absolute path. REA reads and authenticates the file, then projects it
like retained Evidence, so a large file is bounded by the file reader rather
than charged as inline input.

For example, a 334 MB Obsidian application Evidence file yields a summary view
of about 10 KB. Replace the view with
`{"kind": "page", "collection": "modules", "offset": 0, "limit": 32}` for a
module page. See
[JavaScript application workflows](javascript-application-workflows.md) for
views, feature traces and comparisons that take the same saved Evidence.

## Managed assemblies (.NET)

For a .NET PE/CLI assembly, inspect its identity and deployment form before
inspecting members. These commands read metadata and Common Intermediate
Language (CIL) without loading or executing the assembly and require no native
analysis engine:

```bash
rea inspect-managed-artifact /absolute/path/Assembly.dll --json
rea inspect-managed-members /absolute/path/Assembly.dll --json
rea inspect-managed-members /absolute/path/Assembly.dll --type Example.Parser --json
```

Replace `Example.Parser` with an exact `full_name` from the member inspection,
or a declaring type name you already know. Omit `--type` to inspect all members,
or repeat it to select several types.
Selection limits decoding to the selected types; member references remain an
assembly-wide inventory, so the output can still be large.

Choose the workflow from the artifact's contents rather than its `.exe` or
`.dll` extension. The managed parser requires PE/CLI metadata; it does not
unpack .NET single-file hosts or decode IL2CPP. For the image, type and method
names in a Unity `global-metadata.dat`, use
[IL2CPP metadata](il2cpp-metadata.md). NativeAOT method bodies require native
analysis. See the [managed-code guide](managed-code-analysis.md)
for supported deployment forms, selection semantics, and coverage limits.

## SQLite snapshots

For a local database snapshot, use `rea inspect-sqlite-database PATH --json`.
Add `--table NAME --row-limit 20` to read a bounded sample from an ordinary
table. This command does not require a native analysis provider. See
[SQLite database snapshots](sqlite-databases.md) for database/WAL identity,
source-file handling and row-value semantics.

## Native analysis

Inspect embedded Go build metadata without installing Go or configuring a
disassembler:

```bash
rea inspect-go-binary /absolute/path/to/program --json
```

The shared CLI/MCP workflow reports compiler version, modules, replacements,
build settings, original bytes and SHA-256. See [Go binaries](go-binaries.md)
for supported containers and absent or malformed metadata.

Inspect a Godot PCK without running the game:

```sh
rea inspect-artifact game.pck --detail summary --evidence_output evidence.json --json
rea extract-artifact game.pck --json
```

Formats 2, 3 and 4 retain header, directory and integrity facts. Compact delivery
keeps complete Evidence in the requested bundle. See [Godot PCK](godot-pck.md)
for embedded packs, batch queries and unknown encrypted coverage.

Inspect local model declarations without loading weights:

```bash
rea inspect-model-artifact /absolute/path/model.gguf --json
rea inspect-model-artifact /absolute/path/model.safetensors --hash full --json
```

Default hashing reads only headers and leaves full-file identity unknown.
`--hash full` streams the complete file for SHA-256. Both return typed metadata,
original tensor declarations and derived totals. MCP summaries retain complete
Evidence for filtered metadata, tensor and type-total pages; CLI compact delivery
uses `--detail summary --evidence_output FILE`. See [model files](model-artifacts.md).

Inspect Unity IL2CPP metadata names without Unity or a disassembler:

```bash
rea inspect-il2cpp-metadata /absolute/path/global-metadata.dat --json
```

The command decodes a version 24, 27, 29, 31 or 39 `global-metadata.dat` and reports assembly
images, type, method and member names, string literals, index ranges, header
sections and SHA-256. With `--binary PATH` it also reads the matching
`GameAssembly.dylib`, `GameAssembly.dll` or `libil2cpp.so` (never runs it) and
links each method to its code address; `--ghidra-seeds PATH` then writes Ghidra
function seeds. It does not decrypt metadata. MCP defaults to compact counts
with retained Evidence; query indexed rows with filters, batch indices and
selected fields. The CLI defaults to complete Evidence;
`--detail summary --evidence_output FILE` exports the full result to a new file
and returns a compact overview. See [IL2CPP metadata](il2cpp-metadata.md).

Inspect an embedded cargo-auditable Rust dependency list without installing
Rust or configuring a disassembler:

```bash
rea inspect-rust-binary /absolute/path/to/program --json
```

The same workflow reports package names, versions, sources, the root package,
dependency edges, and the section's file range. A missing `.dep-v0` section is
null metadata, not proof that the binary has no dependencies. See
[Rust binaries](rust-binaries.md).

Configure [Hopper or Ghidra](installation.md#hopper), the
[IDA adapter](ida-provider.md), or [Kuna](kuna-provider.md) before analyzing a
native target. Substitute
your target, search text and function name or address in these examples:

```bash
rea analyze /absolute/path/to/program --provider ghidra --json
rea search /absolute/path/to/program "search" --provider ghidra --json
rea function /absolute/path/to/program main --provider ghidra --json
rea decompile /absolute/path/to/program 0x1000 --provider ghidra --json
rea xrefs /absolute/path/to/program 0x1000 --provider ghidra --json
rea trace /absolute/path/to/program "search" --provider ghidra --json
```

`analyze` and `inspect` share the native overview workflow. `function` returns
a function dossier; `decompile` returns pseudocode. For assembly instructions
alone, use `rea instructions`. A macOS `.app` bundle can be supplied directly.

Run `rea --help` or a command's `--help` for arguments and output options.
The [generated catalog](mcp-contracts.md#generated-catalog) lists all CLI commands and MCP
tools. Provider-specific target support is described in the
[native guide](native-investigation.md), [DOS guide](ghidra-dos.md),
[raw binary guide](raw-binary.md), and
[Windows Ghidra guide](windows-ghidra-p0.md).

## Choose a provider

List the available providers and their supported operations:

```bash
rea providers --json
rea capabilities --json
```

These commands describe binary-session providers and auxiliary capabilities.
For the complete MCP surface, use the connected server's tool list and the
session's advertised availability; individual guides describe prerequisites.

With automatic selection, REA uses the single available provider that supports
the target. When several providers support it, select one explicitly:

```bash
rea analyze /absolute/path/to/program --provider hopper
```

Set `REA_ANALYSIS_PROVIDER` for a standing preference. An explicit `--provider`
overrides it. In MCP, pass `provider_id` to `open_binary`:

```json
{
  "path": "/absolute/path/to/program",
  "provider_id": "hopper"
}
```

The selected provider remains bound to the session until an explicit switch
or close. Provider failures are returned with their original reason. For an
`ambiguous` selection error, choose from `details.candidate_ids`; for
`provider_unavailable`, follow `message`, `remediation.action`, and the original
reasons in `details.rejections`. For Hopper, Ghidra, IDA, and JADX, run
`rea doctor --provider ID --json` to diagnose the selected engine. Other adapters,
such as `pwntools-elf`, report their configuration requirements directly and are
not accepted by `doctor --provider`. See
[task readiness](installation.md#check-readiness-for-your-task) and
[provider selection](mcp-contracts.md#identity-and-discovery).

The session reports work still in progress through `analysis_activity`.
A client timeout can end its wait while the provider continues analyzing.
`cleanup_incomplete` identifies resources whose shutdown or removal could not
be verified. See [MCP contracts](mcp-contracts.md) for session lifecycle and
[Ghidra first-query deadlines](mcp-contracts.md#ghidra-first-query-deadlines-and-recovery)
for import, client timeouts and recovery.

If one-shot analysis fails and closing its session also fails, the original
error details remain inline and `details.cleanup_error` describes the later
close failure. Each diagnostic retains its own reported resources; the later
failure does not establish whether an earlier resource was released. Captured
output and partial observations remain in the original details.

## Save and reuse analysis snapshots

A snapshot retains successful analysis results for later queries. REA reuses
an exact result when the target bytes, operation, parameters, provider and
settings match. Mutations and cursor-dependent calls are excluded from the
cache. Snapshot files are local and use owner-only permissions.

Dispatching a metadata write invalidates the active session's snapshot cache,
even if its reply fails: the provider may already have applied the write.
Close and reopen the target before importing or saving another snapshot.

Snapshots retain eligible target-scoped question histories in full, including
mutation Evidence recorded while another target was active. Observations and
related questions must still belong to the saved target. If those dependencies
cannot be retained, the entire history is excluded instead of reverting the
question to an earlier revision or disposition.

```bash
rea analyze /absolute/path/to/program --provider ghidra --snapshot /absolute/path/to/analysis/program.json
# Repeat the same query to reuse its saved result.
rea analyze /absolute/path/to/program --provider ghidra --snapshot /absolute/path/to/analysis/program.json
```

An exact CLI cache hit is normally read before starting a provider process.
On Windows, Ghidra first admits the selected source through its native snapshot
owner, so replay can start that provider.
In MCP, `open_binary` accepts `snapshot_path` to import a snapshot atomically
for its matching target; an MCP provider may still start before returning a
cached result. `close_binary` accepts `snapshot_path` and optional
`overwrite: true` to save before releasing provider resources. A failed save
leaves the session open so the caller can resolve the output failure.

The MCP save receipt reports `primitive_entries`, `workflow_entries`, and
`evidence_records` separately. Zero primitive bindings can still accompany retained workflow
results and Evidence. These are cached observations, not a saved provider
database: only eligible exact queries can reuse a result, and new or live
queries can still require provider startup. The CLI uses the same snapshot
format and preserves these records when loading and updating it.

## Import, export and compare Evidence

Evidence records retain artifact identity, source locations, observations,
inferences and unresolved findings. Validate an existing bundle, export its
canonical form, or compare two supplied bundles:

```bash
rea evidence-import /absolute/path/to/evidence/bundle.json
rea evidence-export /absolute/path/to/evidence/bundle.json /absolute/path/to/evidence/canonical.json
rea compare /absolute/path/to/evidence/left.json /absolute/path/to/evidence/right.json
```

Exports preserve an existing destination unless `--overwrite` is explicit.
For application traces and version comparisons, see
[JavaScript application workflows](javascript-application-workflows.md).
MCP [retained Evidence references](mcp-contracts.md#retained-application-evidence-inputs)
belong to one connection. Separate CLI calls consume full saved records.

## Import historical source

Import an older source tree to compare with the current artifact:

```bash
rea import-reference-source /absolute/path/to/source
rea import-reference-source /absolute/path/to/source --detail summary --outline-depth 2 --json
```

The default (`--detail full`) returns the complete `HistoricalSourceGraph`.
Choose `--detail summary` for a `HistoricalSourceSummary` of that same committed
inventory: its `HistoricalSourceManifest` contains the full graph and root
digests, with provenance, VCS facts, languages, manifest paths, entry and
relationship counts, parse-failure counts, file/directory states, exclusions
and limitations. The summary is a presentation view, not a graph accepted by
source-to-bundle comparison; keep the full output for that workflow.

`--outline-depth` requires `--detail summary` and accepts a nonnegative safe
integer. Depth 1 shows root children, depth 2 (the default) also shows their
children, and depth 0 omits all outline entries. Paths retain canonical Unicode
code-point order. `outline.omitted_entry_count` counts only inventoried entries
hidden by the chosen depth; it does not count unexamined children of excluded or
unreadable directories, or change `inventory_state`. Exclusions and source
limitations remain separate from this presentation omission.

`file_sizes.known_bytes` is the exact sum of known inventoried file sizes as
decimal text, so large sums cannot lose integer precision. Unknown sizes count
in `file_sizes.unknown_file_count`; excluded or unexamined paths are not included
in that total. A zero known-byte sum therefore does not establish an empty source
tree. Full output retains individual file hashes, relationships and parse-failure
diagnostics. Summary mode performs the same import and cleanup, then projects
the committed result without rereading source files. It reduces the selected
output, not the amount of source examined. A shallow tree or many exclusions can
still produce a large summary; depth 0 removes the outline but preserves the
other facts. No fixed output-size or runtime improvement is promised.

The import records hashes and metadata for the supplied files, separately
from observations of the current app. For a directory inside a Git checkout,
it records the HEAD of the nearest enclosing repository; whether the working
tree matches that commit remains unknown. It honors the source tree's `.gitignore`
and applies default exclusions for common generated and dependency paths such
as `node_modules/`, `dist/`, and `*.log`. Pattern-based exclusions record the
matched pattern and whether it came from project, default, caller, or sensitive
path policy. Links into excluded paths retain their internal target metadata;
the exclusion explains why the target has no inventory entry, and the inventory
remains partial. Exclusions record `entry_kind` when the importer observed it;
older saved exclusions without that field have unknown kind. An excluded
ancestor proves an internal descendant only when its kind is `directory`.
Set `REA_REFERENCE_SECRET_PATTERNS_JSON` to a JSON array of ignore
patterns when you want to mark selected paths as sensitive; those patterns are
reported separately as configured-secret exclusions.

Re-import saved graphs whose pattern-based exclusions lack `pattern` before
using them in source-to-bundle comparisons.

Entries that change during an import retain an unavailable-entry diagnostic
alongside readable siblings. If enumeration of an already admitted root fails,
the graph keeps its observed children and records the root failure as a
top-level limitation. That partial inventory does not establish absence among
unexamined children.

JavaScript and TypeScript import parsing requires valid UTF-8. Malformed source
bytes retain their original hashes and sizes with a decoding diagnostic; REA
does not infer module targets from replacement characters.

Historical-source import requires safe no-follow file opens on Linux or
macOS. Native Windows returns `unsupported_host`; use Linux REA inside WSL
or another supported host. See
[source-to-bundle comparison](javascript-application-workflows.md#historical-source-to-bundle-comparison)
for mapping identities, inferences and unknowns.

## Capture runtime behavior

Choose the guide for the target and intended interaction:

- [Browser observation](browser-observation.md): inspect a selected page through CDP.
- [Browser scenarios](browser-scenario-contract.md): run declared interactions and capture their results.
- [Electron observation](electron-observation.md): inspect an Electron renderer or capture an application scenario.
- [Electron fuses](electron-fuses.md): read packaged fuse bytes before expecting `--inspect` to reach an Electron main process.
- [Node/Electron Inspector](javascript-runtime-observation.md): record script locations and execution contexts.
- [Process capture](process-capture.md): run an executable and compare terminal, exit and filesystem observations.

Runtime requests name the target and actions. Launched targets run with your
user permissions; consult the chosen guide for host requirements and effects.

## Serve MCP over streamable HTTP

`rea mcp` speaks stdio to the client that launched it. To serve the same MCP
catalog over streamable HTTP for one local client, such as an agent environment
runtime, start the dispatcher entry with `--http`:

```sh
rea mcp --http --port 8765
```

`--host` and `--port` default to `MCP_HOST` and `MCP_PORT` from the environment,
then to `127.0.0.1` and an ephemeral port. The bound URL is written to stderr as
one JSON log line (`"msg":"MCP transport listening"`) whatever `REA_LOG_LEVEL`
is set to; nothing is written to stdout. `rea mcp --http --help` lists the accepted options. The listener serves
one client at a time: a session ends with the client's `DELETE`, and a client
that connects while another session is open takes it over, so a client that
exited without ending its session needs no restart. The listener runs until
SIGINT or SIGTERM and does not stop when stdin closes. See
[transports](mcp-contracts.md#transports) for the session, `Host` header and
shutdown contract. Client registrations written by setup and the MCP registry
entry keep stdio.

## Serve an environment manifest

`rea environment-serve <manifest.json> --evidence <capture.json> [--host H]
[--port N]` serves an environment manifest projected by `inspect-analysis-view`
as an agent environment: an MCP server at `/mcp` with one tool per manifest
tool, each replaying the retained capture records it cites, the environment
card at `/.well-known/agent-env.json`, and a `/agentenv` data plane that
answers every method with JSON-RPC `-32601`. The manifest's
`parent_evidence_id` must equal the evidence file's `evidence_id`; otherwise
the command refuses with `invalid_request` before binding.

```sh
rea environment-serve manifest.json --evidence capture.json --port 8765
```

`--host` and `--port` resolve like `rea mcp --http`: flags, then `MCP_HOST` and
`MCP_PORT`, then `127.0.0.1` and an ephemeral port. `ENVIRONMENT_NAME` renames
the served environment; set but blank, it is refused as `configuration_invalid`
like a blank `MCP_HOST`. The bound URL is written to stderr as one JSON log line
(`"msg":"MCP transport listening"`). See
[agent environments](agent-environments.md) for what replay returns and does
not establish.

## Export an environment bundle

`rea environment-export <manifest.json> --evidence <capture.json> <dir>
[--package-tarball <path>] [--name <override>]` writes the same manifest and
capture pair as a bundle folder the agentenv framework runs with
`agent-env run <dir>`. It reads each file once, authenticates and cross-checks
the pair with the same checks as `environment-serve`, copies the bytes it
authenticated, refuses to write into a directory that exists and is not empty,
and never overwrites a file.

```sh
rea environment-export manifest.json --evidence capture.json ./grafana-example --json
```

The folder holds a `README.md` with the bundle's provenance, an env folder
`envs/<name>/` with a `Dockerfile` that installs this exact `rea-agents`
version and serves the copied `manifest.json` and `evidence.json` (written
with mode `0600` on POSIX; Windows retains inherited ACLs) with
`environment-serve`, a Python verifier under `artifacts/check_<name>/` and the
smoke task `tasks/smoke.json`. `--package-tarball` copies a packed `rea-agents`
tarball into the env folder and installs it instead of the registry package,
which is how the hosted lane proves a checkout rather than a release. `--name`
replaces the manifest's kebab-case name as the env folder and env id; a device
name Windows reserves (`con`, `nul`, `com1` and the like) is refused. The
command prints one JSON document listing the written files with their sizes
and the pinned package source. See
[agent environments](agent-environments.md#export-a-bundle) for the folder
layout and what the smoke task checks.

## Output and exit status

`rea mcp doctor --json` checks production MCP startup and reports child logs in
`diagnostics`. It drains stderr while retaining at most its first 64 KiB of raw
bytes as text, omitting a final UTF-8 code point if it crosses that byte limit.
`stderr_bytes` counts all observed bytes, including omitted output;
`stderr_truncated` indicates that output exceeded the retention limit. The same
diagnostics appear inside the report when `--full-output` is selected. Log
truncation alone does not change the diagnostic health or exit status.

The default terminal format is TOON. Use `--json` when saving results for a
JSON consumer. Valued output flags (`--format`, `--filter-output`,
`--token-limit`, `--token-offset`) accept `--flag value` or `--flag=value`; a
missing value fails with `MISSING_OUTPUT_VALUE` before the command runs. `--json` is indented on a terminal and compact when piped or
redirected, which keeps large results smaller for agents and scripts; pipe
through `jq .` for indented files. Output selection and formatting do not change
operation status.

`--filter-output` selects fields from successful command data. Classified failures
retain their complete typed diagnostic projection even when the selector matches
a field such as `code` or `message`, or names a missing field. `--full-output`
controls whether the outer `{ok, error, meta}` envelope is included.

For `cutter-command`, `--json-output` requests command-specific JSON from
Cutter when available. This is separate from `--format json`, which selects the
CLI result representation; the global `--json` flag selects that same CLI
representation.

Cutter still accepts deprecated `--json=true` and `--json=false` compatibility
values. When both forms are present, `--json-output` takes precedence in either
argument order. Bare `--json` retains its global meaning of selecting JSON CLI
output formatting.

| Status    | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| --------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `0`       | The operation completed. Its result may include partial evidence, warnings or unresolved questions.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| `1`       | The operation could not complete. Structured output identifies invalid input, permissions, cancellation, timeouts or another failure when available.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| `128 + N` | Signal-derived status. An unhandled signal may have ended the process, with the shell or runtime preserving the conventional status; a command may instead have handled the signal, waited for its operation and cleanup to settle, and assigned the same status (`130` for SIGINT, `143` for SIGTERM). In the handled case, it may also have printed a structured `cancelled` result. |

`rea mcp --http` is long-running and prints no structured result. It exits
`130` on SIGINT or `143` on SIGTERM after closing the listener, the session and
its providers, and `1` when that cleanup fails.

`rea environment-serve` is also long-running: it serves until SIGINT or
SIGTERM, closes the listener, then prints one structured
`{"status":"stopped", …}` document naming the URL, environment and tool count
and exits `130` or `143` through the shared cancellation handler below.
Refusals before binding (unreadable files, non-Evidence JSON, capture Evidence
in a format other than HAR, a manifest whose parent is not the supplied
evidence, an unbindable port) print a structured
error and exit `1`, as does a listener that fails after binding.
`rea environment-export` is one-shot: it prints the written files and exits
`0`, or prints a structured `invalid_request` error and exits `1` for the same
pair refusals, a non-empty or file-occupied directory, a missing package
tarball or a name that is not a kebab-case label or is a Windows device name,
writing nothing in each case.
A write that fails after the first file (a permission, disk-space or
pathname-length failure on a later path) propagates as the host's failure,
naming its cause and, when it failed on one bundle file or the package
tarball, that file. A failure while syncing the finished folder names only its
cause. Either way the partial folder stays in place for inspection; remove it
before retrying, since the next attempt refuses the non-empty directory.

A `cancelled` result does not by itself determine the exit status; it depends on
the command's signal handling. Commands routed through the shared
`withCommandCancellation` handler in the CLI set status `130` for SIGINT or
`143` for SIGTERM after their operation settles. Current source registrations
use that handler for process capture and comparison (`capture-process`,
`compare-process-captures`), JavaScript application analysis (`analyze` when it
selects the JavaScript lane, and `analyze-javascript-application`), selected
browser, web and Electron commands (including `analyze-web-bundle`,
`observe-web-execution`, `capture-browser-scenario` and
`capture-electron-scenario`), and the platform and provider command families
for Android/ADB, Apktool/JEB/Flutter, firmware, PCAP and signal analysis,
WASM/EVM, Go/Rust and binary diagnostics, Frida instrumentation, the Cutter
command, objdump, Rizin and GDB, and the agent environment server
(`environment-serve`). In these paths, a returned structured
`cancelled` result can be printed before the wrapper assigns the
signal-derived status. This describes the current source routing; it is not a
claim that every command or provider runtime has been independently exercised.

When the reader of piped output closes early, as `rea ... | head` does, the
CLI stops writing, prints no error and exits `141` (`128 + 13`, the status of a
SIGPIPE-terminated writer). The operation itself may have completed; only its
output was declined.

`inspect-artifact` also returns a structured cancelled result, but its direct
analysis cancellation path does not set a signal-derived exit status, so it
exits `1`. Setup has its own contract: cancellation exits `0`. Treat the
structured result and process status as separate signals when scripting
cancellation.

`setup --dry-run` returns `planned` and exits `0`; a cancelled setup also exits
`0`. Setup returns `1` for `needs_confirmation` or `needs_human`.
`doctor` returns `1` when required checks in its selected readiness scope fail;
unavailable optional providers remain informational for unrelated tasks.

Enable `pipefail` in a supporting shell so a downstream formatter preserves
REA's failure status:

```bash
set -o pipefail
rea inspect-artifact ./app.asar --json | jq . > inspection.json
```

```

`vendor/rea-docs/docs/client-configuration.md`:

```md
# Client configuration and troubleshooting

Use this reference when a client's configuration paths, profiles, trust settings,
or schema limits affect REA. Start with [installation and setup](installation.md)
for the reviewed setup transaction and [client IDs](installation.md#supported-agents).
The versioned verification notes below describe their stated runs; live service
acceptance is verified only where explicitly recorded.

## GitHub Copilot CLI

For GitHub Copilot CLI 1.0.95, `gpt-4.1` model metadata can block ordinary
chat with REA's full input-schema profile before sending a model request
(`compaction_static_context_blocked`; [#1554](https://github.com/morluto/rea/issues/1554)).
For the native offline OpenAI-compatible BYOK adapter, full-profile chat and
analysis also passed with a distinct `COPILOT_PROVIDER_MODEL_ID` such as
`rea-gpt-4.1`, `COPILOT_PROVIDER_WIRE_MODEL=gpt-4.1`, and that distinct ID selected
through `copilot --model rea-gpt-4.1`. The local fixture requested
`COPILOT_PROVIDER_MAX_PROMPT_TOKENS=1000000`; configure the limit supported by
your backend. This keeps every full schema and the actual wire model intact.
It does not establish the effective client budget or fix the built-in-ID path.
The existing compact profile passed native chat and analysis with the complete
tool inventory on Linux using a loopback model fixture. After setup, add
`"REA_MCP_INPUT_SCHEMA_PROFILE": "compact"` to the `env` object of the
`mcpServers.rea` entry in Copilot's `mcp-config.json`, preserving its other
settings, then restart the client. Compact advertisements can reduce nested
schema constraints; REA still validates complete canonical inputs. Full-profile
`gpt-5.4` metadata is also verified locally. Live model API acceptance and
Windows remain unverified; see [native client verification](testing.md).

## Claude Desktop

Setup registers `mcpServers.rea` in `claude_desktop_config.json`: under
`~/Library/Application Support/Claude` on macOS, under
`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/Claude` (default `~/.config/Claude`) on Linux, and on Windows
in the file the installed app reads:

- Without Claude Desktop's MSIX package storage, setup uses
  `%APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json`.
- The MSIX build (package family `Claude_pzs8sxrjxfjjc`, installed under
  `C:\Program Files\WindowsApps\Claude_<version>_x64__pzs8sxrjxfjjc`)
  virtualizes AppData writes. Once it has saved its configuration, it reads
  the package-private copy
  `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Packages\Claude_pzs8sxrjxfjjc\LocalCache\Roaming\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json`
  and ignores the `%APPDATA%` file. Setup, doctor and uninstall use that
  private copy when it exists. Before the package has saved one, they use the
  `%APPDATA%` file it still reads; with neither file, setup creates the
  private copy.
- If `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Packages` holds a `Claude_<publisher ID>` package from
  another publisher, an `AnthropicPBC.Claude_<publisher ID>` package, or cannot
  be read, REA cannot establish which file Claude
  Desktop reads. Setup, doctor and uninstall report that instead of falling
  back to `%APPDATA%`. Doctor then reports `claude_desktop` as invalid, and
  uninstall stops before removing anything for any client.
  The reported `AnthropicPBC.Claude_fnn82j28hfe8t` build can use the `Claude-3p`
  deployment directory. REA recognizes that package as an unresolved location;
  it does not assume that it reads the legacy AppData file or automatically
  register in `Claude-3p`. See [#4432](https://github.com/morluto/rea/issues/4432)
  for the reported build and manual registration evidence.

Quit Claude Desktop fully before approving setup; closing its window is not
enough. A running Claude Desktop can rewrite its configuration from memory and
drop the registration. This was observed with the Windows MSIX build. Start
Claude Desktop again after setup. If the package saves its private copy after
setup planned to write the `%APPDATA%` file, setup makes no change and asks you
to rerun it.

A process that the MSIX app started, such as a terminal in Claude Desktop's
Code tab, sees the package's private files at their `%APPDATA%` paths even
though it reports no package identity. Setup compares one of those files at
both paths. When it finds that redirected view, the app is running, so setup
and uninstall refuse to change Claude Desktop's configuration; rerun them from
a terminal that Claude Desktop did not start. If the package has no private
file to compare, setup and uninstall cannot rule that out and also refuse; open
Claude Desktop once if it has never run, quit it fully, then rerun. Doctor
reads the same file from either kind of process.

The same process also writes everything under `%APPDATA%` and
`%LOCALAPPDATA%` into the package's private storage, where other apps never
read it. From that redirected view, setup and uninstall refuse to change other
clients' files there (VS Code, Trae, Devin and Hermes) and skill directories
there. `npm install -g` run from such a process installs into the package's
`LocalCache\Roaming\npm`, which other processes cannot see at the `%APPDATA%`
path. Setup refuses to register a launcher stored in any MSIX package's
private storage. Install REA from an ordinary terminal and rerun setup there.

Uninstall removes REA's entry from both the private copy and the `%APPDATA%`
file, including registrations that earlier releases wrote to `%APPDATA%`.

REA recognizes only the MSIX package. A non-MSIX Claude Desktop installed
beside it, which would read the `%APPDATA%` file, is not detected.

The package identity, both file locations, the redirected view, and these
setup and doctor results were observed on Windows 11 with the MSIX build
2.31226.1.0, using read-only `doctor` and `setup --dry-run` runs both inside
and outside the app. On that host, setup run from an ordinary terminal with
the app quit wrote the package-private copy; after the app restarted, the
entry was still present, doctor reported it aligned, and Claude Desktop's MCP
log showed REA starting and answering `tools/list`. Uninstall against the real
app is unverified.

## Claude Code

Claude Code normally defers MCP tool definitions through tool search. It
[turns tool search off](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#configure-tool-search)
when `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` points to a non-first-party host, such as DeepSeek's
Anthropic-compatible endpoint. It then sends every REA tool's name, description
and input schema with every request
([#2019](https://github.com/morluto/rea/issues/2019)). On main at 04089d5be,
with 172 tools, that payload measured about 496 KB with the default profile and
about 290 KB with `compact`. By the o200k and cl100k tokenizers, that is roughly
120k and 68k tokens. Compaction cannot remove tool definitions. If they nearly
fill the window Claude Code assumes, the context refills after every compaction
and Claude Code reports that autocompact is thrashing. To avoid this:

- Make Claude Code assume the model's actual context window. DeepSeek's Claude
  Code guide selects `deepseek-flash[1m]`; the `[1m]` suffix makes Claude Code
  assume a one-million-token window. For other unrecognized model IDs, set
  `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS` to the window the provider documents.
- If the endpoint forwards `tool_reference` blocks, set `ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=true`
  to restore deferred loading. DeepSeek's Anthropic API guide does not list
  `tool_reference` among its supported content blocks, so this setting may cause
  its requests to fail.
- To shrink the upfront catalog, add
  `"REA_MCP_INPUT_SCHEMA_PROFILE": "compact"` to the `env` object of the
  `mcpServers.rea` entry in `~/.claude.json` (`$CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/.claude.json`
  when that variable is set), then restart Claude Code. Setup keeps this
  override.

The sizes above come from REA's own `tools/list`. A live Claude Code session
against DeepSeek's API is unverified.

For a client whose stdio reader rejects the complete catalog frame, add
`"REA_MCP_OUTPUT_SCHEMA_PROFILE": "off"` to REA's `env` object and restart the
client. This omits only advertised output schemas; REA still validates complete
structured results against its canonical contracts. See [MCP output schema
profiles](mcp-contracts.md#output-schemas).

## Kimi Code

Setup registers `rea` in `~/.kimi-code/mcp.json`, or
`$KIMI_CODE_HOME/mcp.json` when set, while preserving unrelated settings and
creating a `.rea.backup` before updating an existing file. Kimi Code infers
stdio from the `command` entry, so setup does not add a `type` field. New
registrations include `startupTimeoutMs = 30000` and a `toolTimeoutMs` derived
from REA's known provider allowance plus 120 seconds of operation
headroom. The default is 450000 ms, covering the default 330-second Ghidra
startup; an explicit Ghidra startup timeout of 2700000 ms produces a 2820000 ms
tool timeout. The startup allowance follows an explicitly selected Ghidra or
Hopper provider, and otherwise uses the larger known Ghidra/Hopper deadline.
An explicit `REA_JEB_MCP_TIMEOUT_MS` request budget also contributes to that
maximum. For `ida` or `auto` selection, a valid IDA registration's parsed
`timeoutMs` also contributes to that maximum; its default is 300000 ms.
Setup forwards these explicitly selected REA deadlines and the input schema
profile into the registration; unrelated process values are omitted. An
explicit `REA_JADX_OPERATION_TIMEOUT_MS` is forwarded with the JADX
registration but does not contribute to the derived tool timeout; raise
`toolTimeoutMs` to cover a longer selected JADX deadline.
This headroom is a practical default, not a guarantee for every analysis
duration. Setup preserves positive timeout values already in the `rea` entry.
You can edit `startupTimeoutMs` and `toolTimeoutMs` there; doctor keeps positive
caller-selected values aligned and reports a non-blocking advisory when a tool
timeout is shorter than the known provider allowance.
Setup selects the compact input-schema advertisement for new or refreshed Kimi
registrations unless their stored configuration or setup environment explicitly
selects `REA_MCP_INPUT_SCHEMA_PROFILE=full` or `compact`. This keeps REA's
canonical tool validation unchanged while avoiding a Moonshot Kimi Code 2.2.0
failure observed with the full catalog: its request was rejected because a
single tool schema exceeded the provider's size limit. The limit is
provider-specific and not an MCP protocol limit. `rea doctor --client kimi`
reports an older registration with no explicit profile as stale. To restore the
compact profile, run `rea setup --client kimi` or add
`REA_MCP_INPUT_SCHEMA_PROFILE=compact` to the registration's `env`, then restart
Kimi Code. An explicit `full` profile remains respected and can still exceed
Moonshot's limit.
Kimi Code also discovers personal skills in `~/.agents/skills` and project-local
`.agents/skills`, so no separate skill root is required; setup still installs
and verifies the matching skill files through the normal shared-skill flow.
Start a new Kimi Code session to pick up MCP and skill changes.

## Pi

For [Pi](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/mcp.md),
setup writes a `type: "stdio"` entry under `mcpServers.rea` in the user-level
`~/.pi/agent/mcp.json` and installs the bundled skill under `~/.agents/skills`.
Use `rea setup --client pi --dry-run --json` to inspect the plan, then
`rea setup --client pi --yes --json` to approve it. Check the registration with
`rea doctor --client pi --json`. Pi reads `mcp.json` as strict JSON, like its
own loader: comments, trailing commas, a byte-order mark, or an empty existing
file are invalid, and setup reports them instead of rewriting the file. Repair
such a file to plain JSON first, then rerun setup.

Setup follows Pi's `PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR`: unset or empty selects the default;
`~` and `~/` expand to the home directory; absolute paths and file URLs select
that directory; relative paths stay relative to the command's working directory.
On Windows, native paths, `~\`, and Git Bash/MSYS, Cygwin, and WSL drive paths
are normalized as Pi does. Run REA and Pi from the same working directory when
using a relative override. Pi has no profiles: `OMP_PROFILE`, `PI_PROFILE`,
`PI_CONFIG_DIR`, and OMP's `enabledServers`/`disabledServers` lists do not affect
Pi registration. Doctor accepts an omitted `type` for stdio but reports a
non-stdio type as invalid; `enabled: false` stays disabled.

REA configures only the user scope. Pi also reads `.pi/mcp.json` in trusted
projects; a same-name project entry can replace the user entry or override its
enabled state and exposure. Check that file if the user registration is aligned
but unavailable in a project. An extension that registers `/mcp` can replace
Pi's built-in MCP support and use its own configuration instead. Run `/reload`
in an existing Pi session after changing servers outside the session.

## Qwen Code

For Qwen Code, setup registers `rea` in the `mcpServers` table of the
user-level `~/.qwen/settings.json`, or `$QWEN_HOME/settings.json` when configured.
Setup and doctor follow Qwen Code's tilde and working-directory-relative home
overrides. Qwen Code also discovers personal skills in `~/.agents/skills`,
where setup installs the bundled workflow.

## Antigravity

Antigravity 2.0 discovers personal skills in `~/.gemini/config/skills`.
Setup installs its selected skill copy there.

## Gemini CLI

Gemini CLI uses `$GEMINI_CLI_HOME/.gemini/settings.json` when that home override
is nonempty, including its shared personal skills at
`$GEMINI_CLI_HOME/.agents/skills`. Setup and doctor check MCP allow/exclude
policies from system defaults, user settings, trusted workspace settings, and
system overrides. Workspace trust follows `GEMINI_CLI_TRUST_WORKSPACE`,
`GEMINI_RESTRICTED_MODE`, the effective `security.folderTrust.enabled` setting,
and the selected `trustedFolders.json` (including
`GEMINI_CLI_TRUSTED_FOLDERS_PATH`). Settings in an untrusted workspace do not
participate. A workspace or system `mcpServers.rea` replaces the entire user
entry; setup stops if the winning definition conflicts with its planned entry.
Review those files manually: setup never edits administrator/workspace settings
or grants workspace trust. Trust supplied only by a running IDE is outside this
standalone CLI check.

## Codex and Devin

Codex treats an unset or empty `CODEX_HOME` as `~/.codex`. Its MCP server
registration supports `startup_timeout_sec` for connection initialization and
`tool_timeout_sec` for each tool call. New REA registrations use a 30-second
startup timeout and a tool timeout derived from the known provider
allowance plus 120 seconds of operation headroom. This yields 450 seconds for
the default Ghidra allowance; an explicit Ghidra startup timeout of 2700
seconds yields 2820 seconds. Setup preserves positive caller-selected timeout
values in the REA entry, and doctor reports a non-blocking advisory when a tool
timeout is shorter than the known provider allowance. An explicitly selected
JEB request budget also contributes to the allowance. A configured IDA
registration's parsed `timeoutMs` contributes for `ida` or `auto` selection.
An explicit `REA_JADX_OPERATION_TIMEOUT_MS` is forwarded with the JADX
registration but does not contribute; raise `tool_timeout_sec` to cover a
longer selected JADX deadline.
These values are client-side deadlines, so increase them in `~/.codex/config.toml` if a
workload needs more time. Devin honors `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` for its
`devin/mcp_config.json` on non-Windows systems.

## OMP

For OMP, setup writes a `type: "stdio"` entry to the user-level
`~/.omp/agent/mcp.json`. It follows `PI_CONFIG_DIR` and
`PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR` (relative to the setup working directory), and the profile selected by `OMP_PROFILE` or
`PI_PROFILE` (`~/.omp/profiles/<name>/agent/mcp.json`). Setup also removes
`rea` from that file's `disabledServers` list, which would otherwise hide the
registration. Doctor treats an `enabled: false` entry as active when
`enabledServers` lists `rea`, as OMP does, unless `disabledServers` also lists
it. Run setup under each profile that should load REA.

## Hermes

For Hermes, setup writes a `mcp_servers.rea` entry to `config.yaml`, preserving
comments and unrelated settings. It resolves that file from `HERMES_HOME`, else
from the platform default Hermes itself uses — `%LOCALAPPDATA%\hermes` on
Windows, `~/.hermes` elsewhere — including any `HERMES_DATA_DIR_SUFFIX`. Hermes
connects an entry unless `enabled` is false, so setup states `enabled: true`.

Hermes personal skills install under the active Hermes home's `skills` directory.
Setup, doctor and uninstall follow the root's `active_profile` selection, as
plain Hermes CLI commands do. An explicit `HERMES_HOME` pointing to
`profiles/<name>` selects that named profile directly. An invalid, missing or
deleted sticky profile is reported instead of writing into the default home;
repair the profile or run `hermes profile use default` before retrying.
REA follows `HERMES_HOME` whitespace trimming, environment-variable expansion,
and home expansion before resolving that profile. Setup previews the resolved
configuration and skill destinations; doctor and uninstall use those same paths.

## Qoder CLI

For [Qoder](https://docs.qoder.com/cli/mcp-reference), setup writes
`mcpServers.rea` into the user-level `~/.qoder/settings.json` (the
`QODER_CONFIG_DIR` override is honored). Entries carry `command`, `args`, and
`env`; stdio is the default transport. Qoder CLI discovers personal skills
from `~/.qoder/skills` (following `QODER_CONFIG_DIR` when set), so setup
installs its skill copy there.

## Factory Droid

For [Factory Droid](https://docs.factory.com/harness/mcp), setup writes
`mcpServers.rea` into the user-level `~/.factory/mcp.json`. Entries carry
`command`, `args`, and `env`. Droid discovers personal skills from
`~/.factory/skills` ([skills](https://docs.factory.com/harness/skills)), so
setup installs its skill copy there.

## Trae

For [Trae](https://docs.trae.ai/ide/add-mcp-servers), setup writes
`mcpServers.rea` into the user-scope `mcp.json` under Trae's VS Code-style
user directory (`%APPDATA%\Trae\User` on Windows,
`~/Library/Application Support/Trae/User` on macOS, and
`~/.config/Trae/User` elsewhere). Entries carry `command`, `args`, and
`env`; stdio is the default transport. Trae discovers personal skills from
`~/.trae/skills` (`%userprofile%\.trae\skills` on Windows), so setup
installs its skill copy there.

The user-level MCP paths follow the editor's VS Code layout. Trae's official
documentation describes the raw JSON editor without specifying those paths;
loading this registration in Trae remains unverified.

## WorkBuddy

For [WorkBuddy](https://www.workbuddy.cn/docs/workbuddy/From-Beginner-to-Expert-Guide/Function-Description/MCP-Guide), setup writes `mcpServers.rea` into the
global `~/.workbuddy/mcp.json` (a standard `mcpServers` JSON file at the user
home root on every platform). Entries carry `command`, `args`, and `env`;
stdio is the default transport. WorkBuddy discovers personal skills from
`~/.workbuddy/skills` (`%userprofile%\.workbuddy\skills` on Windows), so
setup installs its skill copy there.

The global MCP path is a plain JSON file; setup preserves every other server
and top-level key when it upserts `rea`. WorkBuddy also reads a project-level
`<project>/.workbuddy/mcp.json`, which setup does not touch: it registers the
user-level file only. Loading this registration and real REA tool calls
through WorkBuddy are verified.

## ZCode

For [ZCode](https://zcode.z.ai/en/docs/mcp-services), setup registers `rea` in the nested `mcp.servers` table of the
user-level `~/.zcode/cli/config.json`. Entries carry `command`, `args`, and
`env` without a transport discriminator. ZCode discovers personal skills from
`~/.zcode/skills` rather than the shared directory, so setup installs its
skill copy there.

ZCode reads the user-scope `~/.agents/mcp.json` fallback only while the native
`.zcode` config defines no servers at all, with no merging. When setup writes
the first native server into an empty table, it copies the fallback's
`mcpServers` entries into the native table so they keep loading, and leaves
the fallback file untouched. Existing REA environment overrides are preserved
when refreshing its command. A malformed or unreadable fallback file fails setup instead of
being silently suppressed; repair or remove it and rerun. Uninstall removes an
REA-owned `rea` entry from both the native table and the fallback, backing up
each changed file, so an emptied native table cannot load a leftover fallback
registration; other fallback servers, settings and a foreign `rea` entry are
kept. ZCode disables a
server with `enable: false` on its entry; doctor reports such a registration
as stale, and rerunning setup removes the flag to repair it. Native configuration
uses strict JSON; setup refuses comments, trailing commas and a BOM rather than
writing a registration ZCode cannot load.

## DeepSeek Harness

DeepSeek Harness registers MCP clients through a Cordis YAML patch sequence
rather than a `mcpServers` object. `rea setup --client dsh` appends (or
replaces) the REA entry in the home patch `$DSH_HOME/cordis.patch.yml`
(`~/.dsh/cordis.patch.yml` when `DSH_HOME` is unset), preserving unrelated
patches and comments. `rea doctor --client dsh` checks that same entry id.
`rea uninstall` removes it by scanning supported clients; uninstall takes no
`--client` flag. The home patch applies to every Harness profile, so the
registration is written once and no per-profile edit is needed.

Setup, doctor and uninstall resolve `DSH_HOME` and `DSH_AGENTS_HOME` as Harness
does: unset, empty or whitespace-only values use `~/.dsh` and `~/.agents`,
respectively. Bare `~`, `~/` and `~\` expand to the user home; other relative
values resolve against the command's working directory. Nonblank values retain
their original spaces, and the agents root is independent of the Harness home.
Run REA and Harness from the same working directory when using relative overrides.
The written entry is:

```yaml
- insert:
    - id: rea-mcp
      name: "@deepseek-ai/dsh-mcp-client"
      config:
        serverName: rea
        transport: stdio
        command: /absolute/path/to/node
        args: ["/absolute/path/to/rea/scripts/rea.mjs", mcp]
```

Setup preserves caller-owned Cordis expressions and replaces launcher fields
with literal values that doctor can verify. It refuses to edit an expression
that produces the entire REA config, or a group-targeted REA insertion. Use a
literal config and a root-level insertion as shown above.

For a global npm installation, the launcher is under
`$(npm root -g)/rea-agents/scripts/rea.mjs`. Restart Harness after setup; it
exposes tools as `mcp__rea__<tool_name>`. Run `rea setup --skill --dry-run`,
review the destination, then `rea setup --skill --yes` to install the workflow
in `~/.agents/skills` (`$DSH_AGENTS_HOME/skills` when configured); Harness
discovers that directory, and its native `skill` tool can load
`reverse-engineer-anything`.

REA's optional [native client verification](testing.md#end-to-end-integration-and-golden-evidence)
checks headless chat, skill loading, all tool input schemas and actual analysis
using the installed Harness and a local model fixture. This establishes the
Harness integration, with live DeepSeek API compatibility remaining unverified.
See the [Harness MCP guide](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness/blob/639ed015397290b3745d163aafe02ffee4aa3f84/packages/mcp/mcp-client/README.md)
for its native configuration contract.

## Other client settings

For OpenCode, setup writes the V1 `mcp.rea` entry, which OpenCode V1 and V2
both load. If the configuration already uses OpenCode V2's native
`mcp.servers` table, setup registers REA there instead and replaces any earlier
`mcp.rea` entry from REA. Setup honors `OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR` and
`OPENCODE_CONFIG`, preferring the later-loaded JSONC file when both JSON and
JSONC exist. The ordinary XDG global configuration still participates when a
custom directory is selected. Doctor checks the merged user registration; uninstall removes
REA-owned entries from every applicable user file so an older entry cannot
become active again. Malformed applicable files block setup before changes.

Grok Build loads `[mcp_servers.rea]` from `$GROK_HOME/config.toml`, or from
`~/.grok/config.toml` when `GROK_HOME` is unset or empty. Setup edits that server
table, `[mcp_servers.rea.env]`, and a root `disabled_mcp_servers` entry that
names `rea`. It sets `startup_timeout_sec = 30` and leaves every other name
in that list. The shared skill installed under `~/.agents/skills` is already
on Grok Build's skill path.

Grok Bot (`grok_bot`) is detected from `~/.grokbot`, or from `SAND_DATA_ROOT`
when that value is an absolute path. A relative or empty `SAND_DATA_ROOT`
stays on `~/.grokbot`. That directory is not the connector store. Grok Bot
keeps connectors in the signed-in account and runs them on its hosted
computer. It does not import `mcp.json` from the data directory, and it does
not attach a stdio server running on this machine. Setup does not call the
account connector API, does not write a registration file, and does not report
the data directory as aligned. Ask the Grok Bot chat to add a custom MCP
server named `rea` that runs on the Bot's computer:

```bash
npx -y rea-agents@<version> mcp
```

Do not put credentials in that command or its arguments. `rea doctor --client grok_bot`
reports this manual step. `rea uninstall` does not remove the account connector.
