`vendor/rea-docs/docs/ida-provider.md`:

```md
# IDA provider

REA adapts an existing IDA MCP server into its native analysis tools. Existing IDA Pro profiles use [mrexodia/ida-pro-mcp](https://github.com/mrexodia/ida-pro-mcp); an optional native bridge for IDA Pro and IDA Free is described below. Install and configure your selected engine and upstream MCP using their instructions. REA does not install, upgrade, activate, or license them, and does not bundle another IDA server.

Choose one lifecycle mode in an upstream MCP JSON registration. Set `REA_IDA_MCP_CONFIG` to that file, then select `ida` once through `REA_ANALYSIS_PROVIDER`, the CLI's `--provider ida`, or MCP's `open_binary.provider_id`. No provider startup occurs during discovery.

## Supported upstream versions

Each mode accepts one upstream tool profile, checked against `tools/list` before any analysis runs. The attached profile requires the legacy GUI tool names; upstream 2.0.0 renamed those tools, and REA has not established an equivalent attached-mode lifecycle and ownership contract for that catalog. It therefore fails closed with the missing tool names in the error diagnostics.

Startup failures identify the accepted REA analysis operation. Missing-profile and typed startup transport failures retain the original stage in `details.diagnostics.startup_operation`; existing diagnostics, timeout budgets and resource limits remain available. Startup remains shared within a session; each caller receives its own operation attribution. Cancellation retains live cleanup ownership, so a successful retry releases the originating cancellation outcome as well.

The headless profile is defined by the database-supervisor API, not by an upstream version string. The upstream source snapshot [`c133c385`](https://github.com/mrexodia/ida-pro-mcp/tree/c133c3853faa111a9b00ee615c013b720d0c4acd) includes `idb_close` (introduced by [upstream PR #495](https://github.com/mrexodia/ida-pro-mcp/pull/495)) alongside `idb_open` and `idb_list`. Earlier builds may report the same `2.0.0` version while lacking that tool, so REA checks the live catalog rather than treating a version number or branch name as a compatibility guarantee.

| Mode     | Upstream profile    | Known working                                          |
| -------- | ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| attached | legacy GUI tools    | 1.4.0                                                  |
| headless | database supervisor | builds serving `idb_open`, `idb_list`, and `idb_close` |

## Analyze an already-open GUI target

The attached profile supports upstream **1.4.0 legacy tools**, including `get_metadata`, `list_functions`, and `decompile_function`. Copy the upstream registration's `command`, `args`, and optional `env` into a JSON file. An existing `mcpServers` object with an `ida-pro-mcp` entry is also accepted. For example:

```json
{
  "command": "python",
  "args": [
    "/absolute/path/to/ida_pro_mcp/server.py",
    "--ida-rpc",
    "http://127.0.0.1:13337"
  ]
}
```

Use the executable and arguments from your working upstream registration. The legacy GUI's `/mcp` endpoint is its internal RPC endpoint; connect REA through the upstream stdio proxy rather than treating that URL as Streamable HTTP.

```bash
export REA_IDA_MCP_CONFIG=/absolute/path/to/ida-mcp.json
export REA_ANALYSIS_PROVIDER=ida
rea function /absolute/path/to/program main --json
rea decompile /absolute/path/to/program main --json
```

If the registration cannot be read or validated, provider diagnostics retain its
selected `registration_path` and the configuration owner's setting/constraint
facts in `configuration_details.settings`, plus `configuration_remediation`.
`configured` means a path was selected, not that it is valid or an IDA connection
was established; failed registrations remain unavailable. Correct
`REA_IDA_MCP_CONFIG` in the next CLI invocation's environment or the MCP server's
launch environment. Restart/reconnect that server after changing its environment;
an export in another shell does not update a running server.

Open the **original input binary** in REA, not an `.idb` or `.i64` database. Its SHA-256 must match IDA's recorded input hash. REA checks the attached identity and image base around each analysis request. A mismatch or target switch fails with recovery guidance. The original input must remain readable by REA; WSL can use its mounted alias while the GUI runs on Windows. Attached profiles, including native mode, refuse universal Mach-O inputs at admission: every slice shares the recorded whole-file hash, so REA cannot verify which slice the GUI loaded. Open a thin file extracted with `lipo -thin` in both IDA and REA, or use headless mode, which analyzes the selected slice.

REA's close operation releases its MCP connection or proxy. It never saves or closes the existing GUI database. External edits remain visible because results are live and are not replayed from snapshots. These checks do not lock the GUI or prove that the database is unpatched.

## Optional native IDA MCP bridge

IDA Pro and IDA Free can use the separate [ida-free-mcp native plugin](https://github.com/0xshlomil/ida-free-mcp) through an explicit attached registration. Install and start that plugin using its upstream instructions, open the original binary in the IDA GUI, and wait for analysis. The native MCP 1.1.2 release binds `0.0.0.0` without a listen-address setting. Restrict inbound access with the host firewall or use an upstream build that binds only to loopback before starting it. REA's loopback URL restriction does not change the plugin's listener. REA does not install IDA, build the plugin, activate a license, or launch the GUI.

```json
{
  "mode": "attached",
  "protocol": "native",
  "url": "http://127.0.0.1:13337/mcp"
}
```

Set `REA_IDA_MCP_CONFIG` to this file and select `ida` using the same CLI/MCP commands above. Omitting `protocol` preserves existing IDA Pro registrations. Native mode requires `resources/read` for `ida://idb/metadata` and its recorded input SHA-256; it never substitutes a digest of an unrelated local file. The native resource's `path` describes the IDB in the upstream protocol, not the original input path. REA retains it and checks database identity and image base before and after requests.

This experimental profile provides function/string inventory and search, function lookup, assembly, GUI pseudocode, callees, address xrefs, instruction windows, and function dossiers. Direct callers remain unavailable: native code/data xref labels do not prove call edges. It requires neither IDAPython nor idalib. Native headless registrations are rejected.

Native string observations use upstream C-string rendering; other representations remain unknown. Literal searches request conservative candidates and apply REA's original case and Unicode matching rules. Regex searches retain the full scan because native byte-oriented regex semantics cannot replace REA's Unicode regex semantics. All candidate pages are examined, and upstream search errors remain failures.

Native callee resolution batches unique queries and checks each reply's query identity. Results remain live: a recorded input hash does not establish database revision, so cross-request analysis caches cannot prove freshness. For focused questions, use pseudocode, callees, or instruction-window tools; a function dossier requests additional facets and returns more Evidence.

IDA Free's cloud decompiler needs network access and may request consent. Follow its licensing and supported architecture limits; see [IDA Free](https://hex-rays.com/ida-free). Decompilation moves GUI focus and the upstream plugin closes existing pseudocode tabs before requesting fresh output. REA advertises UI/network effects and closes only its MCP connection, preserving the open database. Rendered pseudocode has upstream traversal limits and does not prove complete source recovery. Cloud/widget failures remain explicit failures; retry after the GUI finishes or dismiss its prompt.

Native MCP 1.1.2 can navigate in the previously focused pseudocode tab when switching functions. Use upstream 1.1.3 or a source build including [the navigation correction](https://github.com/0xshlomil/ida-free-mcp/commit/6adf2c615a2a03661059673e9c136ef28d0dc778), which focuses the disassembly view **before** jumping to the requested entry. This REA profile does not repair stale GUI output. Verification must include two different functions before claiming reliable function switching. The initial Linux verification used a locally corrected 1.1.2 plugin; upstream 1.1.3 has not been verified by that run.

Native tool observations retain actual tool names and complete JSON text. Upstream `structuredContent` can be a shortened preview even while text contains the full result. REA reads the full native representation and rejects missing/malformed text instead of treating previews as complete observations.

The legacy producer moves the active GUI as a side effect: assembly and raw function instructions jump to the function, and successful pseudocode opens or reuses a pseudocode view. A function dossier does both. Native GUI decompilation also changes the active view. `binary_session` reports these operations with `effects.may_show_ui: true`; headless operations and the other attached operations report `false`.

## Give REA a target for headless analysis

The headless profile supports upstream's **database supervisor** API: `idb_open`, `idb_list`, `idb_close`, explicit `database` arguments, and modern analysis tools. Legacy 1.4.0 `idalib-mcp`, which accepts one initial filename and serves SSE, does not implement this profile. Follow the [upstream headless instructions](https://github.com/mrexodia/ida-pro-mcp#headless-idalib-session-model) for an installation with the supervisor API.

```json
{
  "command": "idalib-mcp",
  "args": ["--stdio", "--max-workers", "1"],
  "mode": "headless"
}
```

Use an already-installed executable. When required by your existing idalib installation, include `"env": { "IDADIR": "/absolute/path/to/ida" }`. REA neither edits the global activation configuration nor installs dependencies. A configured local Streamable HTTP supervisor can instead use `"url": "http://127.0.0.1:8745/mcp"` and `"mode": "headless"`.

The same CLI commands work in both modes. For a Windows-native REA process:

```powershell
$env:REA_IDA_MCP_CONFIG = 'D:\analysis\ida-mcp.json'
$env:REA_ANALYSIS_PROVIDER = 'ida'
rea function 'D:\samples\program.exe' main --json
```

Headless REA and the configured supervisor must share the host filesystem and native path syntax. Run REA on Windows when the supervisor runs on Windows. The attached profile can span WSL and a Windows GUI because it binds recorded input hashes instead of asking the GUI to open a WSL path.

REA copies the admitted binary into a private temporary directory, checks its digest, and requests an owned worker with `force_headless`. POSIX workspaces are created atomically with owner-only permissions, respecting the process umask; Windows uses the matching package's native private-DACL boundary on a local NTFS temporary directory. It injects the returned database ID into analysis requests. It verifies the active owned worker and input path rather than adopting a user database. On close or failed startup, it releases its session with `save: false`, verifies that it is absent from upstream session discovery, and removes its private input and sidecars. An unverified release retains the workspace and reports incomplete cleanup.

One REA session owns one database. Stdio registrations default `IDA_MCP_MAX_WORKERS` to `1`; the explicit upstream `--max-workers 1` also bounds a supervisor. Database size and engine memory depend on the target and upstream; REA does not impose an engine memory limit. The original binary is never executed or overwritten. Optional `workspaceRoot` selects an existing absolute temporary-directory parent on the REA host. Ensure it has space for the input copy and IDA working files.

When a completed `idb_open` response reports success or is otherwise ambiguous, but no active owned private worker can be verified, REA retains the private workspace even if `idb_list` appears empty. A later close can retry verification if the original owned worker becomes discoverable. A completed explicit `idb_open` rejection retains the existing no-worker cleanup path. This is a local admission/ownership safeguard and **does not** provide a process-termination receipt or change the legacy reaped-worker protocol.

Headless cleanup uses the upstream database lifecycle. Abruptly terminating REA, its proxy, or the supervisor does not establish worker release. Prefer `close_binary` for MCP sessions; after an interrupted process, inspect upstream session inventory and retained workspace diagnostics before removing working files. This adapter does not claim Windows Job Object containment for the upstream detached workers.

## Connect an agent once

Add the registration path to the **REA** MCP entry's environment, keeping the upstream registration in its separate JSON file:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "rea": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "rea-agents@<version-with-ida>", "mcp"],
      "env": {
        "REA_ANALYSIS_PROVIDER": "ida",
        "REA_IDA_MCP_CONFIG": "/absolute/path/to/ida-mcp.json"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Use a package version that actually includes this adapter; repository main can be ahead of the npm release. After reconnecting, call:

```json
{"name":"open_binary","arguments":{"path":"/absolute/path/to/program","provider_id":"ida"}}
{"name":"analyze_function","arguments":{"procedure":"main"}}
{"name":"search_strings","arguments":{"pattern":"license"}}
{"name":"close_binary","arguments":{}}
```

Opening an MCP target starts its selected provider session; headless opening waits for auto-analysis. Set the agent's MCP request deadline long enough for the target. The registration's optional `timeoutMs` defaults to 300000 for upstream requests. An upstream SDK request that reaches this limit returns `provider_timeout` with its operation and actual request budget. A freshly opened headless worker can briefly report `status: "busy"` from `server_health`; REA re-reads health every 100 ms until the worker answers, the caller cancels, or `timeoutMs` has elapsed since the first read. Each health request is capped by the time remaining in that overall wait, so a stalled read cannot extend the readiness deadline by another full request timeout. Expiry while the worker is still busy produces a retryable `provider_timeout`; no further read is started after the deadline. That error names the busy tool from the last observation, or `unknown` when the worker reported none or a value that is not tool-name-shaped. If a health request itself consumes the remaining wait budget, the same last-busy timeout is returned with the stalled request's captured output. Cancellation during the wait produces `cancelled`. Any other unexpected health payload, including a busy payload with an invalid shape, remains `unreadable_output`. Cancellation drains the current upstream request before cleanup; it does not force-stop GUI analysis. An open request that times out without a completed response retains the private workspace because worker inventory alone cannot prove the request has stopped. `binary_session` reports actual tool availability. Repeated doctor/setup calls are unnecessary when the registration already works.

For guided registration, set `REA_IDA_MCP_CONFIG` before `rea setup --client <client>`. Setup includes that file reference in its reviewed plan and preserves it after approval; it does not copy upstream credentials into the agent configuration. For `ida` or `auto` selection, Codex/Kimi setup and doctor use the effective client registration's parsed `timeoutMs` (default 300000 ms) when recommending the agent's per-tool deadline. Existing positive client deadlines remain caller choices. `rea doctor --provider ida --json` validates the registration without starting IDA and explicitly leaves runtime compatibility and target binding for analysis.

## Coverage and evidence

All profiles support procedure/string inventory and literal or regex search, procedure resolution, pseudocode, assembly, raw function instructions, resolved callees, incoming address references, and a function dossier. Inventories and modern pseudocode/assembly follow upstream pagination. Upstream limits on modern xrefs and callees are retained as explicit truncation limitations. In the modern headless profile, targets that are not proven x86-only use processor-neutral `callgraph` edges instead of the x86 instruction checks in upstream `callees` (mrexodia/ida-pro-mcp#549). REA requests depth zero: the pinned upstream emits the root's outgoing edges without scanning child functions, then REA batches function-name lookup for those addresses. The graph covers recognized function destinations only; imports and other non-function targets remain unknown. A server without `callgraph` returns an empty relationship list with an explicit coverage limitation. Graph and path workflows retain those limitations alongside observed edges. A failed or inconsistent graph reply remains an error. A transport-level truncated preview is rejected rather than reported as complete evidence; the error preserves upstream retrieval guidance.

All profiles expose `list_documents` as the single target admitted for the session. Attached mode verifies its digest against IDA metadata before returning it; headless mode binds the digest-checked private input. `inspect_address_context`, `trace_feature`, and `binary_overview` can therefore resolve that identity without upstream document-listing tools. Segment enumeration is optional: when the selected profile cannot provide it, `binary_overview` still returns document and procedure/string counts and omits `segments` and `segment_count`; omission means unobserved, not empty. The modern headless profile also supports `resolve_containing_procedure`. An address resolves through upstream `lookup_funcs` to the canonical entry of the function that contains it; the body stays unavailable like other IDA identities. When no function contains it, REA reads the database-scoped minimal `survey_binary` and reports `not_in_procedure` for an address inside one of its segments (ends are exclusive) and `outside_segments` otherwise. A missing, truncated or inconsistent survey fails the read instead of guessing a reason. `trace_feature` marks a trace truncated, with a residual unknown for that address, when upstream caps the references it returned. Attached profiles do not declare address containment resolution.

The legacy profile additionally supports direct callers. Its producer may report call-site or interior addresses; REA resolves the reported function symbol to its canonical entry. The modern and native profiles do not prove direct callers from its code/data xref labels, so that capability is unavailable and the dossier marks it unknown.

Complete body ranges, typed reference edges, CFG, referenced data, source locals, comment kinds, and database revision are unavailable. Empty unsupported dossier facets mean **unknown**, not observed absence. Whole-symbol inventory, mutation, debugging, arbitrary Python forwarding, and requested GUI navigation are outside this adapter's coverage. Check session availability before composing a workflow that needs those facets.

`provider.version` identifies the REA adapter; the profile explicitly records `version_scope: "rea-ida-adapter"`. The MCP handshake's `serverInfo` is separate and does not establish IDA or Python distribution versions. Raw observations preserve producer metadata and output. Attached hashes identify the recorded original input; headless identity uses the digest-verified private copy and observed worker input path. Neither proves source-code recovery or an unmodified analysis database.

## Verification

Run `npm run verify:ida -- --target /absolute/path/to/program --procedure main` with a configured upstream server. It exercises production CLI and MCP tools, validates their output contracts and Evidence, checks original-input preservation and session cleanup, and keeps local target data out of its console summary. Supply `--package-root` to verify an extracted or installed package. See [testing](testing.md) for the distinction between adapter tests and real-provider evidence.

Native verification requires `--second-procedure other_function --second-marker unique_second_body_text`; these options remain optional for the other profiles. The marker must occur in the second function's pseudocode and be absent from the first; the verifier also checks that returning to the first restores its text.

The verifier requires the resolved procedure in both inventory and procedure search, then compares address, assembly, pseudocode, instruction windows and relationship results with the CLI/MCP dossier. Supply `--expected-string known_literal` to check a known positive string inventory/search result and `--expected-xref 0xSOURCE` to check a known reference source address. Choose those oracles independently from the operation under test. Without them, string and xref correctness are listed in `unverified`; valid output shapes alone do not establish those behaviors. Callee parity does not independently establish semantic completeness. Native callee successes must report an explicit truncation marker; missing markers remain protocol failures.

The initial real workflows use stdio registrations for the legacy Windows GUI profile and a Windows x64 headless supervisor with IDA 9.3. The headless workflow has also passed on macOS arm64 with IDA Professional 9.1 (build 9.1.250226) against the same upstream commit `c133c3853faa111a9b00ee615c013b720d0c4acd`, using a source-built arm64 Mach-O fixture; Mach-O C symbols carry a leading underscore, so the procedure name is `_rea_fixture_add`. Streamable HTTP is tested against a loopback MCP fixture with the pinned client SDK; a real IDA HTTP-supervisor workflow remains unverified. Linux headless engine operation, other IDA releases, architectures, and modern attached GUI tools require their corresponding real workflows before support is claimed.

Native Windows verification uses IDA Pro 9.3 with the public two-function fixture and Windows `whoami.exe`, using upstream `c9d15d98e8a143fc74f6e14037c48f63889b6d6c` with a loopback-listener change. It covers production CLI/MCP parity, distinct-function switching, identity and connection cleanup. See the [correctness and performance measurements](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/experiments/analysis-efficiency/ida-native-windows.md). This follow-up did not run Windows IDA Free or native macOS.

```

`vendor/rea-docs/docs/il2cpp-metadata.md`:

```md
# IL2CPP metadata

`inspect_il2cpp_metadata` / `inspect-il2cpp-metadata` decodes one selected local
Unity IL2CPP `global-metadata.dat` file and returns its assembly images, type
definitions, methods and named members with their owners, plus managed string
literals, by stable index, namespace, range and count,
with the header sections and serialized index widths. It reads the file without
running it and requires no Unity installation, IL2CPP binary, active target,
Hopper, Ghidra or IDA.

Metadata versions 24, 27, 29, 31 and 39 are supported. For example, Unity 2019.4.41f2
wrote version 24, 2020.3.49f1 version 27, 2022.3.30f1
wrote version 29, 2022.3.62f3 wrote 31 and 6000.4.2f1 wrote 39; other Unity
releases that write these numbers have not been checked. Other versions are
rejected as unsupported. Version 24 decoding covers the 264-byte header layout
used by the cited Unity 2019.4 build; earlier 24.x layouts are not inferred from
the version number and are refused when their header or records differ. The path
must name a regular file; directories and symbolic links are rejected.

With `binary_path`, the tool also reads the matching native binary and links
each method to its code address. See [Native method addresses](#native-method-addresses).

## MCP

MCP defaults to a compact summary and retains the complete decoded Evidence in
the session. MCP requires an absolute filesystem path:

```json
{
  "name": "inspect_il2cpp_metadata",
  "arguments": {
    "path": "/artifacts/Data/Managed/Metadata/global-metadata.dat"
  }
}
```

The summary retains the complete decoded Evidence in the session and returns a
linked `inspect_analysis_view` overview: artifact identity, metadata version,
index widths and `counts` (`sections`, `images`, `types`, `methods`,
`nested_types`, `fields`, `properties`, `events`, `parameters` and
`string_literals`) without rows. Use `normalized_result.parent_evidence_id` to page
the original rows without reopening or decoding the file:

```json
{
  "source": {
    "kind": "retained-evidence",
    "evidence_id": "<parent_evidence_id>"
  },
  "view": {
    "kind": "il2cpp-metadata",
    "collection": "types",
    "offset": 0,
    "limit": 64
  }
}
```

Collections are `sections`, `images`, `types`, `methods`, `fields`,
`properties`, `events`, `parameters`, `string_literals`, `method_addresses`,
`return_types`, `field_types`, `parameter_types` and `code_gen_modules`. Every returned row includes
its source `index`, scoped by artifact SHA-256 and collection. All collections
accept batch `indices` and `fields`; collections whose rows have a `name` also
accept exact `names`. Types also accept `image_indices`, `namespaces` and
`declaring_types`; methods, fields, properties and events accept
`declaring_types`. Parameters accept exact `method_indices`, so a batch of
method indices retrieves their parameters without reading the entire parameter
table. `parameter_types` accepts the same `method_indices`, resolved through the
retained `parameters` owners; Evidence without `parameters` refuses that filter. Filters intersect, duplicate indices are returned once, and
rows retain metadata order. An empty filter selects no rows; `fields: []`
returns indices only. Omitted fields return the complete selected rows.

For example, after resolving a type index, retrieve selected method facts:

```json
{
  "source": {
    "kind": "retained-evidence",
    "evidence_id": "<parent_evidence_id>"
  },
  "view": {
    "kind": "il2cpp-metadata",
    "collection": "methods",
    "declaring_types": [1555],
    "names": ["SendMessage"],
    "fields": ["name", "declaring_type"]
  }
}
```

After finding method indices, parameters can be requested directly:

```json
{
  "source": {
    "kind": "retained-evidence",
    "evidence_id": "<parent_evidence_id>"
  },
  "view": {
    "kind": "il2cpp-metadata",
    "collection": "parameters",
    "method_indices": [9785],
    "fields": ["name", "method"],
    "limit": 64
  }
}
```

Historical Evidence that predates these member collections remains queryable.
A missing collection has an unknown (`null`) summary count, and requesting it
reports that it was not collected; it is never presented as an empty inventory. The same holds for Evidence that predates binary linking: its summary
omits `binary`, and `method_addresses`, `method_address_states`,
`return_types`, `field_types` and `parameter_types` counts are `null`.
Existing empty collections retain a zero count. Full Evidence is preserved.

`offset` counts matching rows, not source indices. `limit` defaults to 64;
`coverage.next_offset` continues that filtered page. Coverage describes retained
metadata facts only; runtime behavior and correspondence to native code remain
unknown. Each view preserves the parent Evidence link, artifact identity and
limitations. Queries work after the source file is removed. Select
`detail: "complete"` to return every row inline within the separate MCP response
budget.

## CLI

```bash
rea inspect-il2cpp-metadata /absolute/path/global-metadata.dat --json
```

The CLI defaults to complete Evidence. For compact delivery, explicitly preserve
the full Evidence in a new file:

```bash
rea inspect-il2cpp-metadata /absolute/path/global-metadata.dat \
  --detail summary --evidence_output /tmp/metadata-evidence.json --json
jq -c '{source: {kind: "inline", evidence: .records[0]}, view: {kind: "il2cpp-metadata", collection: "methods", indices: [9785], fields: ["name", "declaring_type"]}}' \
  /tmp/metadata-evidence.json > /tmp/metadata-query.json
rea inspect-analysis-view /tmp/metadata-query.json --json
```

Use the exported Evidence with the CLI's inline Evidence source format described
in [CLI and Evidence](cli.md#run-a-command). Compact delivery requires
`--evidence_output`; existing files are never overwritten. The full export
preserves every decoded row for subsequent queries without the original file.

`--binary PATH` links method addresses and `--architecture arm64|amd64` selects
the slice of a universal Mach-O.

## Observations

The result contains:

- `artifact`: path, SHA-256 and byte length;
- `magic`: unsigned little-endian header signature (`0xFAB11BAF`, delivered as a JSON number);
- `metadata_version`: `24`, `27`, `29`, `31` or `39`;
- `index_widths`: the serialized widths (1, 2 or 4 bytes) of
  `type_definition`, `generic_container`, `parameter` and `type` indices, and
  `type_width_source`. Version 39 derives the type index width from the
  `interface-offsets-record` or the `type-definition-record`; versions 24, 27, 29
  and 31 always use 4-byte indices (`fixed-width-version`);
- `sections`: all version-specific header sections in header order, each with `offset`, `size`
  and `count`. Versions 24 to 31 record no counts, so `count` is `null` and
  record counts come from the section sizes;
- `images`: `name`, `type_start` and `type_count`;
- `types`: `name`, `namespace`, `method_start`, `method_count`,
  `nested_type_start`, `nested_type_count` and `declaring_type`;
- `methods`: `name` and `declaring_type`;
- `fields`, `properties` and `events`: `name` and `declaring_type`, the type
  whose member range holds the row (`-1` when none does);
- `parameters`: `name` and `method`, the method whose parameter range holds it;
- `string_literals`: managed string literals as `value`, or `value_base64` with
  the exact bytes when they are not valid UTF-8;
- `limitations`.

A row's position in its collection is its metadata index, so `type_start`,
`method_start` and `declaring_type` refer to positions in `types` or `methods`.
`nested_type_start` instead indexes the metadata's `nestedTypes` table, which is
not returned; each nested type's `declaring_type` carries that relationship.
A type's `declaring_type` is derived from the `nestedTypes` section and is `-1`
for top-level types. The start of an empty range can retain the original value
`-1`.

The complete inventory of a large game is several megabytes and can exceed
the MCP response budget. Summary delivery and filtered, projected pages keep
unneeded rows out of agent context without discarding the source Evidence.

## Native method addresses

`binary_path` names the native binary built with the metadata: macOS
`GameAssembly.dylib` (Mach-O), Windows `GameAssembly.dll` (64-bit PE) or
Android `libil2cpp.so` (64-bit ELF, AArch64 or x86-64). A
universal Mach-O needs `binary_architecture` (`arm64` or `amd64`); a thin binary
rejects it. The file is read, never loaded or executed.

A position-independent `libil2cpp.so` stores zero in most pointer slots and
keeps the value in `R_AARCH64_RELATIVE` or `R_X86_64_RELATIVE` relocations
(`DT_RELA`). The reader writes those values into a private copy before
searching it, so addresses are the link-time addresses and RVAs are relative to
the first loaded segment. Android packed
relocations (`DT_ANDROID_RELA`) are refused. No target code is executed.

The binary's `Il2CppCodeRegistration` points to one `Il2CppCodeGenModule` per
assembly image. Each module record starts with its module name, its method
pointer count and its method pointer array. The reader finds, for every metadata
image, the single record whose name pointer reaches that image's name string and
whose count equals the image's method count. It then requires exactly one
`codeGenModulesCount`/`codeGenModules` pair that lists exactly those records. No
symbols are needed, so stripped builds work. A method's token row id selects its
slot in the module's method pointer array.

Module records establish names through their declared NUL-terminated string pointers. NUL/0xFF padding, spaces, Unicode and suffix-shared storage are supported. A pointer to a longer string does not match just its suffix; a pointer directly into a shared suffix may name it. Exact reversed UTF-8 matching avoids rescanning the file for every name and retains duplicate-name owners until module records resolve them. A contributor investigated a Linux
`GameAssembly.so` from Unity 2023.2.13f1 whose static registration was not located. When no static pair is resolved on x86-64, the reader searches executable ranges for bytes consistent with RIP-relative LEA/MOV references to module-array candidates. Exactly one referenced array candidate must remain. `code_gen_modules_field` is then `null`, and Evidence is **inferred**: instruction boundaries, the absence of a static registration elsewhere, and runtime use were not verified. The module records and slots themselves remain file observations. Static-table associations are **derived**. Otherwise the result is `code-registration-not-found`.

The binary/metadata pair is caller-selected. Name/count/token agreement is structural evidence, not a cryptographic same-build proof. File-offset locations refer to the primary metadata artifact; linked virtual addresses refer to `binary.artifact`. Both SHA-256 identities remain available in compact native pages as `artifact` and `binary_source`.

Contributor-reported verification (not all rerun by the follow-up): macOS arm64 and x86_64 slices from Unity 2021.3.45f2, 2022.3.30f1, 2022.3.62f3 and
6000.0.84f1 against dSYM symbols; Android arm64 and x86-64 from 2022.3.62f3
against `libil2cpp.sym.so`; Windows x64 from 2023.2.13f1 (metadata version 29,
the MIT-licensed game Between Two Worlds 1.0.5, `GameAssembly.dll` SHA-256
`a3ae7f6ecd1f671297b7d98d12713ef024062d93cd7a4205298102656c93b67a`) against
Il2CppDumper, where all 43,198 linked methods share an address with a
same-named Il2CppDumper method and identical code folding groups 10,448 methods
into 1,735 addresses. A macOS x86_64 build from Unity 2020.3.49f1 (metadata version 27, which Il2CppDumper reads as 27.1) links 10,555 methods, all at addresses where Il2CppDumper names the same method; its other addresses are generic instances. A build from Unity 2021.1.28f1 (also read as 27.1) gives the same result: 10,345 methods linked, every address named the same by Il2CppDumper, and its other 3,486 addresses generic instances.

These checks compare addresses with symbols or with another static tool. They
do not establish that a linked address is the code the game runs (a runtime may
patch, hook or replace it), that builds from other Unity versions, compilers or
obfuscators link the same way, or that a method without an address has no code:
generic instances, adjustor thunks and invokers are not linked, and an
`unknown` row was not looked up at all.

The result adds:

- `binary`: artifact identity, `format`, `architecture`, `image_base`,
  `code_gen_modules_field` (the address of `codeGenModulesCount`, or `null` as
  described above), `code_gen_modules_array` (the module pointer array) and
  `code_gen_modules` (`image`, record `address`, `method_pointer_count`);
- `method_addresses`: one row per method index with `state`, `address` and
  `rva` (address minus `image_base`), both hexadecimal strings. `state` is
  `code` when the module slot holds an unambiguously mapped executable address, `no-body` when an observed slot is zero,
  as for abstract, extern and most generic methods, and `unknown` when no type
  range in any image holds the method or a symbol relocation leaves its slot unresolved.
  `address` and `rva` are `null` unless `state` is `code`. The summary counts
  each state in `counts.method_address_states`. Ghidra seeds are written only
  for `code` rows.

- `return_types`, `field_types` and `parameter_types`: one row per method,
  field and parameter index with `type`, the index into the binary's
  `Il2CppType` table, and `name`, rendered from that table: C# keywords for
  primitives (`int`, `string`, `object`), `Namespace.Outer+Inner` for type
  definitions, `T[]`, `T[,]` and `T*`, generic instances as
  `System.Collections.Generic.List<string>` and generic parameters by their
  metadata name (`TKey`). A trailing `&` marks a by-reference type. `name` is
  `null` only for type index `-1`.

`binary` also records `types_field` and `types_count`: the address of
`Il2CppMetadataRegistration.typesCount` and its value. That record is found as
the single place whose `fieldOffsetsCount` and `typeDefinitionsSizesCount` both
equal the metadata type-definition count and whose type table is file mapped.

Without `binary_path`, `binary` is `null` and the four binary collections are
empty in the complete producer report to indicate unrequested observations. Their summary counts, including state counts, are `null`, and native page requests report unavailable observations. This does not establish an empty native inventory. Missing native fields in historical Evidence remain unknown too.

For metadata version 27, type names are `null` and only type indices are
reported: versions 27.0 to 27.2 share that header number but place the
Il2CppType byref flag in different bits, so a rendered name could gain or lose
`&` without warning.

The builds checked are listed after the module search rules above.

| Reason                            | Category    | Meaning                                                                                           |
| --------------------------------- | ----------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `unsupported-container`           | unsupported | Not a 64-bit little-endian Mach-O, PE or ELF image (ELF: AArch64 or x86-64 with dynamic section). |
| `slice-selection-required`        | unsupported | A universal Mach-O was given without `binary_architecture`.                                       |
| `slice-not-found`                 | unsupported | The requested slice is absent, or a thin binary was given an architecture.                        |
| `unsupported-pointer-encoding`    | unsupported | Mach-O chained fixups or Android packed (APS2) ELF relocations; pointers not decoded.             |
| `malformed-container`             | input error | The container headers are damaged.                                                                |
| `code-gen-modules-not-found`      | input error | An image has no module record; often a binary from a different build.                             |
| `ambiguous-code-gen-module`       | input error | More than one module record matches an image.                                                     |
| `code-registration-not-found`     | input error | No unique module table or executable-byte array candidate was resolved.                           |
| `invalid-method-token`            | input error | A method token is not a method row inside its module's pointer count.                             |
| `invalid-method-pointer`          | input error | A slot is unavailable or its nonzero address lacks unambiguous executable file coverage.          |
| `metadata-registration-not-found` | input error | No single MetadataRegistration matches the type-definition count.                                 |
| `invalid-type`                    | input error | A type index or `Il2CppType` record is out of range, unmapped or malformed.                       |
| `unsupported-type-kind`           | unsupported | A valid type kind has no implemented rendering.                                                   |

Format and selection failures name `binary_path`; capacity refusals remain typed resource errors. Failed linking preserves the metadata source identity, validated counts, selected binary path/architecture and its SHA-256 when observed, plus prior producer observations. It never publishes an incomplete native table as complete. The binary input is bounded to1GiB.

Scans yield cooperatively in bounded batches. Name-address retention and reverse-trie construction are each limited to65,536 entries/nodes and fallback module-array candidates to64 (`native-index-capacity`); exceeding capacity does not prove absence. Rendered type text has a64MiB UTF-8 cache-workspace guard, separate from the64MiB encoded-report admission, and64 nested rendering frames (`native-type-text-capacity` / `type-nesting-capacity`). Genuine cycles are malformed; unsupported type kinds are explicit coverage failures. Native row/text admission runs before allocation or retention. Unused generic parameter names are read on demand from the same stable metadata snapshot. There is no cross-inspection file cache; validated immutable Evidence is reused for session views.

ELF RELATIVE writes into zero-fill are kept as a private virtual-pointer overlay. Unresolved supported-width symbol relocations, including RELA PLT entries, remain unknown; stored zeros never establish no-body. COPY, TLS descriptor, REL, packed APS2 and other unsupported relocation encodings fail closed. Input bytes are unchanged.

Native address queries batch exact64-bit hexadecimal `addresses` and `states` (`code`, `no-body`, `unknown`), intersecting indices and pagination. Numerically equal address spellings match; original row indices and every shared-body alternative survive:

```json
{
  "source": {
    "kind": "retained-evidence",
    "evidence_id": "<parent_evidence_id>"
  },
  "view": {
    "kind": "il2cpp-metadata",
    "collection": "method_addresses",
    "addresses": ["0x180c56ed0"],
    "states": ["code"],
    "fields": ["address", "rva"],
    "offset": 0,
    "limit": 64
  }
}
```

## Ghidra function names

The CLI can turn a linked report into a
[`REA_GHIDRA_SEED_FILE`](installation.md) so Ghidra names every IL2CPP method
before auto-analysis:

```bash
rea inspect-il2cpp-metadata global-metadata.dat --binary libil2cpp.so \
  --ghidra-seeds il2cpp-seeds.tsv --json > /dev/null
export REA_GHIDRA_SEED_FILE="$PWD/il2cpp-seeds.tsv"
```

Each linked method becomes one `function` seed named `Namespace.Type$$Method`
(nested types joined with `.`, whitespace replaced by `_`), the Il2CppDumper
convention. Seeds are at `seed-base + rva`. The default base is where Ghidra's
loaders place the binary: `0x100000` for an ELF linked at 0, and the link base
for Mach-O and PE; `--seed-base 0x...` overrides it for a different import. When
identical code folding gives several methods one address, the first method names
the function and a `# folded <address> <kept> also <names>` comment line after
the seeds lists the others, so the kept name is visibly one of several. Ghidra still names a seeded function that is a thunk after its
target. The file is atomically published with exclusive creation; an existing destination is never replaced. Failed staging retains its cleanup owner for retry. Source digest and link/seed-base comments make the mapping inspectable. Unknown slots are skipped separately from observed no-body slots. `--seed-base` requires `--ghidra-seeds`; overflowing rebased addresses and names/outputs beyond the existing Ghidra protocol limits (2,000 name characters,32MiB file,1,000,000 entries) are refused before publication. The CLI and reusable service use one formatter and owned output workflow; ordinary MCP inspection remains read-only.

## Failures

A file whose magic is not `0xFAB11BAF` fails as an unsupported target with
`unrecognized-magic`. The file may be encrypted or may not be IL2CPP metadata.
A version other than 24, 27, 29, 31 or 39 fails as an unsupported target with
`unsupported-version`.

Damaged metadata returns an input error (`invalid_format`) whose
message names one reason:

| Reason                    | Meaning                                                                                                          |
| ------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `truncated-header`        | The file is shorter than the header.                                                                             |
| `unexpected-header-size`  | `stringLiterals.offset` is not the header size: 264 bytes for version 24, 256 for 27, 29 and 31, 380 for 39.     |
| `section-out-of-bounds`   | A section extends beyond the file, or a non-empty section starts inside the header.                              |
| `section-overlap`         | Two sections overlap. Zero-size sections are exempt and gaps are allowed.                                        |
| `record-size-mismatch`    | A section size does not divide into its records, or the record size differs from the one the index widths imply. |
| `type-index-width`        | The record used to derive the type index width implies no 1, 2 or 4 byte width.                                  |
| `index-out-of-range`      | A serialized index or range points outside its target collection.                                                |
| `nested-type-conflict`    | A type is listed as nested in two types, in itself, or in a cycle of declaring types.                            |
| `declaring-type-mismatch` | A method inside a type's method range names a different type, or a method lies outside its type's range.         |
| `image-range-overlap`     | Two images claim the same type definitions.                                                                      |
| `invalid-string`          | A name index does not start a string, or the name is unterminated or not valid UTF-8.                            |

A version field that disagrees with the file's layout, for example a version
39 file relabeled as 29, usually surfaces as `unexpected-header-size` or
`record-size-mismatch`.

Two checks are stricter than the IL2CPP runtime: a name index must start a
string, and an empty range's start must lie between -1 and the collection size.
Every Unity-written file checked so far satisfies both; metadata rewritten by
other tools may be rejected.

An incomplete inventory is never reported as complete. Failures after a verified
snapshot retain partial source Evidence with its SHA-256, byte length and any
validated section row counts; these counts do not establish that names and
relationships were decoded. A file that changes during reading and a cancelled
request keep distinct errors. Decode checkpoints yield for cancellation, and
close waits for active work. Each reader admits one inspection at a time.
Resource guards bound the selected file to 256 MiB and the encoded complete
report to 64 MiB, checking row counts before allocation and JSON/UTF-8/base64 expansion during
decoding, before serialization. Names and identical literal spans are decoded
once within one stable file snapshot; no filesystem results are cached across
inspections. Ownership assignment also yields to cancellation. MCP also applies its
[response transport budget](mcp-contracts.md); a complete report within the
report limit can still require the summary and paging path.

## Outside this tool

- Decrypting or deobfuscating protected metadata.
- Linking Mach-O binaries that use chained fixups, ELF images with Android
  packed (APS2) relocations, and 32-bit images; generic method instances,
  adjustor thunks and invokers.
- Full method signatures beyond the rendered field, parameter and return type
  names, generic method instances, and type names for metadata version 27.
- Running Ghidra or another disassembler. `--ghidra-seeds` only writes a seed
  file for [`REA_GHIDRA_SEED_FILE`](installation.md); use the
  [native workflow](native-investigation.md) for native code.
- Metadata versions other than 24, 27, 29, 31 and 39.

Names come from the metadata file only. They do not establish which methods
were compiled into the native binary or how they behave at runtime.

## Real producer verification

`npm run verify:il2cpp:metadata -- --metadata PATH` exercises a caller-supplied
`global-metadata.dat` through the public CLI and MCP. It is opt-in, like
`verify:pcap`, because no real game metadata ships with the repository. Normal
inspection does not need it.

The follow-up was checked against the public Cpp2IL
[`Simple_2022_3_35` sample](https://github.com/SamboyCoding/Cpp2IL/tree/b5ad444b82267cb1e4b88b8b373c008105bdea52/TestFiles/Simple_2022_3_35):
version 31, 1,892,268 bytes, SHA-256
`2441635a7c234a1a34deccc6a9906d6f5abcbdab078a38b2bf488a52a4962c48`.
An independent byte-layout oracle matched all 36 images, 2,468 types and 12,409
methods. Corresponding managed DLLs independently matched names and ownership
for 35 images, 2,463 types and 12,406 methods; the generated image has no matching
DLL. This does not establish real-producer coverage for versions 29 or 39.

Compact native summaries omit the `binary.code_gen_modules` table and keep its
count in `counts.code_gen_modules`. Query `collection: "code_gen_modules"`
with batch `image_indices` or source `indices`, selected `fields` and pagination.
Module row `index` is its retained collection position; `image` joins the
metadata image collection. Scalar registration facts and both source identities
remain inline. Complete Evidence retains the original full table.

```md
# Installation and setup

Run REA, connect your selected agents, and check the tools needed for your task.
Setup previews configuration changes and asks for approval before applying them.

| Task                              | Section                                                                                             |
| --------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Connect an agent                  | [Start setup](#start-setup), then [review changes](#review-setup-changes)                           |
| Diagnose one task                 | [Scoped readiness checks](#check-readiness-for-your-task)                                           |
| Configure an analysis engine      | [Hopper](#hopper), [Ghidra](#ghidra), the [IDA guide](ida-provider.md), or [Kuna](kuna-provider.md) |
| Update or remove REA              | [Maintenance](#diagnose-update-and-remove)                                                          |
| Resolve a client-specific problem | [Client configuration](client-configuration.md)                                                     |

## Start setup

```bash
npx rea-agents setup
```

Choose the agents to configure, review the proposed paths and changes, and
approve the plan. npm's package-download approval and REA's setup approval are
separate. Setup asks before changing agent configuration or installing Hopper.
Restart the agents named in the completion message. Quit Claude Desktop fully
before approving, because a running app can overwrite the registration; on
Windows, see [where Claude Desktop reads its configuration](client-configuration.md#claude-desktop).

For the latest published release, use `npx rea-agents@latest setup`.
[Package-runner and global-installation options](#package-runners-and-global-installation)
cover explicit versions, Bun, runtime requirements, and the curl wrapper.

## Review setup changes

`rea setup` first offers the supported agents in a multi-select. Existing REA
registrations are selected by default. Newly detected clients remain available
but unselected: detection gives setup context, not permission to add a new
registration. Clients without a detected configuration can still be selected.
Explicit `--client` flags skip this question.

Setup adds MCP access for selected clients. It installs REA's bundled workflow
with those integrations by default; use `--skill=false` to omit it. If no agent
is selected, setup offers the workflow separately for CLI use, with No as the
default. Hopper is a separate optional choice: setup shows its proposed
installation or connection and requires its own explicit approval. It can also
save verified paths for an existing Ghidra installation.

After selection, review the plan's exact paths and changes and approve before
REA writes files or installs Hopper. You can cancel at any prompt.

Before applying changes, REA checks your current configuration. The plan lists:

- an existing Hopper installation, a verified existing Ghidra installation, or the official Hopper package it proposes to install;
- each detected agent configuration path;
- each selected REA skill destination;
- external software, network origins, integrity evidence, and package-manager
  commands.

Malformed or unsafe existing configuration blocks the whole transaction before
Hopper installation or any file write. Declining or pressing Ctrl-C makes no
changes. Agent configuration writes preserve unrelated entries and comments,
create backups, stage changes in a private directory, and verify their result.
Before publication, they refuse detected changes to the selected configuration.
Replacement uses an explicit destination under the selected canonical parent;
it does not follow a newly inserted destination symlink. First-run setup uses
an exclusive hard link and fails without overwriting a newly created destination;
filesystems without hard-link support cannot publish a first-run configuration.
Setup and uninstall retain an existing `.rea.backup` rather than replacing the
first snapshot.
If that snapshot differs from the current configuration, setup and uninstall
preserve a verified `.rea.backup.<sha256>.recovery` copy of the current bytes
before editing; setup also previews it. Both snapshots remain available.
When an edit made a backup, a failed uninstall update or restore, and a failed
setup readback or rollback, name the backup path that holds the bytes from just
before that edit.
If setup cannot verify a newly created configuration, it retains the file and
reports manual recovery instead of deleting a pathname that may have changed.
For an existing configuration, setup and uninstall recovery refuse a detected
replacement or edit and name the recovery backup. Quit clients before editing their configuration;
these checks do not lock out another writer modifying the same file in place,
or exclude pathname changes between the final check and publication.
Setup also retains valid environment overrides in REA's existing server entry,
such as `REA_MCP_INPUT_SCHEMA_PROFILE`, `REA_MCP_OUTPUT_SCHEMA_PROFILE`, and
`REA_MCP_MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES`.
Detected provider settings replace only matching environment keys.
Setup and doctor report a malformed REA environment map or invalid runtime
setting before setup writes files. Repair the named setting in the client
configuration; setup does not silently discard the rest of the map.
This includes malformed loader/exclusion JSON arrays and a Ghidra compiler
specification without its required language identifier. Valid overrides keep
their original strings, including empty Hopper arguments. DeepSeek Harness
`!!js` environment expressions remain unevaluated and preserved; registration
alignment does not verify the runtime values those expressions will produce.
For layered OpenCode files, each file's values are checked before merging, while
setting dependencies are checked against the effective merged environment.
Setup preserves each layer's overrides instead of copying inherited settings
into the file it updates.

After setup, REA reports which agents, analysis tools, and workflow files passed
its final checks. Restart any agent named in the completion message, then begin
your investigation. Failed steps and diagnostics remain in terminal history.

Select exact clients in scripts with repeatable `--client` flags. Each explicit
client skips interactive selection. Use `--all-detected` only when you intend
to configure every detected supported client. `--skill=false` omits the
workflow, and `--dry-run` returns a read-only plan with status `planned` and
exit code 0:

```bash
rea setup --client codex --client cursor --skill=false --dry-run
```

Prompt UI and progress are written to stderr so stdout remains available for
structured results and pipelines. `NO_COLOR=1` disables color. Use
`--accessible` for sequential, vertically rendered yes/no prompts. Implicit
interactive setup requires stdin, stdout, and stderr to all be terminals; when
any stream is redirected, setup stays non-interactive. Declining or cancelling
returns status `cancelled` with exit code 0.

For automation, `rea setup --json` reports the plan and a compact `.doctor`
readiness projection without applying it. Use `rea doctor --json` for full
health diagnostics and canonical tool catalog details. Pair
`--yes` with explicit scope such as `--client codex`, or use
`--all-detected` when the broad scope is intended. Without a scope flag,
`--yes` is limited to existing REA-owned registrations; it does not select all
detected clients. An unapproved actual apply reports `needs_confirmation` and
exits 1. Installing missing Hopper non-interactively additionally requires
`--install-hopper`:

```bash
rea setup --yes --all-detected --install-hopper --json
```

### Skill destinations

The bundled skill is installed in each selected client's personal skill directory.
See [client configuration](client-configuration.md) for client-specific roots,
profiles, and environment overrides. A mixed selection plans each distinct
destination. Selecting the skill without a client uses `~/.agents/skills`.
Setup leaves existing skill copies in other locations untouched.
Setup refuses symbolic links at the selected skill directory or its managed
`references` directory, matching uninstall and update's ownership rules. Use a
regular skill directory, or select `--skill=false` to configure the client
registration without installing the bundled skill.
The final selected directories are checked before approval and again before
setup changes any client or Hopper installation. Unselected client destinations
do not block other setup choices. Doctor reports linked or non-directory skill
paths as `unmanaged`, names the affected paths, and provides those alternatives;
an unreadable skill identity remains `unknown`. Uninstall retains and reports
files it cannot safely remove, including their ownership manifest.

`rea setup --skill-client claude_code --yes --json` refreshes and verifies the
selected skill destination independently of MCP registration selection. The
final `doctor.scope.skill_clients` records which skill destinations were
checked; `doctor.scope.clients` continues to describe required registrations.
An unselected shared skill does not affect a client-only refresh.

`doctor --skill --json` verifies the selected copies against the bundled
instructions and references. Consumers should use `identity.skill.state`,
`installed_version`, and `installed_tool_count` for skill readiness. The
obsolete `installed_catalog_digest` field has been removed; current catalog
identity remains available at `identity.catalog`.

Setup pins package-runner MCP registrations to the exact installed REA version,
installs the matching skill and on-demand references in the same plan, and adds
`startup_timeout_sec = 30` for Codex and Grok Build. Codex also receives a
`tool_timeout_sec` derived from known provider startup plus operation headroom.

## Limit REA to one project or agent profile

Setup registers REA for the whole client. For Claude Code it writes
`mcpServers.rea` in `~/.claude.json` and installs the bundled skill under
`~/.claude/skills`, so every project that Claude Code opens can call REA. To
offer REA's tools only where they're wanted, use one of the routes below.

Both routes control which sessions discover REA's MCP server and skill. They
leave shell commands, filesystem access and network access available. An agent
under the same OS account can run `rea` from `PATH` or `npx` and read other
profiles and REA output. For clean-room separation, use an implementation
environment with filesystem and network restrictions that prevent reading or
fetching REA, the target and analysis output, including through shared
installations and package registries. A separate account or container must
enforce those restrictions.

For Claude Code, check existing default-profile state before choosing either
route. Setup is additive: a previous user-level REA registration and personal
skill remain active in other projects. Back up the default configuration and
REA skill first, then, with `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` unset, remove the REA user
registration with `claude mcp remove --scope user rea` and remove the known
REA-installed `~/.claude/skills/reverse-engineer-anything` directory. Preserve
unrelated registrations and skills. `rea uninstall` applies to other clients
as well, so it is broader than this Claude-only migration.

**A separate Claude Code profile.** Claude Code keeps settings, skills and session
history under `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`. Setup follows the same
variable: it writes the registration to `$CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/.claude.json` and
the skill to `$CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/skills`.
For REA setup, an empty `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` is treated as unset: registration
goes to `~/.claude.json` and the skill goes to `~/.claude/skills`.

```bash
CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=~/.claude-rea npx rea-agents setup --client claude_code
CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=~/.claude-rea claude
```

A new profile may need authentication. Console sign-ins without an API key are
stored outside `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`; see
[Claude Code authentication](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/authentication#log-in-with-multiple-accounts).
Sessions started without the variable use the default profile's registration,
skill and history.

Inline assignments apply only to that command. Keep the same prefix for every
profile check, setup rerun, update, or removal; bare commands use the current
environment and can otherwise inspect or recreate default-profile state:

```bash
CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=~/.claude-rea claude mcp list
CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=~/.claude-rea npx rea-agents doctor --client claude_code --skill --json
CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=~/.claude-rea npx -y rea-agents@latest setup --client claude_code --dry-run
```

After reviewing an update plan, rerun that same prefixed setup command without
`--dry-run` and approve its exact changes. Profile removal likewise needs the
prefix on `claude mcp remove --scope user rea` and any `rea uninstall` command;
keep the broader client scope of uninstall in mind. Restart the selected
profile after changing its pinned registration.

`claude mcp remove` removes only the registration. To remove REA from this
profile without running the broader uninstall flow, first back up the profile's
REA-managed skill directory, then remove
`$CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/skills/reverse-engineer-anything` as well. Keep other skills
in the profile intact.

The commands above use POSIX shell assignment syntax. In native Windows
PowerShell, select the profile for the whole setup/launch/check session and
restore the previous selection afterward:

```powershell
$previousClaudeConfigDir = $env:CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR
try {
  $env:CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR = Join-Path $HOME ".claude-rea"
  npx rea-agents setup --client claude_code
  claude mcp list
  npx rea-agents doctor --client claude_code --skill --json
  npx -y rea-agents@latest setup --client claude_code --dry-run
  # After reviewing the plan, repeat setup without --dry-run and approve it.
  claude
  # Profile removal, when intended, also belongs inside this selected scope:
  # claude mcp remove --scope user rea
} finally {
  if ($null -eq $previousClaudeConfigDir) {
    Remove-Item Env:CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
  } else {
    $env:CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR = $previousClaudeConfigDir
  }
}
```

Use PowerShell for these Windows examples rather than pasting POSIX assignments
into cmd.exe. Keep profile updates, readiness checks and removal inside the
same selected environment; the `finally` block restores the previous profile
or unsets the variable when it was absent.

**One project.** Install without configuring Claude Code: use the curl
installer's `--no-setup`, or run setup only for other clients. Then register
REA from the project directory at Claude Code's local scope.

This route uses the default Claude profile. Keep `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` unset for
the entire local lifecycle: registration, backup, listing, version replacement
and removal. In POSIX shells run `unset CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`; in PowerShell run
`Remove-Item Env:CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` before these
commands. Record an existing selection first if you intend to restore it after
finishing. The configuration path below is the default profile's
`~/.claude.json`; a different active profile uses its own config root instead.

Register with the variable unset:

<!-- x-release-please-start-version -->

```bash
claude mcp add --scope local rea -- npx -y rea-agents@6.7.0 mcp
```

On native Windows, use the same project directory and wrap the package-runner
shim so the stdio client can launch it:

```powershell
claude mcp add --scope local rea -- cmd.exe /d /c npx -y rea-agents@6.7.0 mcp
```

<!-- x-release-please-end -->

Local scope stores the entry under that directory's path in `~/.claude.json`,
so other projects don't load it. This route doesn't install the bundled skill.
Avoid `--scope project`, which writes `.mcp.json` into the repository where it
can be committed or copied. `rea doctor` and `rea uninstall` read only the
user-level entry, so they don't report or remove a local-scope registration;
remove it with `claude mcp remove --scope local rea` from the same directory.
`rea update` doesn't refresh it either, so it stays on the version it names.
To move it to a newer release, first back up the project entry in
`~/.claude.json` and record its environment and other metadata. In particular,
preserve caller-selected overrides such as `REA_MCP_INPUT_SCHEMA_PROFILE` and
`REA_MCP_MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES`. Run `claude mcp remove --scope local rea` from the
same directory, then recreate it with the platform-appropriate command above
and the new version. Reapply every recorded environment value with Claude
Code's `mcp add --env NAME=value` options and restore any other retained entry
metadata before restarting the project session. Removal and re-addition do not
preserve these values automatically. Running setup for Claude Code instead
would add a user-level entry for every project.

Check the separate profile with the prefixed `claude mcp list` above and compare
with the default profile with `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` unset. For local scope, run
`claude mcp list` from the selected project and again from another project.

## Check readiness for your task

Run `rea doctor` when you need diagnosis. It reads host prerequisites and agent
configuration without changing them. Without options, it audits every detected
registration, the installed skill and optional analysis engines; its overall
`healthy` value can be false while your chosen workflow works.

Doctor's `providerInspections` are host-level engine and registration checks,
not a readiness row for every advertised MCP adapter surface. `tools/list`
remains the complete stable catalog. Call `binary_session` with `{}` before
choosing an operation; it works before a target is opened, and
`result.tool_availability` reports per-operation availability, reasons and
client requirements for the current session state. It does not guarantee that
a particular caller-supplied input will be valid. See
[MCP discovery](mcp-contracts.md#identity-and-discovery).

Select the part you want to check:

| Task                                | Readiness check                                                          |
| ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Static JavaScript/Electron analysis | Run `rea analyze-javascript-application PATH --json` directly.           |
| One analysis engine                 | `rea doctor --provider ghidra --json` (or `hopper`, `ida`)               |
| One agent registration              | `rea doctor --client codex --json` (see [client IDs](#supported-agents)) |
| Installed workflow instructions     | `rea doctor --skill --json`                                              |

A scoped report has `scope.mode: "explicit"`. Its `scope_checks` determine
`healthy` and the exit status. Other checks appear in `informational_checks`;
`environment_healthy` summarizes the full audit. `--target` adds a target check,
but the report remains audit-wide unless a scope option is also supplied.

An invalid `REA_LOG_LEVEL` fails every scope, including one client or the
installed skill, because the executable rejects it before any command. A
selected client also fails for every other setting that MCP startup rejects,
including `REA_GHIDRA_STARTUP_TIMEOUT_MS` and `REA_HOPPER_STARTUP_TIMEOUT_MS`.
Those settings still fail a selected provider and the audit-wide result. A
skill-only report leaves them informational.

Follow the remediation for the failed check. If a native target has several
available providers, choose one with `--provider` on the CLI or `provider_id`
on `open_binary`. A `capability_unavailable` failure carries
`details.selection_reason`: `ambiguous` asks you to choose from
`details.candidate_ids`, while `provider_unavailable` asks you to repair the
selected engine. See [provider selection](cli.md#choose-a-provider).

### Linux owned-process prerequisite

On Linux, REA's shared process supervisor requires a procps-compatible `ps`
on REA's `PATH` for ownership checks before launching a child. Ghidra, JADX,
firmware tools and static JavaScript/Electron analysis use these checks.
Install your distribution's `procps` or `procps-ng` package, or put another
procps-compatible `ps` on `PATH` before
running those workflows. A missing or incompatible command causes a refusal
before the supervised child starts.

The public error code varies by caller: `capability_unavailable`,
`provider_unavailable` or `execution_failure`. Some provider adapters report
only a generic startup error. Check this prerequisite before following
provider-specific recovery advice.

## Diagnose, update, and remove

`rea doctor --json` is strictly read-only. `rea update` updates only the npm or Bun global installation that owns the running CLI. Source checkouts and package-runner copies must be updated through the mechanism that owns them; a fresh package-runner invocation can use `npx rea-agents@latest` or `bunx rea-agents@latest`. `rea uninstall` removes only REA-owned agent registrations and skill files; `--purge-data` additionally removes REA cache and state paths.

```bash
rea update
rea uninstall
rea uninstall --purge-data
```

Uninstall preserves Hopper, Node.js, Evidence files, captures, unrelated skills
and other MCP servers. Purging removes only REA's cache and state under
`~/.rea`. A client configuration that is malformed, unreadable, or at an unsafe
path stops the operation before anything is removed, and a client that fails
while being updated stops the remaining removals. Uninstall reports each
candidate `configuration_path` with its outcome. A client with multiple files
keeps their individual `actions` alongside its aggregate status and detail,
including earlier removals when a later file fails. The paths name
the discovered configuration candidates, not resolved physical file identities.
For JSON clients, uninstall removes every repeated `rea` member in the effective
server table only when each registration is REA-owned. An unowned earlier
member, or an unowned OpenCode V1 entry that removing V2 would expose, stops
preflight before any
removal. Repeats inside an inactive earlier copy of the server table stay
unchanged. A purge path that is a
symbolic link is retained and reported rather than followed. Uninstall checks
REA's managed shared and Claude Code personal skill locations. See the
[CLI guide](cli.md#output-and-exit-status) for exit statuses.

### Update the owning installation

`rea update` installs the exact resolved
release into the npm prefix or Bun global directory that owns the running
package, then checks the new executable's version before reporting success. It
does not reopen onboarding. For npm installations, release lookup and
installation both use npm's configured registry. Bun global updates require
Bun 1.2.17 or later, which introduced `bun info`. The updater checks `bun --version`
first and stops with an instruction to upgrade Bun manually if the version is
older or cannot be parsed; it does not upgrade Bun itself.
For supported Bun global installations, `bun info` and
`bun add --global --ignore-scripts` use Bun's configured registry
and run inside the owning Bun global directory (`BUN_INSTALL_GLOBAL_DIR`, else
`$BUN_INSTALL/install/global`, else `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/.bun/install/global`,
else `~/.bun/install/global`), never in the caller's current project. A Bun
global directory without its `package.json` is not treated as an owned
installation, because Bun would install into the nearest ancestor project
instead.
Its maintenance plan selects only existing REA registrations and an already
installed REA skill. Run the returned scoped setup command to review and approve
those changes, then restart affected agents. The plan is returned in terminal,
non-TTY, and JSON modes without applying configuration changes.

## Released package and main

Repository main documents its current code and generated catalog. `@latest`
selects the npm release, and persistent MCP registrations are pinned to the
version that performed setup. Installing newer instructions does not update a
running server or its registration.

The npm release checked on **2026-10-11** was **6.4.0**, published from
[`a56f7bb6`](https://github.com/morluto/rea/commit/a56f7bb668ab23fec8d33f7af353ac7ed2fe1895).
The actual registry package accepted dry-run setup plans for the 17 client IDs
in that release, including Qwen Code, Pi and Hermes. Seven client IDs are
included from 6.5.0 and were absent from the checked npm 6.4.0 package: `droid`,
`dsh`, `kimi`, `qoder`, `trae`, `workbuddy` and `zcode`.
The 6.4.0 registry check does not establish 6.5.0 publication or live DeepSeek
API integration.
OpenCode's plan selected
`OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR` even when that directory did not yet exist. These checks
used an isolated home on macOS with Node 24; they verify planning and argument
admission, without writing client configuration or establishing live integration
with every client. This resolves the npm 6.3.0 setup gaps tracked in
[#1650](https://github.com/morluto/rea/issues/1650).

Main's catalog describes the current code. A source build or a subsequent
release containing changes after this checkpoint is required for newer
functionality. Package startup alone does not verify a provider's real
platform workflow.

To check the published version, run `npm view rea-agents dist-tags.latest`.
Use the connected server's actual tool list and advertised input schemas for
feature selection. The same package version string in a development checkout
does not establish that its bytes match the npm tarball. Update a registration
through a reviewed, scoped setup plan, then restart/reconnect the agent.

## Skill-only installation

```bash
npx skills add morluto/rea --skill reverse-engineer-anything
```

This installs agent instructions and bundled references, not REA MCP
registration or analysis engines. Follow the skill's
[conditional connection guide](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/.agents/skills/reverse-engineer-anything/SKILL.md#connect-only-when-needed).
Working tools can be used immediately. If tools are missing, inspect the current
client's registration with `doctor --client codex --json` (substitute its client
ID), then plan repairs with `setup --client codex --dry-run --json`. Show and
approve the exact changes before applying that scope. An aligned registration
with tools absent from the active session needs a restart/reconnection;
`doctor` checks files and prerequisites, not the live agent connection.

Guided setup installs the package's matching skill by default. The skills.sh
route can select newer repository instructions, so follow actual server schemas
and the release boundary above. Static JavaScript CLI inspection can proceed
while MCP is unavailable:

```bash
npx -y rea-agents@latest analyze-javascript-application /absolute/path/to/app --json
```

It returns the complete Evidence record directly and requires no native engine.
Provider failures in doctor do not prevent unrelated target-free tools. To check
readiness for one task instead of auditing every integration, see
[Check readiness for your task](#check-readiness-for-your-task).

## Hopper

Hopper is separate commercial software with its own license. Its free demo has
vendor-defined limits, and a paid license is optional. REA reuses any detected
installation and preserves Hopper during uninstall.

The automated Hopper installer supports macOS 12+, Ubuntu 24.04+, Fedora 41+,
Nobara 44+, 64-bit Arch Linux, CachyOS, or Omarchy. REA itself runs on any
Linux distribution with a recognized apt, dnf, or pacman package family, where
an existing Hopper launcher is selected through `HOPPER_LAUNCHER_PATH`. Ghidra
and IDA have their own provider-specific host requirements; Windows Ghidra uses
the [experimental P0 boundary](windows-ghidra-p0.md).

On macOS, approved setup downloads the official DMG, checks its published size
and digest, validates the application bundle, and atomically installs it to
`~/Applications/Hopper Disassembler.app`. REA then opens Hopper so the
operator can choose its demo mode or activate an existing license. Homebrew and
administrator access are not used.

The Hopper launcher action used by REA creates a document from an executable;
its supported command-line interface does not attach to an already-open
document. While another live REA session owns the same target and loader
profile, a second session reports the owning run ID instead of opening a
duplicate document. On macOS, closing the owning REA session releases this guard;
Hopper keeps its document open. A later REA session can therefore open another
document for the same target. REA does not currently identify, focus, or reuse
that existing GUI document, and the supported launcher exposes no attach or
reuse action for it.

REA currently declines saved Hopper database (`.hop`) targets on macOS because
the native `open database` launch route does not run REA's bridge script. To
analyze that program with REA, select its original executable as the target and
open it through Hopper; this starts the supported bridge route. This does not
recover database-only annotations or analysis changes. Saved-database analysis
on Linux continues to use its supported demo-launch route.

Hopper lease directories must be readable and owned by the current user.
REA validates and secures an opened directory before reserving a lease. If
opening that directory fails with a permission error, the diagnostic identifies
the path and recovery steps while leaving its permissions unchanged. Check
ownership and parent-directory access, then restore owner-only read, write, and
search permissions (`0700`) on a directory you own before retrying.

On supported Linux distributions, approved setup verifies Hopper's official
`.deb`, `.rpm`, or Arch package before invoking the native package manager.
The official release feed selects the current public demo without a version
