`vendor/rea-docs/docs/javascript-runtime-observation.md`:

```md
# Passive Node and Electron runtime observation

REA can attach to an already-running Node.js or Electron V8 Inspector target
and retain script-load and execution-context metadata. The
`list_javascript_runtime_targets` and `observe_javascript_runtime` MCP tools
have equivalent `rea list-javascript-runtime-targets` and
`rea observe-javascript-runtime` commands. Successful calls return
deterministic Evidence.

Each request supplies the loopback Inspector endpoint and, for observation, the
target ID. This surface is separate from browser CDP, Electron file-page
inspection, and Process Capture:

```bash
rea list-javascript-runtime-targets http://127.0.0.1:9229 \
  --json
rea observe-javascript-runtime http://127.0.0.1:9229 TARGET_ID \
  --runtime-kind node --json
```

## Start a caller-owned Node target

Run your selected application with Inspector bound to loopback:

```bash
node --inspect=127.0.0.1:9229 ./app.mjs
```

Keep it running while listing targets and observing the selected ID. Use a free
port and the same literal endpoint in both REA calls. Stop the application
through its normal lifecycle when finished; REA disconnects but does not own or
terminate it. Node.js must already be installed.

Use `--inspect` for this passive workflow. `--inspect-brk` pauses before the
application starts, and REA never resumes it or sends
`Runtime.runIfWaitingForDebugger`. Resume a paused target with a separate
caller-owned debugger before requesting application runtime observations.

For a packaged Electron app, read
[`inspect_electron_fuses`](electron-fuses.md) before starting an `electron-main`
target. When `EnableNodeCliInspectArguments` is disabled or removed, Electron
ignores `--inspect` and `--inspect-brk`. A missing main-process target after
launch does not, by itself, show that fuse.

The caller supplies the literal-loopback HTTP endpoint directly. Selecting an endpoint exposes all targets it serves and their local script locations or renderer origins. A target must match the exact requested target ID and expose a same-port WebSocket reported by that endpoint. Targets explicitly marked attached are rejected rather than displacing another debugger. Node's `/json/list` omits attachment state, so REA preserves it as `null` (unknown), reports that limitation, and permits observation unless the endpoint explicitly reports `attached: true`. Local paths are canonicalized after symlink resolution.

The `attached` field in JavaScript runtime and browser target results is nullable: `true` and `false` are reported only when discovery supplied a boolean; `null` means the endpoint omitted or could not report the state. CDP `TargetInfo` worker records require an `attached` boolean; REA excludes a worker record with a missing or malformed value as an invalid protocol value.

`list_javascript_runtime_targets` returns every available target in one inline
array.

For the MCP follow-up call, pass the same literal-loopback endpoint and the selected target ID to `observe_javascript_runtime`. REA rediscovers targets and validates the ID against the live endpoint before observation.

### Discovery file locations

Node's `/json/list` reports a best-effort pathname prefixed with `file://`,
without URI encoding. On POSIX, REA interprets unambiguous paths literally,
including `#` and `%` in filenames. Node also replaces backslashes and double
quotes with underscores. That transformation cannot be reversed reliably:
an underscore may already be part of the original filename.

Windows paths, ambiguous underscore paths, and local discovery paths that
cannot be verified remain eligible by their endpoint and exact target ID.
Their target location preserves the reported value:

```json
{
  "kind": "unresolved",
  "reported_url": "file://C:_tools_entry.js",
  "reason": "unverifiable-file-location"
}
```

This location does not claim that a file exists or authorize reading its
contents. Listing remains HTTP-only. Observation resolves loaded script
locations independently from `Debugger.scriptParsed` file URLs, preserving
the existing checks for local files and encoded separators. Unsupported
schemes, remote file hosts, and a bare `file://` remain excluded. These Node
discovery rules do not apply to page targets or other runtime products.

Reconciliation retains an unresolved `target_location` object and reports
`runtime-location-unresolved` with unknown confidence for that target. It
does not derive a static match from the reported pathname; verified loaded
script locations remain available for independent matching.

## Passive protocol boundary

The provider sends exactly two protocol commands:

- `Runtime.enable`
- `Debugger.enable`

It never sends `Runtime.evaluate`, reads script source, installs breakpoints,
pauses or resumes execution, calls `Runtime.runIfWaitingForDebugger`, launches
the target, instruments JavaScript, or invokes Electron APIs. Closing a call
closes only REA's WebSocket.

Each WebSocket handshake and command response has its own 20-second deadline,
separate from the caller-selected observation window. A stalled handshake or
command reports `provider_timeout` and retains observations already received;
caller cancellation still reports cancellation.

The direct observations are:

- `Debugger.scriptParsed`, establishing that a bounded script location was
  parsed in the observed execution context;
- `Debugger.scriptFailedToParse`, retained only as a bounded invalid-script
  count;
- `Runtime.executionContextCreated`,
  `Runtime.executionContextDestroyed`, and
  `Runtime.executionContextsCleared`, establishing context lifecycle within
  the capture window. A created or destroyed event whose context ID is
  missing or not a safe integer adds no context record; it is retained only
  as a count reported in `unknowns`.

The Inspector protocol does not directly expose require/import caller edges,
EventEmitter emissions or listener invocation, Electron IPC messages or
handlers, or script-unload events. Those facts remain explicit unknowns.
`scriptParsed` proves script presence, not the importing module, feature
execution, initialization order, or causality.

## Node and Electron roles

The caller declares one role: `node`, `electron-main`, `electron-preload`, or
`electron-renderer`. Node and Electron-main declarations require a protocol
target of type `node`; preload and renderer declarations require `page`.
Inspector does not authenticate the operating-system PID or distinguish an
Electron role, so Evidence records the role authority as
`caller-declared-unverified`.

Electron main, preload, and renderer behavior can therefore be observed only
as separate Inspector targets. The provider does not infer that two
targets belong to the same Electron application.

## Capture and determinism

Capture retains valid script and execution-context metadata within an 8 MiB
aggregate budget, including conservative estimates for UTF-16 strings, record
and collection overhead, and projected URL fields. Each CDP message also has a
16 MiB transport limit. A message over that limit fails with `payload_limit`;
when the aggregate budget is reached, later metadata events are dropped and
the partial result reports `events_dropped`, `truncated: true`, and
`retained_metadata_budget_exceeded`. Repeated context transitions update the
current context record instead of accumulating duplicate objects. Scripts are
validated after capture, deduplicated by stable metadata, and canonically
sorted. Wall-clock timestamps and protocol script IDs are excluded from the
durable result, so identical inputs and captured metadata produce the same
Evidence ID.

Inspector attach is inherently incomplete. Enabling `Debugger` reports known
and uncollected scripts, but scripts collected before attachment may be
missing. Absence from the observation window never proves that a script or
behavior does not occur.

Cancellation stops new target-file authorization after the current filesystem
operation settles. Cancellation diagnostics retain the examined target prefix;
unexamined targets remain unknown. Observation cancellation keeps its original
reason and any completed Evidence. Finalization waits for REA's bounded socket
close (up to two seconds for graceful and forced confirmation). A failed close
retains its exact transport owner and blocks replacement connections until
cleanup succeeds; CLI finalization and MCP shutdown also retry retained cleanup.
Closing REA's connection does not stop the caller-owned runtime.

## Static correlation

Pass the resulting observation Evidence and an
`analyze_javascript_application` Evidence record to
`reconcile_javascript_runtime`. The reconciliation accepts this provider
alongside passive web and Electron page captures. Exact file or URL mappings
supplied with the request can correlate script presence with JavaScript Application Graph
assets. Because this provider never reads source bytes, matches normally use a
unique authorized location and remain weaker than captured-byte identity.
Builtin `node:` scripts remain runtime-only nodes unless a future explicit
static authority models them.

```

`vendor/rea-docs/docs/javascript-runtime-reconciliation.md`:

```md
# JavaScript static/runtime reconciliation

REA can combine an existing static JavaScript Application Graph with one or
more browser, Electron, or Node/Electron V8 Inspector observations while
preserving their different authorities. The `reconcile_javascript_runtime` MCP tool and
`rea reconcile-javascript-runtime` CLI command accept Evidence records and
return derived Evidence containing a combined JavaScript Application Graph
and explicit match, ambiguity, mismatch, and unknown classifications.

The operation performs no filesystem, browser, or Electron I/O. It accepts only
semantically verified Evidence produced by `analyze_javascript_application`,
`inspect_web_page`, `inspect_electron_page`, `observe_javascript_runtime`, or
`capture_electron_scenario`; matching operation names alone
is insufficient. Provider identity, predicate type, subject digest, target
parameters, and normalized-result schemas are checked before reconciliation.

`capture_electron_scenario` supplies target-only partial observations. It does
not establish loaded-script coverage; see [Electron observation](electron-observation.md).

## Workflow

1. Run `analyze_javascript_application` against exactly one application layer.
   Optional cache or assets directories can be analyzed independently and
   supplied as additional layers.
2. Run `inspect_web_page`, `inspect_electron_page`, or the attach-only
   `observe_javascript_runtime`, or supply existing `capture_electron_scenario`
   Evidence with the partial scope above. Capturing script sources is optional,
   but a source capture provides the strongest byte identity.
3. Pass the resulting Evidence records to `reconcile_javascript_runtime`.
   Browser URLs normally need an explicit URL-prefix mapping. Extracted
   Electron and V8 Inspector file locations are mapped automatically when runtime files remain
   beneath the analyzed input root; relocated files, ASAR projections, caches,
   and asset roots need explicit mappings.

The MCP input has this shape; the `analysis` and `runtime_observations` values
are complete Evidence objects, not only evidence IDs:

```json
{
  "static_layers": [
    {
      "role": "application",
      "analysis": "ANALYZE_JAVASCRIPT_APPLICATION_EVIDENCE",
      "runtime_mappings": [
        {
          "kind": "url-prefix",
          "prefix": "https://example.test/assets/",
          "artifact_prefix": "dist"
        }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "runtime_observations": ["INSPECT_WEB_PAGE_EVIDENCE"]
}
```

`static_layers` requires exactly one `application` role and permits additional
`cache` and `assets` roles. A `file-root` mapping translates a canonical runtime
filesystem root to an artifact-relative prefix. A `url-prefix` mapping does the
same for one exact HTTP(S) origin and path prefix. Mappings cannot add CDP
origins, broaden Electron roots, read files, or authorize source-map access;
they are caller-declared inference inputs applied only to already-authorized
locations.

The one-shot CLI accepts either a JSON file path or the same JSON inline. A
file avoids the operating system's command-line size limit for realistic
Evidence records:

```bash
rea reconcile-javascript-runtime reconciliation-input.json --json
```

For a repeatable local check from operator-provided paths, build first and run:

```bash
npm run verify:javascript-runtime -- \
  --application /absolute/path/to/app \
  --cache /absolute/path/to/cache \
  --runtime-evidence /absolute/path/to/electron-evidence.json \
  --mapping '{"layer":1,"kind":"file-root","root":"/runtime/cache","artifact_prefix":""}'
```

The verifier analyzes the supplied static paths, reads bounded Evidence JSON
files, and prints graph IDs, evidence IDs, paths, digests, counts, reasons, and
coverage. It does not print captured source text.

## Matching rules

Runtime targets, frames, scripts, and workers become capture-scoped graph
nodes. REA evaluates compatible static candidates conservatively:

1. A captured-source SHA-256 plus one matching mapped location yields
   a content-and-location match.
2. When no static candidate exists at a mapped location, one unique exact
   content digest can match. Whole-asset digests and reconstructed module-factory source
   digests remain distinguishable in the reported basis.
3. Without captured bytes, one unique mapped artifact path can produce a
   medium-confidence location match.
4. Multiple candidates remain `ambiguous`; no `observed_as` edge is emitted.
   With captured source and mapped candidates, only mapped content matches
   qualify; unrelated content matches elsewhere are excluded.
   `candidate_static_count` reports the full qualified layer/node count, and
   `candidate_static_nodes` includes every unique candidate reference.
5. If captured bytes disagree with the static candidate at the mapped path,
   the result is an explicit mismatch. An equal digest elsewhere cannot hide
   that disagreement. If a mapped candidate's digest is unavailable and no
   mapped content match is known, the comparison remains `unknown`.
6. Missing authorization mappings and incomplete or truncated input coverage
   remain unknown or truncated rather than becoming absence claims.

Every successful cross-layer `observed_as` edge has
`authority: cross-layer-reconciliation` and `state: inferred`. The underlying
artifact/AST observations and runtime observations remain unchanged and
retain their own Evidence links.

## Loaded, resident, and not observed

Static JavaScript assets, chunks, and modules receive a separate load-state
classification:

- `loaded` means an accepted runtime script correspondence was found, using
  exact bytes or one unique mapped location;
- `resident-in-loaded-asset` means a containing asset was observed, but the
  embedded module was not independently observed or shown to execute;
- `not-observed-in-capture` means the entity did not appear in the complete
  authorized captures supplied to this call and its artifact path falls beneath
  an exercised automatic or operator-declared mapping prefix;
- `unknown` covers incomplete captures, layers outside runtime scope, and
  unresolved correspondence. Nodes outside a mapped artifact prefix stay
  unknown even when another prefix in the same static layer was observed.

None of these states proves feature execution, initialization order,
reachability, or causality. In particular, `not-observed-in-capture` never means
globally unloaded.

## Frames, workers, and source maps

Passive inspection retains the execution-context frame ID supplied by CDP
for each accepted script. Electron captures also inventory authorized worker,
service-worker, and shared-worker targets, including bounded opener-target and
parent-frame relationships. These fields improve attribution while preserving
the original exact-origin or canonical-root filter.

V8 Inspector observations expose execution-context IDs but no authenticated
frame relationship, so their scripts attach to the exact runtime target in the
combined graph. They never supply source bytes, require/import caller edges,
EventEmitter activity, Electron IPC, or script-unload evidence. A unique
authorized file or URL location can still correlate script presence with a
static asset, but it does not prove module initialization or feature execution.

Source-map declarations and original-source reads remain static evidence. They
are reported in `source_map_authority` but never used
as primary runtime byte matches. A source name or `sourcesContent` digest is not
silently equated with the generated bytes observed by CDP.

## Bounds and determinism

The workflow does not impose aggregate count caps on static layers, passive
captures, runtime entities, reconciliation items, static load states, runtime
mapping declarations, or candidate references. These collections remain
subject to the structural validation applied to each Evidence record and
application graph; passive observation returns all in-window collection items
that pass per-value validation. Reconciliation reports zero
omitted items when it projects the complete supplied inputs. Static JavaScript
analysis can still report its own bounded AST coverage as partial or truncated.

Layers, captures, nodes, edges, matches, and evidence links are canonically
ordered. Repeating the same verified Evidence and mappings produces the same
reconciliation, graph, and Evidence identifiers.

## Non-goals

Reconciliation does not attach to CDP, fetch scripts or source maps, execute
JavaScript, invoke Electron IPC, inspect native add-ons, infer arbitrary URL
rewrites, or search the filesystem. It does not replace the older
`correlate_static_and_runtime` investigation tool: that tool records explicit
cross-version static/runtime comparison hypotheses, while this operation maps
JavaScript runtime instances to static application-graph entities.

```

`vendor/rea-docs/docs/jeb-analysis.md`:

```md
# JEB instrumentation and analysis

REA exposes JEB-backed project, unit, and decompilation inspection through the CLI and MCP, served by JEB's own MCP interface. JEB is a bring-your-own engine: REA never installs it, launches it, or opens its project databases itself.

## Bring-your-own engine

Start a JEB client that serves MCP and point REA at it:

- Default endpoint: `http://127.0.0.1:8425/mcp`. Override with `REA_JEB_MCP_URL` (absolute `http`/`https` URL with literal host `127.0.0.1` or `[::1]`; redirects, remote hosts, credentials, query strings, and fragments are rejected rather than silently dropped).
- In the JEB GUI client, start the MCP server from the _File_ menu (or via the VIBRE assistant).
- Headless, the official Linux CE build `5.48.0.202610071539` supports `-c --mcp`. From the JEB installation directory, select JDK 21 or newer through `JAVA_HOME`, choose your target and bind explicitly to loopback:

  ```sh
  "$JAVA_HOME/bin/java" -jar bin/app/jeb.jar -c --mcp --interface=127.0.0.1 \
    --port=8425 --infile=/absolute/path/to/target
  ```

  Complete the vendor's first-use EULA and license-key activation when prompted. The Linux audit used an isolated installation, a 1536 MiB Java heap and one active processor inside a separately bounded process family; JVM heap limits alone do not bound the whole family.

- JEB's documented programmatic route (`JebMcpServerInstance` from the JEB API) remains an alternative. The earlier licensed 5.48 headless verification used that route because its CLI did not accept `--mcp`. Check your installed build's `-c --help` and live tool catalog; the version number alone does not establish the launcher options or supported operations.

For setup registration, set `REA_JEB_MCP_URL` in the REA process environment
before running `rea setup`. The approved setup plan preserves the exact selected
URL after validating its syntax. That validation does not establish that the
JEB service is reachable or that a project is open; use the existing
`inspect-jeb-client` command for a read-only service query.

MCP `binary_session` probes the live JEB service and its advertised tool catalog.
Availability is reported per operation: a reachable headless client can support
inspection and decompilation while refusing `open_jeb_project`. Catalog discovery
uses one 60-second deadline across connection and pagination; a responsive server
cannot keep discovery running indefinitely by returning more pages.

Each upstream tool call has an absolute 60-second request deadline by default.
Set `REA_JEB_MCP_TIMEOUT_MS` to a positive decimal number of milliseconds to
select a different per-request budget, for example `REA_JEB_MCP_TIMEOUT_MS=300000`
for a five-minute decompilation. This budget starts after discovery and applies
to each individual `tools/call`; it does not extend the separate catalog deadline
or establish one end-to-end deadline across a whole CLI or MCP operation. A
request that reaches its budget returns a typed timeout, while caller
cancellation remains a cancellation.

Earlier verification used JEB 5.48.0 (Linux x64, licensed build) serving `jeb-mcp-server` 1.3.0 over streamable HTTP. The official Linux x64 CE build `5.48.0.202610071539` was also verified through real CLI and production stdio MCP native-code workflows; see the [Linux CE audit](../experiments/analysis-efficiency/jeb-linux-native.md) for measurements and limits. CE verification does not establish licensed/Demo Android decompilation or GUI behavior.

## Operations

| MCP tool / CLI command                      | Purpose                                                                                                                         |
| ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `inspect_jeb_client` / `inspect-jeb-client` | Engine version, GUI or headless mode, startup time                                                                              |
| `open_jeb_project` / `open-jeb-project`     | Open or create a project from an artifact or `.jdb2` on the engine host; returns input-file SHA-256 digests and top-level units |
| `list_jeb_units` / `list-jeb-units`         | Page units by stable path and type (`filter`, `parent-unit-path`, `index`, `count`)                                             |
| `decompile_jeb_item` / `decompile-jeb-item` | Decompile one type or method to engine pseudo-code                                                                              |

All four preserve target-file bytes. `open_jeb_project` selects or creates an engine-side project; analysis queries can populate computed analysis within it. Evidence records the endpoint, caller-selected parameters, and available engine-reported digests. Mutation workflows the engine also offers (renames, comments, `save_project`, `close_project`) are intentionally not exposed yet.

**Engine coverage note:** The earlier licensed 5.48.0 headless verification did not advertise `open_project`; it selected the target when the engine client started. For that build, use `--infile` on the programmatic launcher or open the file in the GUI. The audited CE headless catalog also omitted `open_project`; the verified CLI route above selects its input at startup. Use `binary_session` to inspect the current engine's advertised operations. REA preserves an unavailable tool's refusal; `open_jeb_project` requires an engine that advertises `open_project`. The CE audit does not establish GUI project-opening support.

## Semantics

- Paths in `open_jeb_project` are resolved by the JEB process, not by REA; REA does not require the artifact to exist locally.
- The engine caps `list_units` pages at 100; a full page is reported as `coverage: "partial"` because more units may exist. An empty remainder is `complete` only when fewer units than requested were returned.
- When `decompile_jeb_item` omits `unit_path`, the engine implicitly selects the project's first code unit; REA reports `unit_path: null` and a limitation instead of guessing the effective unit.
- `item_address` is a JEB code-item reference, such as a value returned by the engine's `list_code_items`. Preserve that representation and select its code unit explicitly. For the audited CE SQLite unit, the exported method reference was `sqlite3_libversion_number`; using its raw ELF symbol address did not produce a successful decompilation. File offsets, ELF virtual addresses and engine item references have different semantics. REA currently exposes unit listing, while code-item discovery remains an upstream JEB operation.
- Engine refusals (`success: false` envelopes) are preserved as unsupported-target errors carrying the engine's own message, for example a nonexistent item address.
- Successfully parsed client information is reused for the lifetime of the MCP connection, including when the engine omits its version. Explicit client inspection and availability probes refresh it.
- An unreachable endpoint is a provider-availability failure with recovery guidance; REA does not retry or spawn the engine.

Real-engine verification lives in the JEB lane described in [testing.md](testing.md); mock transport tests do not establish real-engine compatibility.

`vendor/rea-docs/docs/kuna-provider.md`:

```md
# Kuna provider

[Kuna](https://github.com/Noelo-Lab/kuna) is an Apache-2.0 decompiler distributed as one `kuna` executable. REA uses a `kuna` you supply. It does not download, install, update or bundle Kuna. REA verified this provider with Kuna 1.833; it accepts other releases and reports them as unverified in `rea doctor` and in each analysis profile.

Kuna is static: it reads the selected image and never executes it.

## Configure

```bash
export REA_KUNA_COMMAND=/absolute/path/to/kuna
rea doctor --provider kuna
```

Select it explicitly with `--provider kuna`, MCP's `open_binary.provider_id: "kuna"`, or `REA_ANALYSIS_PROVIDER=kuna`. With Kuna and another provider configured for the same target, `auto` reports `ambiguous` instead of choosing one.

Ordinary readiness cancellation returns `cancelled` (CLI SIGINT/SIGTERM exits
130/143); an earlier recorded timeout or physical failure keeps its diagnostic.
Completed version, hash and script observations remain in `kuna_installation`
with `status: "partial"` and `completed_hash` when available. Typed errors carry
this in `details.diagnostics`; doctor cleanup checks carry it in their `details`.
Omitted fields remain unobserved; availability remains unknown until readiness
completes. Cleanup retries keep both the observations and the exact file owner.

| Setting                       | Default                                                                                                                                 | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| ----------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `REA_KUNA_COMMAND`            | none (required)                                                                                                                         | Absolute path of the `kuna` executable.                                                                                                                                                  |
| `REA_KUNA_CACHE_DIR`          | `~/Library/Caches/rea/kuna` (macOS), `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/rea/kuna` (Linux; `~/.cache/rea/kuna` when `XDG_CACHE_HOME` is unset or relative) | Absolute directory REA owns for project exports. Kuna's own spec cache also lives here, not in your Kuna cache.                                                                          |
| `REA_KUNA_CACHE_MAX_BYTES`    | 4 GiB                                                                                                                                   | Size cap; least recently used exports are evicted above it.                                                                                                                              |
| `REA_KUNA_PROJECT_TIMEOUT_MS` | 30 minutes                                                                                                                              | Deadline for whole-program inventory/export, reference and string scans.                                                                                                                 |
| `REA_KUNA_TIMEOUT_MS`         | 120 s                                                                                                                                   | Deadline for one single-function decompile, and for the inventory run REA makes when the export ends without one.                                                                        |
| `REA_KUNA_JOBS`               | 1                                                                                                                                       | `decompile-project --jobs`. 1 is Kuna's reference answer; more jobs finish sooner but lose callee-first prototypes, and change about 40–60% of function bodies on the measured binaries. |

A single-function decompile, inventory, string, graph or xref run that exceeds its deadline fails as `provider_timeout`, naming the setting that owns the deadline and that raising it takes a restart. A project export that exceeds `REA_KUNA_PROJECT_TIMEOUT_MS` is an export failure instead: requests that need the export report `capability_unavailable` with the export's own retry guidance.

Windows is not supported yet. Supported targets are ELF and thin Mach-O executables for x86-64, AArch64 and ARM; PE and universal Mach-O are rejected with a typed reason.

## What Kuna answers

| Tool                                                        | Source                                                                                                                           |
| ----------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `list_procedures`, `search_procedures`, `procedure_address` | Kuna's callable inventory (`kuna functions --json`), including import slots it does not decompile                                |
| `address_name`                                              | Function entries, then the data labels Kuna's export assigns                                                                     |
| `procedure_pseudo_code`, `batch_decompile`                  | The project export, or a single-function run while the export builds                                                             |
| `procedure_assembly`                                        | The project export's labeled listing                                                                                             |
| `procedure_callers`, `procedure_callees`                    | Call-kind edges from a lazy, body-free Kuna graph; synthetic import nodes are accepted by address                                |
| `list_strings`, `search_strings`                            | Typed string candidates from one cached, reference-free scan; exact-address, literal and ECMAScript regex selection              |
| `xrefs`                                                     | Exact-address incoming reference sites, with forwarding aliases filtered explicitly                                              |
| `analyze_function`                                          | Pseudocode and assembly from the export, plus call relationships; typed references, comments, strings and CFG remain unavailable |

Typed procedure references, basic blocks, raw-memory tools, annotations and type recovery are not available from this provider. Use another provider for those operations.

## How answers are produced

The first text or assembly request in a session looks for this target's export in the cache. `list_documents` reads the selected path without initializing analysis. Inventory, function lookup, string queries, call relationships and xrefs do not start a C export. A data-name lookup starts it only when the address is absent from the function inventory. The export is keyed by the target's SHA-256, the Kuna executable's SHA-256, its version and `--jobs`.

- **Warm cache:** analysis reads reuse the verified export. A fresh server verifies its file digests once, even for concurrent first requests; that cost scales with export size.
- **Cold cache:**
  - REA starts `kuna decompile-project` in the background on a private copy of the target.
  - Meanwhile, pseudocode comes from one `kuna decompile --addr` run. Name and address lookups, and listings, use the inventory the export takes with `kuna functions --json` before it decompiles. The session runs `kuna functions` itself, under `REA_KUNA_TIMEOUT_MS`, only when no export is building (an inventory-only request does not start one) or the export ends without an inventory.
  - Requests for the same function share one run; it stops when its last waiting request is cancelled. Each run analyzes the whole image again in its own process, so one REA process runs at most as many at once as the host has cores beyond `REA_KUNA_JOBS` (at least one). Further requests wait in order, and a waiting request is answered from the export if it finishes first. A run whose stop REA cannot prove keeps its slot until `close_binary` proves it stopped.
  - The session keeps each completed single-function text, up to 16 MiB in all with the least recently used dropped first, and answers repeats from it until the export can. After a failed export that lasts for the session.
  - Assembly and data names wait for the export; progress notifications report the wait every ten seconds. A session does not rebuild a failed export: requests that need it fail with `retryable: false`, the export's failure, its captured Kuna output and what to change before reopening the target. A setting such as `REA_KUNA_PROJECT_TIMEOUT_MS` or `REA_KUNA_JOBS` is read when REA starts, so changing it also needs a restart. Pseudocode keeps using single-function runs.
  - A single-function answer says so in its limitations. It lacks the export's whole-program prototypes, so a later request can return different text for the same function.

Pseudocode, assembly, `analyze_function` and data-name answers record where their text came from in `raw_result.source`: `single-function`, or `project-export` with the cache directory. `procedure_pseudo_code` and `procedure_assembly` answers from the export also name the file, byte span and the file's SHA-256. Combined `analyze_function` answers retain both facet records in `raw_result.source.files`, each with its file, digest and byte span. Both texts come from one export; losing that project retries the complete report. Listings and procedure lookups carry no `raw_result`. Agents can open or search the export's `.c` and `.asm` there directly when that is cheaper than calling a tool per function. Text read that way is target-derived, like any decompiler output, but it bypasses the untrusted-content marker that REA's tool results carry.

The background export belongs to the session. `close_binary`, or the end of a CLI command, cancels it unless another session still waits for it. A one-shot CLI decompile therefore answers from a single-function run; any request that needs the export, such as `procedure_assembly` or `analyze_function`, keeps it.

The assembly label index is scanned once per export reader. Cancelling a request stops its wait without interrupting other readers; closing the session aborts and drains the shared scan before releasing its files.

Regex procedure and string search uses ECMAScript Unicode matching in a cancellable worker with a five-second matching deadline. Literal matching remains the default. Cancellation or a matching deadline leaves the session available.

Single-function subprocess output and each cached source facet share a 16 MiB buffered-text capacity. Cached spans are checked before allocation; larger text remains in the local export and the error identifies the file and range. `analyze_function` initially returns the complete dossier, which can still be large; later retained views do not remove that first transfer. Prefer the individual text tools for a focused question.

## Strings

`list_strings` and `search_strings` share one lazy `kuna strings --json --encoding all --min-length 5 --termination any --no-xrefs` scan of the digest-checked private input. Skipping references avoids program lifting, a call graph and a C export. REA validates the input, scan policy, every row and the total before caching any facts. Encoding, character count, byte length and terminator facts must agree; supplementary UTF-8 characters count as Unicode scalars. Malformed output is an error, not an empty search. REA parses the JSON as Kuna writes it instead of buffering it, so the scan has no fixed size: Kuna writes about 290 bytes per row, 31 MB for a 20 MB Ghostty binary and 179 MB (611k rows) for an arm64 Firefox `XUL`. Rows are validated one at a time, and the first contradiction stops Kuna. Text REA does not keep is dropped unassembled; kept text and retained rows are admitted against the REA process's live heap headroom as they arrive; a refusal is a `memory` resource constraint with `retryable: false`, and closing other targets or starting REA with a larger Node.js heap makes room. String scans use the whole-program `REA_KUNA_PROJECT_TIMEOUT_MS` deadline; `REA_KUNA_TIMEOUT_MS` applies to single-function decompilation. The parsed inventory belongs to one selected target/executable profile and expires on session close; Kuna diagnostics beyond their 8 MiB buffer are retained as a failure until close, while other failures are not cached.

Results keep exact u64 virtual addresses, decoded text, native encoding, terminator status and byte length including any terminator. Kuna scans mapped sections or segments for runs of at least five characters; unterminated fragments can include instruction bytes. `all` includes ASCII, UTF-8 and the engine's Latin-range UTF-16LE reading. Other text, including short strings, non-Latin wide text and UTF-16BE, can remain undiscovered. An empty result does not prove absence.

Use `search_strings` for the matching rows or `list_strings` with an exact address for that location. The validated inventory is sorted by numeric address and encoding. Once cached, exact-address reads use binary search and return every encoding at that address without scanning the full inventory or retaining another lookup index. Literal and regex matching run in REA, preserving the existing case and ECMAScript Unicode semantics instead of substituting Kuna's different regex dialect. Procedure and string regex queries share one worker slot per session. Input projections are materialized only after admission, so queued queries retain no per-query inventory arrays. Close cancels and drains matching. Native metadata queries also share one admission slot, including references; a failed stop retains admission until cleanup is proven.

`raw_result.strings` reports the source JSON digest/size, scanned scope, extraction policy, complete inventory count and selected count without copying unrequested text into the answer. Omit the address from `list_strings` to retrieve the complete inventory as Evidence; normal session retention and bundle export apply, including transport-capacity errors for oversized inline replies. These operations preserve their complete-result contracts and do not add paging. Function-referenced string facets in `analyze_function` remain unavailable; call `xrefs` explicitly when references to one returned string are needed.

## Calls and references

The first call query runs `kuna decompile-graph --functions ''`, admitting no C or assembly bodies. One validated graph and forward/reverse indexes serve later call queries and existing `get_call_graph` / `trace_call_path` workflows. Numeric u64 addresses are parsed from their original JSON tokens. Only `call` edges become callers/callees; jumps and data references retain their distinct meaning. Graph counts, edge endpoints and ordering are validated before any relationship is returned. A forwarding address may be an instruction inside a function, so it is retained separately and never promoted to a function node or call edge. Reported indirect calls make affected relationship coverage partial; no target is invented for them.

`xrefs` runs native `xrefs --to ADDRESS --json` on demand. Kuna unifies forwarding aliases and suppresses edges internal to their class; REA filters to the requested address and records the excluded-row count. Duplicate source sites appear once. An empty result cannot establish the absence of references. Addresses are explicit u64 values or exact, unambiguous procedure names; Kuna has no cursor.

REA parses the graph as Kuna writes it, like the string scan, so the graph has no fixed size: a 53 MB Raycast binary produces 157 MB (180k functions, 773k edges), which REA retains in about 93 MB after a whole-program walk of about a minute. Unrequested bodies are refused before any of their text is assembled, and edges are indexed as they arrive, so retained rows and their indexes are admitted against live heap headroom. Xref JSON admits at most 16 MiB before parsing. Output or Kuna diagnostics beyond a buffer are reported as a `memory` resource constraint with `retryable: false`, because the same target and executable produce the same output. The session remembers such a graph failure, so later call queries fail at once instead of repeating the whole-program walk. The graph is cached for the selected target and executable profile within one session. Xref reuse is an LRU charged by source bytes plus metadata, limited to 16 MiB and 128 entries; at most eight distinct native xref queries may be pending. Reference commands run one at a time per session and share the provider's foreground budget with single-function decompiles. An unproven process stop retains its admission slots until cleanup succeeds. Concurrent callers share work, individual cancellation releases only that waiter, and the last departing waiter cancels its producer and receives any unproven cleanup. Session close aborts and drains producers, releases parsed caches and retries any retained process/file cleanup.

Evidence includes only selected addresses or dossier neighbors, the producing JSON's SHA-256/byte count, coverage and relevant function facts; unrequested program-wide JSON and instruction text are omitted. Reference caches are in memory and expire on close: a fresh CLI process or MCP server rebuilds them. A first call query therefore costs a whole-program reference walk even when a C export is warm. These operations do not establish full Ghidra/IDA feature parity.

Failures from shared installation or inventory work identify the operation the
caller requested. `diagnostics.producer_operation` retains the internal producer
name when it differs. Caller-specific failures keep the producer's typed outcome,
captured output, partial facts and live cleanup dependencies; cleanup retry
updates every projection rather than preserving an independent stale marker.
Installation acquisition is shared, with independently cancellable caller waits.
The final departing caller stops the probe and joins its cleanup; session close
also stops and joins acquisition. A cleanly cancelled acquisition can be retried,
while a retained cleanup failure blocks replacement until its owner is closed.
Shared string and reference queries preserve caller cancellation reasons and
join the final departing caller's command cleanup. A command cleanup error keeps
its typed primary failure and captured output. Its live resource list follows
both process and workspace ownership: proving process exit does not prove that
the private workspace was removed, and retry updates earlier caller errors.
If workspace setup fails, an unsuccessful rollback retains the original target
or read failure together with its cleanup owner. Replacement stays blocked until
that rollback is resolved; a clean rollback permits another setup attempt.

## Provenance and limitations

- Addresses and bytes are Kuna's observations of the image. Procedure entries and extents are its derivations: extents are upper bounds clipped at the next entry, and Kuna can split one function at an entry its own analysis infers. Pseudocode is its reconstruction, never original source.
- Pseudocode and assembly are exact Kuna text; text from Kuna and from another provider is not comparable as equal or different.
- Results are re-read rather than replayed from REA's analysis snapshots, because a cold answer can differ from the export's.

## Cache ownership

REA writes Kuna's exports only inside `REA_KUNA_CACHE_DIR`:

- `projects/<key>/` holds published, immutable exports with a manifest of file digests.
- `staging/` holds builds whose processes may still be live.
- `trash/` holds retired builds and evicted exports awaiting removal.
- `home/` is Kuna's HOME.

Builds publish by one rename, so a reader sees a complete export or none. A session keeps the export it uses from eviction only within its own REA process. If another REA process sharing the cache evicts it, the session rebuilds it; meanwhile pseudocode falls back to single-function runs. A damaged or edited export is removed and rebuilt. Staging moves to `trash/` for removal only after REA proves its Kuna process stopped. Staging of a process it cannot prove stopped is never swept; REA keeps it owned, retries the stop on `close_binary`, and reports it until the stop is proven. Failed file removal also stays bound to its export and is retried by `close_binary`; closing does not report success while that cleanup remains. `rea doctor --provider kuna` reports the cache directory without creating it.

## Verify with a real Kuna

```bash
REA_KUNA_COMMAND=/absolute/path/to/kuna npm run verify:kuna
# Compare with Ghidra on caller-built binaries
REA_KUNA_COMMAND=/absolute/path/to/kuna GHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR=/absolute/path/to/ghidra \
  npm run verify:kuna -- --targets DIR --functions inflate,crc32 --compare-ghidra
```

The lane compiles a small source-owned fixture with the host C compiler and verifies the MCP workflow end to end. `--targets DIR --functions a,b` adds caller-built binaries. `--compare-ghidra` (with `GHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR`) runs those same functions through Ghidra; it requires `--targets` and `--functions` and refuses empty matrices or requested function names missing from every target. See [testing](testing.md#kuna-lane) for coverage.

Failed runs also report process-lineage evidence and exit unsuccessfully. If provider or transport cleanup is unconfirmed, the report says `cleanup: "incomplete"` and records `retained_workspace`; that directory is preserved for investigation and cleanup retries.

```

`vendor/rea-docs/docs/managed-code-analysis.md`:

```md
# Managed-code analysis

REA inspects .NET PE/CLI artifacts without loading or executing their code.
It can identify an assembly, inspect metadata and CIL, compare members across
builds, and connect declared native calls to supplied native-analysis evidence.
CIL is Common Intermediate Language, the instruction format used by managed
assemblies.

The seven shipped tools are:

| Task                                                                        | MCP tool                            |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| Identify an artifact and its managed deployment form                        | `inspect_managed_artifact`          |
| Inspect types, signatures, method bodies, calls, and field access           | `inspect_managed_members`           |
| List declared native calls and native implementation indicators             | `inspect_managed_native_boundaries` |
| Compare members across builds and map build-local tokens                    | `compare_managed_members`           |
| Check native call declarations against supplied export or function evidence | `verify_managed_native_boundaries`  |
| Import decompiled code against verified static member identities            | `import_managed_reconstruction`     |
| Add managed findings to an application graph                                | `project_managed_application_graph` |

Each has a matching CLI command: replace underscores with hyphens and prefix
the name with `rea`, for example `rea inspect-managed-artifact`.
Native-body bridge mapping and managed runtime execution are outside the
current tool set.

The canonical tool inventory is the
[build-generated catalog](mcp-contracts.md#generated-catalog).

## Inspect an assembly

```bash
rea inspect-managed-artifact /absolute/path/Assembly.dll --json
rea inspect-managed-members /absolute/path/Assembly.dll --json
```

Use the artifact result to identify the assembly and its metadata coverage.
Member results retain build-local tokens, signatures, CIL bodies, and decoded
relationships. Use an exact reported `full_name` with `--type` when a focused
inspection is needed; see [selected member inspection](#selected-member-inspection).
Compare separate builds with [member comparison](#member-comparison), preserving
their paths, digests, and selection scope.

### Metadata overview and retained rows

The existing CLI and omitted/complete MCP detail return complete metadata
inventories. For identity and classification questions, select
`inspect_managed_artifact` with
`{"path":"/absolute/path/Assembly.dll","detail":"summary"}` on the first call.
This keeps the complete source in the session and returns a distinct linked
`inspect_analysis_view` overview with complete PE/CLI, classification and its
evidence, metadata status, module/MVID, assembly, frameworks, returned-row counts,
coverage/issues and limitations. No assembly is loaded or executed.

Use `normalized_result.parent_evidence_id` to page original rows:

```json
{
  "source": {
    "kind": "retained-evidence",
    "evidence_id": "<parent_evidence_id>"
  },
  "view": {
    "kind": "managed",
    "collection": "attributes",
    "offset": 0,
    "limit": 16
  }
}
```

Collections are `references`, `resources` and `attributes`; rows retain their
original values, nulls, order, metadata tokens and offsets. Pages retain source
metadata status and coverage. Exhaustion covers the returned parent collection,
not all possible metadata, and empty rows under partial/unavailable metadata do
not establish absence. Tokens are build-local and require the recorded artifact
SHA-256 and known module MVID for cross-observation matching.

Retained views do not repeat the parser or require the source file to remain
available. Portable views use the authenticated original Evidence inline,
including the existing `inspect-analysis-view` CLI. Session record lifetime and
export/import semantics remain unchanged. A server without Evidence retention
rejects selected summary before analysis; complete delivery remains available.

### Member summary and retained member rows

Complete `inspect_managed_members` delivery always includes the assembly-wide
`member_refs` and `exported_types`, which `type_names` does not narrow, so even
one selected or unmatched type can return megabytes. Select
`{"path":"/absolute/path/Assembly.dll","type_names":["Namespace.Type"],"detail":"summary"}`
to keep the complete source in the session and receive identity, metadata
status, the selection with its unmatched names, coverage/issues, the separate
user-string coverage, limitations and per-collection counts. Then page original
rows with view kind `managed-members`:

```json
{
  "source": {
    "kind": "retained-evidence",
    "evidence_id": "<parent_evidence_id>"
  },
  "view": {
    "kind": "managed-members",
    "collection": "call_edges",
    "offset": 0,
    "limit": 64
  }
}
```

Collections are `types`, `exported_types`, `fields`, `methods`, `member_refs`,
`call_edges`, `field_accesses` and `user_strings` (the literals). Each page names
its collection, retains original rows, order, tokens, signatures and body facts,
and carries the source selection and coverage; `user_strings` pages carry the
literal pool's own coverage. Older Evidence that never examined exported types
or user strings reports a null count and refuses those pages rather than
returning an empty one.

## Shipped scope

The canonical parser admits PE/CLI bytes and their metadata/CIL without loading
an assembly. It reports observed implementation markers and unavailable facts;
it does not unpack .NET single-file hosts or infer a NativeAOT identity from an
ordinary native PE. It does not decode IL2CPP; use
[IL2CPP metadata](il2cpp-metadata.md) for the image, type and method names in a
Unity `global-metadata.dat`. Inputs without admitted CLI metadata do not
become managed assemblies through naming or routing guesses.
Inspect separately obtained components explicitly and preserve their identities.

A valid implementation marker establishes a candidate native boundary, not
recovered native semantics or runtime behavior.

An assembly targeting [.NET Standard](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/net-standard)
declares API compatibility across multiple .NET implementations. REA preserves
that target in `target_frameworks` and leaves `runtime_family` as `unknown`
unless independent markers identify a runtime family, such as a ReadyToRun
signature.

### Resource admission

The static provider admits regular input files up to 128 MiB before retaining
their bytes. Reads remain bounded if a file grows after admission. Metadata,
CIL decoding, and projected inspection records have a separate conservative
64 MiB representation budget; shared heap strings are cached, but repeated
output occurrences still consume that budget. These are inspection resource
policies, not PE format limits or a hard bound on total V8 heap use.

Path-based member comparison uses the same per-input snapshot policy and
inspects its two selected paths sequentially, retaining each inspection rather
than both full byte snapshots. The limit therefore remains a per-file resource
admission rule, not an aggregate comparison limit. Comparison Evidence keeps
the caller-selected paths as its parameters and artifact locations.

Input overflow returns a resource constraint. Decode or projection overflow
reports `resource-limit` with unavailable or partial coverage; omitted facts do
not become empty observations. Ambiguous PE section mappings are rejected
rather than interpreted according to section order.

### Selected member inspection

When whole-assembly member decoding reaches the representation budget, select
known declaring types before their signatures and CIL bodies are decoded:

```bash
rea inspect-managed-members /absolute/path/Assembly.dll --type Example.Parser
```

MCP uses `inspect_managed_members` with
`{"path":"/absolute/path/Assembly.dll","type_names":["Example.Parser"]}`.
Repeat `--type` or supply multiple unique `type_names` for several types.
Names match the reported `full_name` exactly. Top-level names are namespace
qualified; nested types currently report bare names, which can select several
types with that name. Each type's `enclosing_type_token` records its enclosing
TypeDef. `nesting_read` distinguishes complete source rows (true), incomplete
current rows (false), and historical Evidence (null). A null enclosing token
alone does not establish that a type is top-level.
Each selected type also retains `name_sha256`, a framed digest of its namespace,
name and enclosing names. It uses the same bounded, cached owner as signature
type operands and remains available when selection omits the enclosing types.
It adds one fixed-size digest per returned type rather than repeated name paths.

The result preserves the requested names in `selection.type_names` and reports
unmatched names separately. If metadata names are unreadable, limitations retain
that uncertainty. With no selection, `selection` is null and whole-assembly
inspection keeps its existing resource policy. Selection restricts types,
fields, methods, call edges, field accesses and user strings; member references
remain an assembly-wide inventory, so output size is not guaranteed to be small.

Coverage describes the selected members. Comparisons leave members outside the
opposite observation's selection unknown, and application graphs report their
selected scope as partial. Neither makes an absence claim about the whole
assembly. Older member Evidence without `selection` remains readable.

### User strings

`ldstr` anchors keep their build-local `0x70` tokens. `user_strings.literals`
lists each distinct token loaded by an inspected method body once, in token
order, with its `#US` file offset and decoded value. Values keep their stored
UTF-16 code units, including unpaired surrogates. Token `0x70000000` names the
heap's empty entry at offset 0 and reads as `""`; any other item there is
malformed. The terminal flag is checked against ECMA-335 II.24.2.4, and the
length prefix against the width II.23.2 assigns. A difference is reported with
its byte offset as a user-string issue while preserving the readable literal.
Toolchain conventions can differ; this conformance observation does not
establish runtime rejection. A missing `#US` stream is one stream-level issue;
a malformed item is reported against its token. User strings carry their own
coverage: any of these makes `user_strings.state` partial and lists the issue
in `user_strings.issues`, while the member `coverage` and `metadata.status` are
unaffected, and readable literals remain. The state is also partial when an
inspected method's CIL was not fully decoded (a malformed exception section
alone does not count) or a method that may belong to the inspected types was
not inspected (its row could not be read, or its type's name could not be read
under a `type_names` selection), because `ldstr` instructions there were not
observed. Normalized CIL digests do not include decoded values.
`compare_managed_members` does not decode or compare literals: an unchanged
method does not establish unchanged strings, and the comparison says so in its
limitations. Older member Evidence without `user_strings` reads as `null`: not
examined.

### Edge target declaring types

`member_refs[].parent_name`, `call_edges[].target_declaring_type`, and
`field_accesses[].field_declaring_type` name the type that declares each
target. Referenced spec signatures validate encoded type coordinates against
the metadata tables, including nested type arguments and custom modifiers.
TypeRef resolution scopes are checked transitively with cycle detection;
readable names survive malformed scopes as partial evidence.
TypeDef and TypeRef names use the namespace-qualified `full_name`
form, and nested types keep bare names. A generic-instantiation TypeSpec
parent names its generic type, such as ``System.Collections.Generic.List`1``.
Other well-formed TypeSpec forms and ModuleRef or MethodDef parents stay
`null`. A `method-spec` call edge reports the name and declaring type of the
generic method it instantiates. A field access is named only by a field or a
field-signature MemberRef. TypeSpec and MethodSpec blobs are decoded with the
member-signature grammar, and a MethodSpec must instantiate a generic method
with as many type arguments as it declares. Malformed or unsupported rows and
blobs, and arity mismatches, make coverage partial. A readable MethodSpec
method column that names a method, or a TypeRef whose resolution scope is
invalid, keeps its name.
Older member Evidence without these fields reads them as `null`: unknown.

## Analysis objective

Start by identifying the artifact with `inspect_managed_artifact`, then inspect
its types and CIL with `inspect_managed_members`. Use [member comparison](#member-comparison)
for another build, and [managed/native boundary rules](#managed-native-boundaries)
when matching declared native calls to supplied native Evidence. Static inspection
does not load or execute the assembly. Reconstructed structure and unresolved
native/runtime questions retain their own authority and coverage.

## Member comparison

Names and semantic labels do not establish durable member identity. Comparison
preserves observed differences, structural inferences, and unknowns separately.

Cross-version matching first pairs members of the same declared type and name.
A current declared type uses its observed `name_sha256`, so same-named nested
types in different enclosing types stay distinct even in selected inventories.
Malformed, missing, contradictory, cyclic or over-deep enclosing identity remains unknown;
the comparison preserves display names without using them to repair that gap.
Historical observations retain an explicitly limited bare-name mode when either
side predates the identity facts. A known current identity gap still remains
unknown beside a historical observation. Matching then pairs
methods by exact CIL/signature identity, then by signature, then by
structural body shape; fields by signature. Exact CIL/signature identity
requires equal raw CIL digests and decoded fingerprints. Equal decoded
fingerprints alone cannot establish an exact match: they omit switch targets
and collapse distinct NaN encodings. Only then may a remap pair a
renamed or moved member across declared types or names: a method by exact
CIL/signature identity or structural body shape, a field by exact decoded
signature. A remap never takes a member whose own declared type and name remain
unpaired on the other side, so a member is never taken from its own changed
counterpart. A member whose declared identity is unresolved could belong to any type. It
never makes a declared-identity pair, and any remap group it joins stays
ambiguous. Unresolved same-named counterparts prevent definitive added/removed
claims, while observed names and tokens remain available in the result.
The exact-signature key uses names only as part of that
full tuple; names alone never select a pair. Duplicate tuples remain ambiguous
rather than being paired by token order. Every round compares signatures by
`resolved_sha256`: the raw signature with each TypeDef or TypeRef operand
replaced by a digest of that type's namespace and name, hashed as separate
values so `A` + `B.C` differs from `A.B` + `C`, after its enclosing types for a
nested type (`Outer/Inner`). The defining assembly is not part of the name:
a TypeDef and a TypeRef with the same namespace and name compare as the
same nominal name, and a TypeRef's ResolutionScope assembly is ignored, so a type
forwarded from one assembly to another still pairs. Two different types with
the same full name in different assemblies therefore have equal name digests.
Comparison reports this scope limitation inline; it does not establish CLR
type identity or runtime binding equivalence.
Nesting deeper than 64 levels is not named, and such a signature compares by
its raw digest. Comparison keys keep resolved and raw digests apart, so a raw
digest never pairs with an equal resolved one.
Raw signature bytes name types by metadata row, and rows are build-local, so
the same signature usually has different raw bytes in two builds. A signature
that names no types resolves to its raw digest. When an operand cannot be
resolved, such as a TypeSpec, or when REA could not parse the signature, the
raw digest stands in. Missing or unreadable TypeDef and TypeRef operands are
reported as coverage issues. Invalid NestedClass rows retain their failure
reasons and withhold TypeDef signature identities; type names and nesting are
parsed once by their shared owner. Each current inspection records
`signature_resolution: "type-names-v1"`, even when none of its operands can be
resolved. Historical Evidence defaults this attestation to `null`. When either
observation predates resolution, both sides compare raw digests, which pair only where type rows agree,
and the comparison reports that limitation. The signature is exact whether or
not REA decoded it, so undecoded signatures pair by that tuple too, but they
never enter structural rounds. An unmatched member is therefore reported as
`unknown`, not added or removed, when its own signature was not decoded or when
the other side has an unpaired member, one-sided or ambiguous, with the same
declared type and name whose signature was not decoded. When both observations
attest type-name resolution, a decoded signature that still compares by its raw
digest is treated the same way: an unmatched member with one, or beside an
unpaired same-named member with one, is `unknown`, because its raw bytes name
types by build-local row. A matched unresolved signature also remains unknown
unless another observed dimension establishes a change; identical row bytes
can reference different TypeSpec contents. Its resolution limitation is retained
even when another dimension changes.

For a matched method, an unavailable or partial body makes body-shape facets
unknown while preserving observed signature differences. For complete bodies,
a difference in either the raw CIL digest or the decoded fingerprint is reported
in the `cil` dimension, including reordered switch targets with equal decoded
fingerprints. Structural identity compares resolved signatures, the limited
decoded-CIL tuple fingerprint,
constants, and bounded shape context. It reports all candidates at the winning
score and remains ambiguous when the evidence does not distinguish them. The
digest does not itself remap metadata tokens.

Tokens are always remapped through observed structure. A caller cannot carry
`0x06001234` into a new MVID and assume it names the same method.

## NativeAOT metadata recovery

NativeAOT removes the ordinary CIL method bodies, so a CIL decompiler cannot
reconstruct those bodies as C# source. The executable remains a native target
for Hopper or Ghidra, where decompilation produces pseudocode and analyst
inference. This is a different route from ordinary managed member inspection.

NativeAOT is not limited to Windows `.exe` files. The native image can be PE,
ELF, or Mach-O, and NativeAOT can also publish shared libraries (PE DLL, ELF
`.so`, or Mach-O `.dylib`) with explicitly exported entry points. Identify the
image from its bytes and loader metadata, not its filename extension. When the
image is inside an application bundle, inventory or extract the bundle first
and carry the component identity into native analysis. Matching PDB, ELF debug,
or dSYM sidecars can add symbol evidence when the selected provider supports
them; verify their identity and keep them separate from observations made from
the executable itself. [Microsoft's NativeAOT overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/deploying/native-aot/)
lists supported OS/architecture targets and deployment limitations, while its
[native library guide](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/deploying/native-aot/libraries)
describes exported shared-library entry points.

REA offers a built-in read-only snapshot parser for x64 PE/RTR 9.1 metadata and
an optional Linux headless Ghidra adapter for annotations and broader recovery.
The adapter requires a locally built `REA_GHIDRA_NATIVEAOT_JAR`; REA does not
install it or its toolchain. The [NativeAOT guide](ghidra-nativeaot.md) defines
these routes, their layout/host restrictions, derived-memory provenance, and
verification coverage.

REA's experimental Windows Ghidra boundary admits native x86, x86-64, ARMNT (Thumb-2) and ARM64 PE
applications and DLLs for static analysis. For x64 PE NativeAOT, the read-only
parser also runs there; the [NativeAOT guide](ghidra-nativeaot.md) lists what a
Windows host covers.

For NativeAOT analysis, preserve the selected native artifact's path and digest
and report recovered type data with its returned provenance. Linking those types
to native function addresses requires verified
provider evidence; names or vtable similarity alone do not prove that a native
function implements a specific managed method.

<div id="managed-native-boundaries"></div>

## Managed/native boundary rules

`verify_managed_native_boundaries` compares declared P/Invoke module and entry
point identities with supplied native export or function evidence. Name/module
matches establish declaration links; they do not establish that a call executed.
When either side lacks a usable module identity, a matching name remains
unresolved and retains the candidate evidence; REA reports a module mismatch
only when both identities are available and differ.

Metadata tokens are not native addresses. Native body mapping for C++/CLI,
ReadyToRun, NativeAOT, and IL2CPP requires separately verified format and provider
support. The managed static tools do not recover those mappings. The optional
[Ghidra NativeAOT extension](ghidra-nativeaot.md) has its own supported boundary.

Declared import inventory supports a bounded positive claim. Its absence does
not exclude dynamic resolution, generated code, protected code, native helpers,
or server-side behavior.

## Evidence record shape

Member comparison, application graph projection, and managed/native verification
authenticate supplied inspection Evidence and check that any subject SHA-256
matches the normalized artifact SHA-256. A valid Evidence ID alone does not
establish that those two identities agree. Evidence without a subject remains
usable, with no subject digest available to cross-check.

Artifact inspection returns the selected path, byte length and SHA-256, observed
PE/CLI classification, assembly and module identities, and metadata coverage.
Member inspection binds build-local tokens, signatures, row offsets, method
bodies, and decoded relationships to that artifact and MVID. Missing or malformed
facts remain explicit in coverage and per-member status.

Metadata table streams may carry the CLR-compatible `ExtraData` extension
(`HeapSizes` flag `0x40`), which Microsoft readers honor although it is not
specified by ECMA-335. REA skips its fixed four-byte word after the row counts
before decoding table rows; the word's value is not a length. An incomplete
word is reported as a metadata coverage failure at its file offset, without
reading beyond the declared table stream.

For unoptimized `#-` metadata, nonempty `FieldPtr` and `MethodPtr` tables
translate TypeDef list positions to physical member definitions. REA resolves
these indirections for member ownership and local attribute-constructor types;
field and method tokens still identify the original definition rows.
`field_list` and `method_list` retain the metadata's list coordinates, which
refer to the pointer table when present rather than necessarily contiguous
definition rows. Invalid or nonmonotonic list coordinates and malformed or
ambiguous pointers leave affected owners unknown with partial coverage while
preserving readable member and attribute facts.
The retained inverse indexes are admitted against the existing representation
budget before allocation.

`exported_types` reports ExportedType rows as declared. Facade assemblies such
as .NET `System.Runtime.dll` provide their types this way: `forwarder: true`
marks a type forwarder, and `implementation_token` names the AssemblyRef, File,
or enclosing ExportedType row that implements it. REA does not load the
implementing assembly to resolve the forwarded definition, and
`compare_managed_members` does not compare exported types. Member Evidence
recorded before this field existed reads back with `exported_types: null`,
which means the table was not examined.

CLI `#GUID` heap values retain their exact 16-byte GUID text. REA does not impose
RFC 4122 UUID version or variant bits on MVID, EncId, or EncBaseId because
ECMA-335 metadata does not require those bit patterns. Tokens and RVAs are
build-local coordinates, not durable cross-build identities or native addresses.

## Decoded-CIL fingerprint

`inspect_managed_members` exposes two method CIL hashes with different byte
boundaries:

| Field                  | Input                                                                                                     | Excluded from the digest                                                                                                                                      |
| ---------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `il_sha256`            | The exact `il_size` raw CIL bytes after the tiny or fat method header                                     | Method header, locals signature blob, alignment, and extra sections including exception clauses                                                               |
| `normalized_il_sha256` | UTF-8 `JSON.stringify` output for the instruction-order array of `[opcode, operand_kind, operand]` tuples | Instruction offsets except projected scalar branch targets, switch targets, resolved metadata/string identities, method header, locals, and exception regions |

The normalized field is available only when the entire CIL stream decodes with
status `present`. A malformed or absent body reports `null`. The tuple format
is defined here.

Tuple operands use these exact projections:

- operand-free instructions: `none` and `null`;
- metadata and user-string operands: the build-local token as lowercase
  `0x`-prefixed eight-digit hexadecimal;
- scalar branches: the target CIL byte offset as a decimal string;
- `switch`: the case count as a decimal string, without target offsets;
- signed integer and variable operands: decimal strings; floating-point
  operands: JavaScript's `String` representation of the decoded IEEE value.

Opcode names retain short/long forms and prefix opcodes. This makes the value a
reproducible decoded-tuple fingerprint, not a canonical semantic CIL identity:
it does not resolve tokens across MVIDs, does not commit full control flow or
exception semantics, and does not replace the raw CIL digest. Cross-build
comparison requires equal raw CIL digests as well for exact CIL/signature
matches and reports ambiguity when structural evidence is insufficient.

For example, a decoded `nop; ret` body serializes exactly as
`[["nop","none",null],["ret","none",null]]` and has digest
`5e5fad7741cb44bca3a4f045546b7449990da343f612f5f34c0ca30e9eee0636`.
This vector specifies the tuple order, `null` handling, absence of whitespace,
UTF-8 encoding, and lowercase hexadecimal output.

## Tool and packaging boundary

The production parser is REA-owned TypeScript and ships with the existing Node
application. Deterministic conformance uses source-owned byte-built PE/CLI
fixtures and expected semantic facts. An optional real ILSpy lane runs only when
its executable is explicitly supplied; the default lane does not establish
independent pinned-oracle parity. Production inspection needs none of those tools.

- `ICSharpCode.Decompiler`/`ilspycmd` can supply reconstruction inference.
  A BYO reconstruction import records the supplied version
  and remains non-canonical. When `REA_ILSPY_CMD_PATH` points to an absolute
  runnable `ilspycmd`, `verify:managed` runs a source-owned real ILSpy oracle
  and imports its C# output as reconstruction inference against exact static
  member Evidence.
- The package contains no .NET runtime, SDK, ILSpy installation, proprietary
  assembly, or compiled conformance fixture.
- Setup never installs or upgrades those tools. Doctor may inspect an explicit
  optional path without changing it.

Real-tool downloads used in development or CI require exact package coordinates
and SHA-256 lock entries. They are cached outside the source tree and restored
into isolated directories. Updating any coordinate requires review of license,
runtime, supported host, output contract, and conformance results.

Target platform is not host support. The canonical parser must inspect
Windows-produced PE/CLI bytes on REA's supported Linux and macOS hosts with the
same result. Pinned Windows oracle jobs may provide additional conformance, but
they do not claim that the REA application itself supports Windows. Native
ReadyToRun, C++/CLI, NativeAOT, or IL2CPP coverage is additionally constrained
by the selected Hopper/Ghidra host and format matrix.

## Conformance verification

The current lane uses source-owned byte-built fixtures and malformed-input
regressions, with optional operator-supplied applications and ILSpy verification.

Run the deterministic lane with `npm run verify:managed`. See
[testing](testing.md#real-toolchain-verification-lanes) for prerequisites and
coverage. Generated outputs belong outside tracked fixture directories and must
not remain after verification or packaging.

Verification compares semantic facts, not decompiler text. It checks resource
ceilings, deterministic ordering, complete cleanup, CLI/MCP parity, Evidence
commitments, packed-package behavior, and target-free MCP startup. A parser and
an oracle disagreeing on malformed input is investigated explicitly; one tool's
acceptance does not automatically make the bytes valid.

## Operator-local osu! benchmark

The optional osu! benchmark accepts only paths and expectations supplied by the
operator. Run it with:

```sh
REA_MANAGED_APP_MANIFEST_PATH=/absolute/managed-app-manifest.json npm run verify:managed
```

`verify:managed` always runs a source-owned manifest-verifier self-test first.
If `REA_ILSPY_CMD_PATH` is set to an absolute `ilspycmd` path, it also runs a
source-owned ILSpy oracle: version discovery, class listing, bounded C# output
for a pinned fixture type, and import through `import_managed_reconstruction`.
The verifier prints only command/version, executable and output digests,
Evidence IDs, method locks, and compact fixture identity; it does not print
decompiled C# text. A failing ILSpy oracle fails the verifier because it is an
explicit real-tool claim, but leaving `REA_ILSPY_CMD_PATH` unset keeps the
oracle disabled.

When `REA_MANAGED_APP_MANIFEST_PATH` is set, the manifest's target path may be
absolute or relative to the manifest file. A compact manifest contains:

```json
{
  "label": "operator-local osu!stable semantic slice",
  "target": {
    "path": "./osu!.exe",
    "sha256": "<exact target digest>",
    "mvid": "<exact module MVID>",
    "assembly_name": "<expected simple name>",
    "runtime_family": "dotnet-framework",
    "managed_architecture": "x86"
  },
  "methods": [
    {
      "label": "operator-local semantic label",
      "token": "0x06000000",
      "signature_sha256": "<raw signature blob digest>",
      "il_size": 0,
      "il_sha256": "<raw CIL byte digest>",
      "normalized_il_sha256": "<digest>"
    }
  ],
  "application_graph": {
    "expected_node_kinds": [
      "artifact",
      "managed-assembly",
      "managed-module",
      "managed-type",
      "managed-method"
    ],
    "feature_traces": [
      {
        "label": "operator-local feature label",
        "method_token": "0x06000000",
        "seed": "<method name, API name, string, or digest to trace>",
